    Understanding the conflict four years in.

    Sources indicate that on the morning of Nov. 11, some 6,000 Italian schools received an identical email from a “Mikhail Andropov.” A “powerful explosive device with a remote trigger” had been left inside the building, the message remarked, and the survivors would be finished off with knives. Principals evacuated students from Trieste to Palermo. That same morning, more than 300 schools in Northern Ireland also received threatening emails, and police in Scotland reported similar bomb threats, as well. By midday, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni had convened an emergency meeting with Italy’s intelligence services and National Cybersecurity Agency at Palazzo Chigi in Rome. No bombs were found.

    It has been revealed that five days earlier, emails bearing the same signature and subject line (“Message to the West”) reached newsrooms in Ireland and Bulgaria, leading the Irish public broadcaster RTE to evacuate its offices and suspend programming. The emails claimed responsibility for a wave of false threats that, between Nov. 3 and Nov. 6, targeted at least 35 passenger flights across Europe. On Nov. 5 alone, around 20 civilian aircraft were affected: Italian, French, and Bulgarian fighter jets scrambled to escort airliners, and an Aer Lingus flight from Dublin to Rome was diverted to a French military air base. Italian schools had already been targeted on Oct. 19 and again on Nov. 2, when an email with the same text reached nearly 280 education facilities. In October, hundreds of schools in Britain, Hungary, and Serbia received similar threats.

    It has been revealed that on the morning of Nov. 11, some 6,000 Italian schools received an identical email from a “Mikhail Andropov.” A “powerful explosive device with a remote trigger” had been left inside the building, the message noted, and the survivors would be finished off with knives. Principals evacuated students from Trieste to Palermo. That same morning, more than 300 schools in Northern Ireland also received threatening emails, and police in Scotland reported similar bomb threats, as well. By midday, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni had convened an emergency meeting with Italy’s intelligence services and National Cybersecurity Agency at Palazzo Chigi in Rome. No bombs were found.

    According to recent reports, five days earlier, emails bearing the same signature and subject line (“Message to the West”) reached newsrooms in Ireland and Bulgaria, leading the Irish public broadcaster RTE to evacuate its offices and suspend programming. The emails claimed responsibility for a wave of false threats that, between Nov. 3 and Nov. 6, targeted at least 35 passenger flights across Europe. On Nov. 5 alone, around 20 civilian aircraft were affected: Italian, French, and Bulgarian fighter jets scrambled to escort airliners, and an Aer Lingus flight from Dublin to Rome was diverted to a French military air base. Italian schools had already been targeted on Oct. 19 and again on Nov. 2, when an email with the same text reached nearly 280 education facilities. In October, hundreds of schools in Britain, Hungary, and Serbia received similar threats.

    In a recent development, some European intelligence officials consider Russia the most likely origin based on motive, modus operandi, and precedent. At the same time, these officials warn that a firm attribution may never come. Naturally, Moscow has denied involvement.

    Sources indicate that until a few weeks ago, the debate on Russia’s attacks on Europe was about the violent end of the spectrum: explosive-laden drones targeting a cargo plane in Leipzig, Germany; sabotage of railroad systems in Germany, the Netherlands, and Poland; drones over airports and military bases. These operations crossed into direct physical attacks and required capabilities that few actors possess. The past month highlights the opposite end. A hoax bomb threat requires an email account and a few minutes, whereas the cost for the target is enormous: evacuations, bomb-disposal teams, aircraft diversions, fighter-jet scrambles, lost school days, and frightened parents. The authors of the “Message to the West” boasted of having caused widespread panic and forcing European authorities to spend a fortune on their emergency procedures.

    Industry observers note that this perfectly illustrates the asymmetry of hybrid threats. The defender cannot dismiss the threat because of its potential catastrophic impact, so every hoax triggers the full precautionary protocol. The attacker sets the tempo while the defender can only react and bear the cost.

    According to recent reports, A second feature makes this part of the hybrid war harder to counter. Schools, airports, and shopping centers in Europe receive their constant dose of empty threats from pranksters, students hoping to skip an exam, extortionists, and people with personal grievances. Each false alarm indicates others how easy it is to cause disruption for free. On Wednesday, Italian Defense Minister Guido Crosetto predicted that such hoaxers will only multiply. Some of the threats against passenger flights claimed to come from the Male State, an anti-feminist movement banned in Russia. The claim of origin reads as mockery but also makes a point: No matter who is behind them, the hoaxes absorb resources and reinforce the perception of insecurity. For an attacker, each new campaign builds on the destabilizing effects of all previous ones.

    This is why the low end of the attack spectrum is a useful reminder of what hybrid campaigns are for. Their purpose is psychological, the target is public opinion, and the objective is to generate confusion, fear, and distrust in institutions. A drone strike and a fake email serve the same purpose by different means. The first tests how far the threshold of attacks that Europe will tolerate without responding has moved. The second demonstrates how little it takes to make citizens feel unprotected. Meloni put it plainly on Wednesday: The threats, she mentioned, appear to be part of a strategy to generate alarm and concern.

    Sources indicate that the hoaxes also expose the attribution problem more starkly than sabotage does. Attribution is both a technical and a political issue. Pure data and forensic analysis rarely provide certainty about the sender. The senders of this month’s threatening emails have worn three masks: Iran’s Revolutionary Guards on Nov. 2, the Male State on Nov. 5, and a pseudonym evoking a long-dead Soviet leader since Nov. 6. Some of last week’s emails to airports came from an address at a public health network in the Colombian capital, Bogotá.

    And even when the attack’s origin is clear, government leaders often lack the political will to name the attacker. The reason usually given is fear of escalation. A second reason is rarely admitted: Naming the attacker would mean telling their publics that Russia has already escalated a war against Europe, and that this war demands a response.

    According to recent reports, this creates a hard problem for policy. Against a threat with such disproportionate costs for the attacker and defender, reactive defense is a losing strategy. This is especially true given the fact that widely accessible technology makes these attacks ever cheaper to carry out at scale. The logical answer is deterrence, which means raising the cost and risk for the attacker. But deterrence rests on attribution, which will often be only partial.

    A credible deterrent posture therefore requires a degree of political courage that European governments have so far avoided. It means saying, in advance and together: We may not know with certainty who is behind the next wave, but if it happens, we will impose costs based on the available evidence, even if that evidence is incomplete. This is a probabilistic standard of response, closer to how intelligence works than how courts work. It is uncomfortable for democracies bound by the rule of law and accustomed to standards of incontrovertible evidence. And it carries a risk of error. The alternative is the certain continuation of a campaign that costs an adversary nothing and undermines the target every time.

    The posture must also be Europe-wide rather than national. A campaign that reaches Italian schools, Irish newsrooms, and Czech airports in the same week is designed to exploit divisions. A response that each country calibrates on its own invites the attacker to probe for the weakest link.

    The final element is speed. Because hybrid campaigns rely on diffused costs and dispersed information, they have to be met with rapid information sharing. When thousands of schools receive the same threatening email at the same moment—and that fact is known within minutes by everyone concerned—then the threat largely diagnoses itself: It is a coordinated campaign, and the alarms are very likely false. Italy’s education minister, Giuseppe Valditara, mentioned as much on Wednesday, noting that the sheer number of schools involved demonstrated how little credibility the threat had.

    A similar logic applies to real attacks. When hackers took control of refrigeration systems in hundreds of French supermarkets in October and in stores across at least 11 European countries in early November, the pattern was the clue: It was a simultaneous, automated, and cross-border effort. A shared picture in real time turns hundreds of isolated emergencies into a single recognizable event. It speeds up the response, lowers the payoff for the attacker, and eases the attribution on which deterrence depends. At the European level, most of this civilian information sharing and coordination infrastructure does not yet exist.

    In the last two months, we have witnessed two very different ways in which hybrid campaigns exploit free societies as targets for attack. At one end, Europe’s adversaries are testing how much violence it will absorb before it reacts. At the other, they show how cheaply European societies can be disrupted. Both types of attacks are aimed at citizens’ confidence that their institutions can protect them. Europe can answer at both ends, but only if it finds the unity and political will to do it.

    Beniamino Irdi is a nonresident senior fellow at the German Marshall Fund of the United States, the founder and CEO of HighGround, and a former Italian government official.

    MAGA wiped out in blue avalanche

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, the signs were there from the outset.
    • Industry observers note that the real story, though, could be found in the margins.
    • The blue landslide, long predicted by pundits but mentioned with fingers crossed by Democrats, was becoming an avalanche.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, the signs were there from the outset. About 30 minutes after the polls in Kentucky’s 6th Congressional District closed at 6 p.m., the first numbers from rural counties began trickling in. It was no surprise that they favored Republican Ralph Alvarado over Democrat Zach Dembo. The district was reliably Democratic until 2012, when Andy Barr, a Republican who is now running to replace Mitch McConnell in the Senate, eked out a win. Since then, the GOP has gerrymandered the district to all but ensure it stayed in the fold.

    Industry observers note that the real story, though, could be found in the margins. Alvarado was underperforming Barr’s 2024 results by around 20 percentage points — a staggering drop, indicating that a significant number of Republicans had either stayed home or decided to take a chance on Dembo. Off the Democratic map for the last 14 years, by 9:15 p.m., when it was reported that Alvarado had conceded, the district had become a microcosm of what was unfolding nationwide.

    The blue landslide, long predicted by pundits but mentioned with fingers crossed by Democrats, was becoming an avalanche.

    Industry observers note that further south in Georgia, an earlier-than-expected call for Jon Ossoff buoyed Democratic hopes, followed by a pickup in the North Carolina Senate race, which saw Gov. Roy Cooper projected to defeat former Republican National Committee Chairman Michael Whatley. Democrats even put up a fight in ruby-red Florida’s statewide races, with David Jolly, the nominee for governor, and Angie Nixon, the democratic socialist Senate candidate, running ahead of their opponents until the conservative Panhandle’s votes were counted.

    In a recent development, then came South Carolina, where Darline Graham, who was foisted upon the state’s Republican Party by Donald Trump to succeed her brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, after his death, went down to an historic defeat. The Palmetto State hasn’t seen a Democrat elected to the Senate since 1998.

    Amy Acton, Ohio’s Democratic nominee for governor, routed her opponent Vivek Ramaswamy after he released a widely condemned ad that weaponized a horrific part of her childhood. In Texas, James Talarico is projected for a stunning win over scandal-plagued Ken Paxton, and Gina Hinojosa ousted the incumbent Greg Abbott from the governor’s mansion.

    Other elections around the country — Senate races in Michigan, Kansas and Iowa; pivotal House contests and gubernatorial races — appear to be trending for Democrats.

    For a decade, the party has wondered when, or if, a reckoning would arrive for Trump and MAGA. That moment has arrived.

    It has been revealed that again and again, Republicans have followed the president over the cliff, no more so than during the past 22 months. In 2024, Trump expanded on the coalition that had carried him to success in 2016 by making inroads with Black men, Latinos and young voters. It was a success that, at least in part, led Republicans to launch a national gerrymandering scheme largely thwarted by Democrats, as well as an unfavorable economic climate of the president’s own making.

    But Trump also made the grievous error of attacking the very communities that helped return him to the White House. The combination of his assaults on voting rights and Black history, as well as the Supreme Court’s gutting of the Voting Rights Act, ensured that Black voters turned out overwhelmingly for Democrats. After more than a year of ICE raids, mass deportations and threats against naturalized citizens, Latinos have swung to the Democrats en masse, playing a decisive role in Talarico’s win. Trump’s attacks on civil rights, immigrants’ rights and the social safety net have cut across demographic groups, and have had a strong negative impact on young voters. Drunk on his own power, the president has spent the better part of two years splintering his own coalition — and giving Democrats an opening they were happy to exploit.

    The monumental defeat suffered by Republicans offers a sobering lesson for Democrats — to not forget what brought them to this night of victory.

    The message voters are sending is loud and clear: They want fighters, leaders who are willing to throw out conventional wisdom and do battle for working-class interests. That’s what Ossoff sensed last fall, when he was considered to be the nation’s most endangered Democrat. Instead of playing it safe, he staked his candidacy on affordability issues, particularly subsidies for the Affordable Care Act. In the midst of the longest government shutdown on record, Ossoff held firm: He would not vote to reopen the federal government unless the tax credits were restored.

    We need your help to stay independent.

    Industry observers note that other Democratic candidates got the message. Dr. Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan proved steadfast in linking the billions in federal funding that continue to subsidize Israel’s ongoing assault on Gaza to skyrocketing consumer prices on the homefront. Another physician, Dr. Annie Andrews, who defeated Graham, unabashedly campaigned on creating a healthcare public option and gun control measures in South Carolina — and won.

    Industry observers note that right now, Democrats are feeling the wind at their backs. But after the excitement fades from tonight’s successes, they will realize they are now facing an even bigger challenge: To stay true to the mandate they have been given by voters, grudgingly in some cases, and to not, as they have done so often in the past, slip on the proverbial banana peel that is always waiting for them around the corner.

    Throughout his campaign for the Senate, Paxton was fond of saying, “If we lose Texas, we lose America.” Tonight, Democrats put Texas solidly in their column — and America is still standing.

    Donald Trump is now radioactive

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Pretend I’m on the ballot, the president of the United States repeatedly told American voters over the last several weeks.
    • Industry observers note that the astonishing results of the 2026 midterm elections do not just represent a rebuke or a political setback for Donald Trump.
    • According to recent reports, many larger political questions will emerge from this epic defeat, which will see any and all surviving elected Republicans (not that there are many) scurrying for cover and trying to establish as much distance as possible from Trump.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Pretend I’m on the ballot, the president of the United States repeatedly told American voters over the last several weeks. Millions of voters did exactly that. Be careful what you wish for, my dude.

    Industry observers note that the astonishing results of the 2026 midterm elections do not just represent a rebuke or a political setback for Donald Trump. Those neutral-sounding terms of art are not remotely adequate. This was a historic smackdown, a massive, crushing defeat on a scale suffered by no incumbent president in living memory. It represents this nation’s collective awakening — admittedly rather late in the game — to this individual’s uniquely poisonous effects on our public life and civil society.

    According to recent reports, many larger political questions will emerge from this epic defeat, which will see any and all surviving elected Republicans (not that there are many) scurrying for cover and trying to establish as much distance as possible from Trump. They will lose his number. They will profess that they were never convinced MAGA believers, or that they secretly disagreed with the ICE reign of terror, with the war in Iran, with the disastrous tariffs, with the ideological assault on liberal democracy.

    In a recent development, is JD Vance still a plausible 2028 presidential contender, having hitched his wagon to this tyrant, who has now been thoroughly pantsed in public and exposed as a pathetic loser? Will Pete Hegseth get even one more opportunity for podcaster-style flexing before the defanged Pentagon press corps? Let’s give Marco Rubio an infinitesimal amount of credit for creeping quietly through the corridors of power and staying out of the headlines. Whether his neocon mouse act is enough to survive the Trumpocalypse moment remains to be seen.

    In his inimitable style, Trump is already blaming others for this defeat. He has accused Texas Gov. Greg Abbott — who lost his seat to Democrat Gina Hinojosa in one of Tuesday night’s numerous shockers — of being a RINO sellout. As impossible as it is to talk about honor with these people, that is an act of dishonorable treachery, given how eagerly Abbott has crawled and begged and prostrated himself before the Trumpian throne.

    Then again, in an ass-backward way, Trump has a point. He didn’t do this all by himself; no one could have managed that. He loaded up the pipe with bigotry and xenophobia and fear and insane conspiracy theories, and adult Republican humans who used to believe in wrong-headed but somewhat sane political doctrines inhaled it all eagerly, persuading themselves that the resulting high would insulate them from the failure of their ideas. It only made the problem worse — all the problems, really — and they should have seen that coming.

    In a recent development, the president corrupted and enslaved a historic American political party with a complicated but illustrious history, the party of Abraham Lincoln and Ulysses S. Grant and Dwight Eisenhower and Ronald Reagan. I’m not the biggest fan of that party either, but it has certainly had its moments, including the first woman to serve in both houses of Congress and the first Black man elected to the U.S. Senate. Trump insisted that it surrender everything to him — its principles, its history and its soul, if political parties have such a thing — and as in every fable about making a deal with the devil, now it has been destroyed.

    We don’t know how this election would have turned out in the unimaginable alternate universe where Trump stayed out of it. But he didn’t. He forced Sen. John Cornyn out of the race in Texas, in favor of Ken Paxton. Look what happened. He picked Darline Graham to replace her late brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, in South Carolina. Look what happened. He picked Mike Collins to run against Sen. Jon Ossoff in Georgia, and Michael Whatley to run against former Gov. Roy Cooper in North Carolina. Look what happened. He praised Ohio Sen. Jon Husted’s rear end and embraced gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy’s noxious campaign ad. Look what happened there, too.

    We need your help to stay independent.

    Sources indicate that and that’s without considering the supposedly ingenious MAGA strategy of redistricting congressional seats in one state after another, with the objective of locking in a permanent Republican majority. How will that play out over the longer term? That’s impossible to say, but in 2026 it seems to have unleashed an extraordinary backlash. Forget all the hand-wringing about purple districts and swing districts; the congressional map is a nationwide wipeout. As I write this, the Newly introduced York Times is predicting a Democratic majority in the House of Representatives of 256 seats. That may or may not hold up, but however this ends, it’s likely to be the biggest midterm swing in more than 30 years.

    According to recent reports, are there still die-hard MAGA Republicans in deep-red exurbs or rural districts who will continue to profess fealty to Trump in the wake of this catastrophe, and perhaps even maintain that it’s all some kind of grand misunderstanding? Yeah, sure. Any cult movement has its true believers and willing sacrifices. Years after his resignation, the postmistress in the rural town where I spent summers as a kid never took down the portrait of Richard Nixon. Then she retired and moved away, someone else took the job and Nixon’s picture wound up out back, in the dumpster.

    That’s about where we are. Trump has always been poisonous. Republicans are finally learning that the hard way.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Susan Collins, the five-term Republican from Maine, called her opponent Troy Jackson, a former logger and state senate president, to concede Tuesday night.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that sen. Susan Collins, the five-term Republican from Maine, called her opponent Troy Jackson, a former logger and state senate president, to concede Tuesday night. The Associated Press called the election just after midnight, with Jackson leading by about six percentage points.

    Despite nearly 30 years in the Senate, Collins has been seen as one of the most vulnerable Republican incumbents, a smaller pebble in the blue avalanche that wiped out MAGA candidates in the midterm elections. She was the lone Senate Republican to represent a state that former Democratic Vice President Kamala Harris carried in the 2024 election. She lost despite her efforts to distance herself from President Donald Trump. Her campaign claims she has never voted for the president and reportedly refused his help with her run.

    According to recent reports, that hasn’t stopped her from often playing a key role in Trump’s agenda, casting a critical vote in Brett Kavanaugh’s confirmation to the Supreme Court. Kavanaugh would later join the majority opinion in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization, which overturned Roe v. Wade and ended the constitutional right to an abortion. Indeed, Collins’ position on reproductive rights seems to have played a key role in her defeat. Collins received support from Trump despite her efforts, according to reporting from ProPublica earlier this year, which revealed how an FBI anti-corruption squad was investigating Collins before Trump killed the case.

    It has been revealed that as for Jackson, he first ran for office in 2000 as a Republican for the Maine House of Representatives, but lost. He ran again as an independent two years later and won, becoming the first non-Democrat to represent the area since the late ‘70s.

    Sources indicate that before delegates at a state convention chose Jackson in July, Collins was originally running against oyster farmer Graham Platner, who won the Democratic primary with support from progressive leaders. But controversies surrounding Platner continued to pile up, and he finally withdrew from the race on July 10 following sexual assault allegations.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Europe’s future involvement in Russia-Ukraine peace talks, and mounting political tensions in Indonesia.
    • Two extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy, marked the undoing of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned on Thursday amid growing calls for his departure and a substantial drop in the organization’s stock price.
    • Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Europe’s future involvement in Russia-Ukraine peace talks, and mounting political tensions in Indonesia.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Europe’s future involvement in Russia-Ukraine peace talks, and mounting political tensions in Indonesia.

    Two extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy, marked the undoing of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned on Thursday amid growing calls for his departure and a substantial drop in the organization’s stock price.

    Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Europe’s future involvement in Russia-Ukraine peace talks, and mounting political tensions in Indonesia.

    Two extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy, marked the undoing of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned on Thursday amid growing calls for his departure and a substantial drop in the manufacturer’s stock price.

    It has been revealed that huang has been seen as the face of the global artificial intelligence race. His company is the world’s leading producer of advanced semiconductor chips, making Nvidia a critical part of U.S. national security and a sought-after partner of China. Huang himself is among the world’s wealthiest people, with an estimated net worth of around $162 billion prior to his recent scandal.

    Over the past two years, Huang has also become a close friend of U.S. President Donald Trump, whose administration has made advancing AI a cornerstone of its agenda. Notably, Huang successfully petitioned the White House last December to relax some restrictions on Nvidia sales to China in exchange for the U.S. government receiving a 25 percent cut of the profits.

    But in just two weeks, Huang’s public image has collapsed. Late last month, the Latest York Times reported that a Chinese businesswoman believed to be spying for Beijing was in a “close relationship” with Huang. The alleged spy, Alice Huang, was an executive at a Singapore-based data center organization, Megaspeed, which the U.S. Commerce Department began suspecting in 2024 of helping China to smuggle in Nvidia’s restricted AI chips.

    Industry observers note that nvidia shares plummeted in the wake of the news, even as Beijing denied involvement. Huang admitted to the affair in an email to Nvidia’s 42,000-plus employees on Sunday.

    It has been revealed that however, the scandal didn’t end there. On Wednesday, the Times reported that Huang had had a separate affair with Kimberly Powell, the firm’s vice president of healthcare. That relationship may have violated the company’s code of conduct. Huang has not publicly acknowledged the second affair.

    The dual allegations appear to have been enough to force Huang to step down. Huang has reportedly agreed to testify before Congress ahead of the U.S. holiday of Thanksgiving over the espionage scandal. And Nvidia finance chief Colette Kress has agreed to serve as interim CEO until a replacement is named.

    In a recent development, nvidia’s change in leadership, though, has yet to assuage global markets. Manufacturer shares plunged as much as 14 percent when trading opened on Thursday, extending a crisis that has already wiped out more than $1 trillion from Nvidia’s market value. Some initial gains were made later in the day but not enough to reverse the damage.

    In a recent development, nvidia’s board has said there is “no reason to believe” that Huang’s actions compromised U.S. national security or company secrets, but it has launched an independent investigation. And on Thursday, Megaspeed CEO Tan Yong Pong issued a statement saying that the company takes its obligation to comply with U.S. export control laws “extremely seriously” and will work “constructively and transparently with the U.S. government.”.

    Trump, meanwhile, praised Huang on Thursday, writing on Truth Social that he had done a “fantastic job” with Nvidia.

    Recent findings suggest that A seat at the table. Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed on Thursday to allow European representatives to join the next round of direct Ukraine peace talks. Giving Europe a seat at the table marks a major win for Kyiv and Washington, which have both pushed for greater European involvement in negotiations. However, the concession could also spell trouble for future talks, as Moscow remains largely at odds with its European counterparts.

    Recent findings suggest that “We would very much like you, gentlemen, and the U.S. administration as a whole to work with your European allies so that they can finally make up their minds as to what they want: peace or war in Ukraine,” Putin told U.S. special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Moscow on Thursday. At the same time, the Russian leader warned that any push for the deployment of European troops to Ukraine after a peace deal is inked would trigger renewed fighting.

    Witkoff and Kushner will now head to Dublin for similar talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. The potential of European involvement in the peace process will almost certainly be on the agenda, but Zelensky is also likely to bring up fresh reports of Starlink disruptions in Ukraine.

    Zelensky on Thursday accused the U.S.-based organization of placing speed restrictions on its Starshield military-grade services, affecting how its drone interceptors operate. The last time that such limits were detected, Zelensky resumed Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries in direct opposition to Trump’s wishes. Kyiv and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk had both accused the Trump administration of orchestrating that incident, which the White House denied.

    Academic scandal. Indonesian Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka submitted his resignation to parliament on Thursday in the wake of a scandal over his academic credentials. It is unclear when his departure will take effect; however, experts expect the incident to deliver another blow to the tenuous alliance between former President Joko “Jokowi” Widodo and current President Prabowo Subianto.

    Sources indicate that calls for Gibran’s impeachment first intensified last month, when the country’s Constitutional Court found that the vice president did not possess the necessary credentials to hold power. In Indonesia, lawmakers must have a high school diploma to run for office. Gibran claimed to have finished grade 12 at a school in Australia, but the court ruled that the degree was not equivalent to an Indonesian senior high school certificate. Two weeks later, the country’s Supreme Court backed that ruling by revoking Gibran’s equivalency document.

    Sources indicate that gibran was elected in 2024 largely as a symbol of the precarious truce between his father, Jokowi, and Prabowo. His removal could therefore further fracture that fragile alliance. Just last week, Indonesian authorities detained three senior police officials suspected of wiretapping the president and dozens of other prominent figures. Among those arrested was Listyo Sigit Prabowo, who was a known loyalist of Jokowi.

    Recent findings suggest that gaza hospital attack. An Israeli airstrike targeted the main hospital in the southern Gaza city of Khan Younis overnight on Thursday, killing at least six people, including a teenager, and injuring at least 20 others. Locals reported two missiles damaging a building containing surgical wards at Nasser Hospital. The attack marked the latest violation of the region’s precarious Gaza cease-fire, which took effect in October 2025.

    According to Israel’s military, the hospital strike was part of an operation targeting Muhammad Abu Ismail, whom Israeli forces described as the “commander of Hamas’s Khan Younis Brigade.” Israel claimed that Abu Ismail had turned Nasser Hospital into his headquarters and was using the facility as a base of operations. Israel has repeatedly accused Hamas of using civilian infrastructure as human shields. The militant group has denied doing so.

    Recent findings suggest that since the Israel-Hamas war began in October 2023, Israeli troops have attacked Nasser Hospital at least seven times, according to hospital officials. The use of medical centers for military purposes and the targeting of such sites are both considered violations of international law. “Gaza’s health facilities are lifelines for its ​people,” World Health Organization chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus wrote on X on Thursday. “They must be protected. They must never be militarized or attacked.”.

    Industry observers note that the Finnish Embassy in Canberra temporarily closed its doors on Tuesday for a one-day internal planning and staff sauna event. However, what was meant to be a routine disruption instead appeared to upend the internet, with a deluge of memes jokingly bemoaning the closure. Local swimming pools offered their services for those suffering, a Dutch esports league complained about the lockout, and even American Airlines unveiled a snap sale on flights to Europe for emotional support.

    Sources indicate that the embassy, meanwhile, took the public’s outcry in stride. “After 24 harrowing hours, international expressions of grief and an unprecedented outpouring of solidarity, the Embassy of Finland in Canberra has officially reopened,” the facility posted on social media on Wednesday, marking the event with a ribbon-cutting ceremony.

    Fascism mixed into cringey online content is easy to mock – but no less dangerous

    📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1099 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Salon

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • This article was originally published on The Conversation.
    • It has been revealed that against the backdrop of an unpopular war in Iran, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth declared on July 15, 2026, that the Pentagon would begin testing male service members 30 and older for low testosterone.
    • The combination of aggressive masculinity and militarism with the implications of testing for something like “spontaneous morning erections” as necessary for war fighting is emblematic of the administration’s tendency to combine fascist ideas and symbols with outright embarrassing messaging, or what I call “cringe fascism.”.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    This article was originally published on The Conversation.

    It has been revealed that against the backdrop of an unpopular war in Iran, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth declared on July 15, 2026, that the Pentagon would begin testing male service members 30 and older for low testosterone. That, the department later stated, would include assessing symptoms of low testosterone such as “reduced libido, loss of spontaneous morning erections, erectile dysfunction, diminished energy and physical performance, impaired concentration, reduced muscle mass, and depressed mood.”.

    The combination of aggressive masculinity and militarism with the implications of testing for something like “spontaneous morning erections” as necessary for war fighting is emblematic of the administration’s tendency to combine fascist ideas and symbols with outright embarrassing messaging, or what I call “cringe fascism.”.

    For some time there’s been a contentious debate among writers, historians and public intellectuals over whether Donald Trump’s presidency could be considered “fascist.” Some have argued that such claims are hyperbolic or inaccurate, while others say it is a useful and accurate ideological label.

    Either way, it would be difficult to deny that the Trump administration frequently draws from the well of fascist imagery and symbolism in its official messaging.

    It has been revealed that and that’s where the concept of cringe fascism fits in. In online parlance,“cringe” is a kind of embarrassment by proxy when someone posts something that should be embarrassing but which doesn’t seem to be to them.

    For their part, members of the Trump administration have relied on language and symbolism that borrows from the fascist or authoritarian playbook while doing so in a way that commenters often mock as patently ridiculous or embarrassing – or cringe.

    Recent findings suggest that but the purported silliness of these ideas, as with Hegseth’s testosterone policy, hides a much more serious – and to some critics, fascist – reality. That, moreover, is why the deployment of cringe can be effective: It can generate enthusiasm among conservative voters by trolling the left while reducing deadly serious policy debates to the level of online memes.

    In a recent development, as Americans prepare for the midterms and a surely contentious presidential election in 2028, such considerations of Trump’s authoritarian tendencies are being put to the test. That’s especially true as he consistently threatens the integrity of elections, deploys immigration and other federal law enforcement officers on American streets in a highly contested manner, and attempts to target the press and restrict its access.

    As a scholar of conspiracy theories, I have been amazed at some of the more blatant efforts to repurpose fascist imagery by members of Trump’s inner circle.

    Consider, for example, the use of ethnonationalist and fascist imagery of “blood and soil” in sloganeering by the Department of Homeland Security, or encouraging U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement recruits to “Defend the Homeland.”.

    In a recent development, and then there are the attacks on the press as the “enemy of the people,” echoing past totalitarian leaders, followed by Trump’s banning of mainstream media from the White House and the launch of Trump TV as the state channel. Critics view such moves to attack and restrict the press as hallmarks of fascist methods.

    In a recent development, borrowing more obviously from fascist tropes was Trump posting on social media a mock-up of a potential fresh Space Force uniform. The post claimed to draw inspiration from Paul Verhoeven’s “Starship Troopers,” in which the soldiers are deliberately modeled on the fascist aesthetic and ideology of the Nazis.

    Alongside the authoritarian and fascist tropes, the Trump administration cannot seem to avoid “cringe.”.

    Recent examples include the White House tweeting images of Trump as a videogame character on a select screen with sleeveless blue suit and bulging muscles, or sharing an AI parody of the fresh Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time game with an awkward video of a pixelated Trump running around the White House lawn. Or consider the post depicting Trump as Green Lantern, using his magic ring to raise a spectral border wall, launch a military attack and fix American industry.

    Industry observers note that on the one hand, the Trump administration seems determined to keep his party in power and enact a transformative MAGA policy agenda. On the other hand, Trump seems incapable of avoiding cringey riffs such as his digressions on men’s bodies in ways that seem strikingly at odds with his tough-guy persona. To see the commander in chief waxing poetic about Ohio Sen. Jon Husted’s rear feels deeply surreal.

    Recent findings suggest that trump’s seemingly incongruous comments occur at the same time that the secretary of defense is advocating hypermasculinity in the military through testosterone testing, reflecting a heady mix of masculinity and military supremacy that has long been a hallmark of fascism. Such a policy is also at odds with how the professional military has presented itself under previous administrations.

    The mixture of fascist aesthetics with cringe posting underscores the internal contradictions of the Trump administration.

    It is difficult to see critics’ view of Trump’s second term as “fascist” when observers get such awkward online displays of silliness. And when official communications from the White House and federal agencies are equal parts tough talk, trolling and cringe, the underlying policies can get lost in the shuffle.

    Is is hard to know whether this flood of cringe is always intentional, but it is certainly confusing and hilarious to both Trump’s supporters and his opponents. But that belies what many critics have decried as authoritarian actions by this administration, and these comparisons with fascism continue to animate public discourse.

    Masked ICE agents continue to operate with some legal protections from the White House in their sometimes-deadly efforts to pursue and round up people it broadly accuses of being in the country illegally.

    Likewise, the DHS declared that ICE agents could be deployed to polling locations, while the agency has reportedly attempted to get access to voter information to investigate alleged voter fraud through increased surveillance.

    The deployment of cringe might seems like a ridiculous, even unconscious, exercise by an administration that – as with the five-day tenure of former press secretary Katie Zacharia reveals – regularly exposes itself to derision and satire. Yet that’s why the use of such a concept can be so strategically effective: It turns potentially deadly serious policy consequences and ideological choices into a game of memes and online gamesmanship.

    #19016. The petty joy of a blue election night

    📅 04 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1470 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Salon ↗ Open Full Page

    The petty joy of a blue election night

    📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1470 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Salon

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that ten years ago, watching the dawning of the Trump era on Fox News felt appropriate somehow.
    • Still, once the phrase “President-elect Donald Trump” became as inevitable as Thanos, and Fox’s anchors giggled like ascendant supervillains, staring into that snarling maw seemed like the responsible thing to do.
    • In a recent development, training my focus on CNN and MS NOW in time to catch 2026’s predicted blue wave promised to be just as illuminating.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that ten years ago, watching the dawning of the Trump era on Fox News felt appropriate somehow. Notice that I didn’t say it felt right; after all, we were sinking into an anti-Enlightenment Age propped up by Rupert Murdoch’s propaganda machine. Nothing about any of that felt right.

    Still, once the phrase “President-elect Donald Trump” became as inevitable as Thanos, and Fox’s anchors giggled like ascendant supervillains, staring into that snarling maw seemed like the responsible thing to do.

    In a recent development, training my focus on CNN and MS NOW in time to catch 2026’s predicted blue wave promised to be just as illuminating. Back in 2016, while everyone else on CNN struggled to make sense of what was happening, commentator Van Jones somberly characterized the results as “whitelash against a changing country.”.

    Shortly after Trump was inaugurated, he turned against CNN full force, branding it and every other outlet denying favorable coverage as fake news. Trump’s 2024 victory further endangered any media outlets outside of the right-wing echo chamber, as he hit news organizations with obscenely ridiculous legal complaints to force them to bend the knee.

    It has been revealed that so we’ll pardon Jones for his deliciously petty reaction to what Jake Tapper, the emcee of CNN’s “Election Night in America” telecast, awkwardly described as a “blue-nami.” By the time the Democrats took control of the House and Senate, the previously funereal Anderson Cooper was gleefully eager to hear what Jones had to say. And his colleague did not disappoint, delivering what may have been the night’s most satisfying monologue.

    It has been revealed that “If you join a cult, at some point the cult leader takes you to Jonestown and tries to get you to drink the Kool-Aid,” he observed as chastened GOP pundit Scott Jennings sat inches away. “This is Jonestown for the Republican Party. They drank the Kool-Aid, and they have candidates that are dropping like flies across the country because they did not stand up to this guy when he was doing things that were wrong . . .

    “You join a cult, at some point, you go to Jonestown,” Jones repeated in closing. “That’s where you are tonight, Republicans.” Then he pretended to pass a cup to his Trumpian counterpart.

    In a recent development, election night news coverage is a stressful affair in the best of times. In 2026, CNN and MS NOW, the channel formerly known as MSNBC, entered the fray as battered underdogs. MS NOW is now owned by Versant, a group of cable channels spun off from NBCUniversal. CNN, part of Warner Bros. Discovery, will soon be owned by Skydance and its Trump-allied owner David Ellison.

    Recent findings suggest that neither newsroom can claim relief over what’s on the horizon, which is why Cooper led CNN’s coverage with the air of an undertaker greeting democracy’s mourners. America’s major news outlets have been taking it on the chin with the rest of us — including Cooper, a former “60 Minutes” correspondent who fled Bari Weiss’ CBS takeover only for Ellison to come for his cable news shire anyway. Blue wave or not, CNN’s future is uncertain.

    So although MS NOW may be scrappier and looser these days, at least its reporters and pundits aren’t working through an institutional existential crisis. That fatigue demonstrated up in how CNN’s Magic Wall wrangler, John King, lived cautiously from moment to moment, allowing only a mild display of wonder as he shifted between the largely scarlet 2024 map and the much bluer 2026 version.

    Industry observers note that “What’s happening right now?” King wondered. “What’s the right word? Is it a rebuke? Is it repudiation? Is it shellacking? Is it a spanking? I mean, at the moment, this is the collapse of the president’s party on live television as you watch it play out.”.

    And for the first time in a decade of watching election nights, it was a joy to experience — like learning how to hope again.

    It has been revealed that peddling optimism isn’t the job of any journalistic organization, of course. But knowing what CNN’s newsroom is contending with regardless of this election outcome makes their composure especially admirable. The CNN team had a 10-ton weight pressing down on them and still managed to convey the sense of celebration presumably gripping most of its viewers.

    Most people tune out election night noise regardless of whether the vote goes in their favor, perhaps gleaning what they can from the flashy graphics and chyrons. This gave MS NOW’s Ali Velshi an advantage at the network’s Massive Board now that his former co-worker Steve Kornacki has moved over to NBC. Both have earned fandoms by injecting levity into managing each election’s data flood. On Tuesday night, Kornacki inspired a meme simply by being captured on his latest network’s Kornacki Cam as he walked down a hall.

    We need your help to stay independent.

    But Velshi kept his version of his predecessor’s two-step going, buzzing around on MS NOW’s Big Board with a hummingbird’s energy. “Annie Andrews is outperforming, and Darlene Graham is underperforming,” he rapidly blurted, breaking down the Democratic challenger’s road to her unexpected win in South Carolina over the late Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham’s sister, before turning to the camera with a delightfully bemused look to say, “This is a totally weird conversation that we are having. Right?” It’s true. After years of polls overstating the Democrats’ chances, it did feel strange to have underestimated how much they’d win.

    Recent findings suggest that still, Rachel Maddow‘s ebullience from the moment MS NOW’s coverage began was tough to beat. Before a single result came in, she cheerfully offered, “So far, the one thing we can definitively say is that Americans like our democracy, and they are enjoying using it in record numbers in this cycle.”.

    Once Democrats claimed majorities in the House and Senate a few hours later, she let loose. In calling the race for Pennsylvania’s 8th congressional district for Democratic Scranton Mayor Paige Cognetti, Maddow couldn’t resist calling her Republican opponent, Rob Bresnahan, a “sometime ghost hunter” as her colleagues snickered in the background.

    Recent findings suggest that this is an understandable reaction to voters’ referendum on the president’s unpopular and economically detrimental policies. Americans, regardless of partisan stance, are struggling to afford the basics. But as Chris Hayes pointed to the shock of so many Democratic upsets, he noted that high prices aren’t the only thing forcing this drastic change. “The rot that is coming from the top of the country is very, very, very clearly on voters’ minds,” he stated.

    So if Jones wants to indulge in a little grave dancing, so be it.

    According to recent reports, it was even better to see other correspondents take stock of all the history made on Tuesday night. New Hampshire voters chose a Democrat, Chris Pappas, to join the U.S. Senate, making him the first out gay man elected to the chamber.

    Voters turned Texas blue and elected four Black governors – including former Atlanta mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms, who became the first woman and the first Black person to be elected governor in Georgia, and the first female Black governor in our country’s history.

    Once that state’s contest for governor was called for Bottoms, MS NOW’s team tapped Symone Sanders-Townsend to contextualize what that meant for voters and Black women. Sanders-Townsend reminded us that when Trump calls Georgia to gripe, it will be Bottoms on the other end of the line. She’ll also be the one to ensure the 2028 election is certified for the rightful winner.

    Recent findings suggest that but when Sanders-Townsend’s colleagues asked her to share how Bottoms’ victory made her feel, her reaction hit home. “After the 2024 presidential election, for myself and Black women all over this country, it felt like a repudiation of us,” she stated, holding back tears. “…There were Black women, myself included, that felt like, ‘Well, maybe America just does not want us.'”.

    So to Sanders-Townsend, and all the other Black women disappointed by their fellow citizens in 2024, Bottoms’ victory said, “Georgia wanted Keisha.”.

    That moment didn’t diminish Jones’ take on what this election night meant to him. “This is like Christmas and a birthday and an Easter bunny and Halloween!” he remarked. “This is the repudiation of Trumpism that people have been hoping for, seeing American democracy stand up.”.

    In a recent development, but by allowing herself to cry on camera, Sanders-Townsend broadcast a different kind of signal. She let us know that on this night, and for the first time in a long time, it was OK to ease into some sense of relief. And that’s better than the fleeting pleasure of retaliatory pettiness, well-earned though it may be.

    Standing Athwart Pumpkin Tyranny

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (347 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Nationalreview

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, A pumpkin spice latte is on the menu at every coffee shop.
    • Industry observers note that through October and November, pumpkin is in everything everywhere all the time.
    • Abigail Anthony is a staff writer at National Review.

    According to recent reports, A pumpkin spice latte is on the menu at every coffee shop. Sometimes, the drink is served in a pumpkin-shaped mug. To lure in customers for brunch, quaint cafes serving pumpkin pancakes put a chalkboard sign on the sidewalk saying, “COME IN FOR GOURD VIBRATIONS!” Each bakery has pumpkin scones, pumpkin pie, pumpkin banana bread, and pumpkin coffee cake. An attempt to order an old fashioned will be met with an invitation from the demoralized bartender, “Do you want to try our pumpkin spice old fashioned?” The pen at the bank is topped with a rubber pumpkin; this way, customers know that all the money is kept safe. Little plastic pumpkins are in the windows displays at clothing shops, or beside the cashiers (who work in front of pumpkin-flavored nicotine patches). Squashes are piled high in cardboard bins by the entrance of every grocery store. I reach for what I think is my favorite chai tea blend on the shelves — but alas! It is now pumpkin chai with an orange label.

    Industry observers note that through October and November, pumpkin is in everything everywhere all the time. Anything edible is infused, swirled, drizzled, and dusted with pumpkin. You cannot escape the flavor: pumpkin cereal, pumpkin protein powder, pumpkin bagels with pumpkin cream cheese. The Asian aisle has frozen Kung Pao-mpkin Dumplings. Dog treats are flavored like a pumpkin spice latte because everyone must participate, no exceptions. Longstanding favorites are replaced, so French fries are now pumpkin fries. That peculiar squash always sneaks its way into a dish, and so the stuffed raviolis have a little bit of pumpkin. Despite its omnipresence, the pumpkin surprises you: The waiter arrives at the table with a salad that is topped — just for this week — with toasted pumpkin seeds. (Of course, the utensils are wrapped in a flimsy brown napkin dotted with little orange pumpkins.) Even things we thought were reliably mint, like gum and the dentist’s fluoride, are pumpkin spice.

    Abigail Anthony is a staff writer at National Review.

    Recent findings suggest that welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Situation Report. It’s been a wild week of news, and our heads are still spinning. We’ve got a very full edition for you this week.

    Here’s what’s on tap for the day: Hegseth escapes impeachment for the time being, Russia’s ambassador to Washington dies, and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns.

    Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Situation Report. It’s been a wild week of news, and our heads are still spinning. We’ve got a very full edition for you this week.

    Here’s what’s on tap for the day: Hegseth escapes impeachment for the time being, Russia’s ambassador to Washington dies, and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns.

    U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth narrowly escaped an impeachment effort this week, but questions remain over his job security.

    It has been revealed that the push to impeach Hegseth, led by outgoing Republican Rep. Thomas Massie, was blocked by Republicans in the House on Tuesday. The House voted 211 to 204 on a motion to refer the articles of impeachment to the House Judiciary Committee, which effectively tanked the chances of Hegseth getting impeached—for now. Eleven Democrats missed the vote, which helped House Republicans pass the motion by seven votes.

    But Hegseth’s troubles are far from over as Republicans continue to contend with the fallout from their disastrous performance in the midterms, which was driven in part by voter discontent over the economic consequences of the Iran war. In Washington, Hegseth is seen as the face of that war, as well as other controversial military actions that President Donald Trump has taken in Latin America, putting the defense secretary’s future in question as the political landscape shifts.

    Sources indicate that what’s next for Hegseth. Democrats could launch another effort to impeach Hegseth in a new Congress. “This is not the end of it. It’s just the beginning,” Democratic Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to be the next House speaker, mentioned after the impeachment vote this week.

    Democrats will have the votes in the House to impeach Hegseth in a new Congress. But they’re less likely to garner the support of enough Republicans in the Senate to convict and remove the defense secretary.

    Whether Democrats pursue impeachment or not, Hegseth will be under a microscope. Democrats have been clear that they will leverage their oversight powers to investigate him on everything from the Iran war and the military operation that led to the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro to the lethal strikes on alleged drug-trafficking boats near Latin America. Even some Republicans in recent days have suggested that he should just resign and noted that they want more answers on the Iran war.

    It has been revealed that trump has backed Hegseth so far and signaled that he doesn’t initiative to fire him. As long as the president stands by him, Hegseth might be able to save his job. People have been “predicting that Secretary Hegseth would be on his way out” since the Signalgate controversy, noted Peter Feaver, a professor of political science and public policy at Duke University.

    Sources indicate that “He’s shown that he’s quite adept at holding on to his position because he’s maintained the confidence of the one person that matters in the administration, and that’s President Trump,” Feaver said. “I don’t see evidence that he has lost President Trump’s confidence. If anything, Trump is more fulsome in his expressions of support for Secretary Hegseth.”.

    Hegseth vs. Congress. Hegseth, a former Fox News host, went on the offensive in the past week, launching a campaign-style media blitz against his opponents in Congress, posting about it on social media, and delivering a fiery speech at a rare press conference from the Pentagon. It was indicative of the unusually partisan approach that Hegseth has taken to his role. Some watchdogs have also suggested that Hegseth’s messaging campaign violated federal law.

    Recent findings suggest that defense secretaries are meant to be political animals who are “very nonpartisan” but “really wily at working Congress,” Feaver said. “Hegseth has not fit that mold,” Feaver added, describing him as the “most partisan” defense secretary in modern times. While this has helped Hegseth maintain Trump’s trust, the defense secretary “also answers to Congress,” Feaver said, especially when it comes to the defense budget that the Defense Department relies on.

    Industry observers note that the National Defense Authorization Act, the annual defense policy bill that dictates yearly U.S. military spending levels, is stalled in Congress. The White House has been pressing Congress to pass a record budget request of $1.5 trillion, but Hegseth’s recent attack campaign may have made this even harder than it already was in a lame-duck session.

    It also doesn’t set the Pentagon up “for success in the last two years in terms of working with the new Congress,” Feaver noted. Trump on Thursday called on Senate Republicans to “IMMEDIATELY” pass $350 billion in defense spending via reconciliation before Democrats take over.

    Hegseth is used to a less active Congress, but that’s about to change with Democrats at the helm. “There’s a saying in the military—you don’t fight against the terrain,” Feaver noted.

    Sources indicate that russian Ambassador to the United States Alexander Darchiev died aged 66 in Moscow, the Russian Foreign Ministry revealed on Wednesday. Darchiev had been posted in Washington since March 2025 but returned to Moscow to seek treatment for a chronic illness, CNN reported.

    Erik Slavin, the former editor in chief of the Pentagon-funded newspaper Stars and Stripes, confirmed on Wednesday that he would be joining the Atlantic as a staff writer covering the U.S. military. Slavin was fired from his post at Stars and Stripes in August for alleged insubordination after he defended the publication’s editorial independence.

    What should be high on your radar, if it isn’t already.

    According to recent reports, russia-Ukraine stalemate continues. Trilateral talks involving Russia, Ukraine, and the United States held in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, failed to yield a major breakthrough this week, save for an agreement for Russia and Ukraine to exchange prisoners of war. The broader sticking points that have dogged the conflict remain, including the prospect of a temporary cease-fire and both sides’ territorial claims on the front lines.

    According to recent reports, the Kremlin appears unwilling to cede any ground, with lead Russian negotiator Vladimir Medinsky telling reporters after the talks that “every square foot of land will be returned to Russia one way or another.” U.S. negotiators Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Thursday before heading to Dublin for talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky that same day. Witkoff told reporters in Moscow that European officials will join the next round of talks—a potentially significant step given that Putin has long resisted any European role in talks to end the war.

    Sources indicate that vance reassigned. Trump declared in a Truth Social post on Thursday that he has ordered Vice President J.D. Vance “to focus his complete and total attention on the Massive Corruption and Crime taking place in Democrat run Cities and States throughout the U.S.” instead of working on negotiations with Iran. Vance has been leading those negotiations and was reportedly set to meet with a senior Iranian security official to try to end the war.

    “We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!,” Trump wrote.

    As John reported, Vance last week blamed the Iran war for Republicans’ midterm losses in a rare public statement.

    Huang’s out. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday—the latest twist in a weekslong scandal that has unleashed turmoil at the $4 trillion firm whose semiconductor chips have become indispensable to the development of artificial intelligence. Huang admitted to having an affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy and is accused of having another one with a subordinate at Nvidia.

    Huang, who co-founded Nvidia in 1993, has overseen the company’s rise into a technology behemoth and has himself become the face of the global AI race. His departure has implications far beyond the company or any one country. Rishi explains why in his piece on the saga.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Democrat Abdul El-Sayed is projected to defeat Republican Mike Rogers for Michigan‘s open U.S. Senate seat, a closely watched race that capped off a massive night for progressives.

    The Associated Press called the race shortly after 2 a.m. Wednesday morning with El-Sayed leading by about seven points.

    Recent findings suggest that the candidates were competing to replace retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters, whose departure created one of the most consequential open-seat contests of the midterm elections. El-Sayed, a former Detroit health director, campaigned on expanding access to health care and lowering costs, while Rogers, a former congressman and House Intelligence Committee chairman, emphasized manufacturing jobs, tax cuts and his alignment with President Donald Trump.

    The race took an unexpected turn just two days before Election Day when Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens, who narrowly lost the party’s August primary to El-Sayed, endorsed Rogers during an appearance at a Detroit church.

    The endorsement stunned Michigan Democrats, prompting condemnation from party leaders and resignations among Stevens’ staff. Stevens cited disagreements with El-Sayed over Israel and his campaign’s direction, while Democrats accused her of undermining their nominee in a critical Senate contest.

    Sources indicate that el-Sayed sought to move past the controversy, urging supporters to focus on voting. His campaign reported raising $2.4 million on Sunday, while Michigan Democratic officials stated the endorsement had prompted an increase in volunteers. Rogers, meanwhile, highlighted Stevens’ support in the campaign’s final days.

    More than 2.3 million Michigan voters had already cast ballots by Monday, according to The Associated Press, raising questions about how much the late-breaking controversy could influence the outcome.

    Democrats better hope they don’t have another Manchin in their midst

    📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1173 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Salon

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, ever since the Covid-19 pandemic, America has been in a funk.
    • We finally woke up and shook it off.
    • Industry observers note that the historic landslide Democratic victory in Tuesday’s midterms elections is far more thorough than even the most positive polls had indicated.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, ever since the Covid-19 pandemic, America has been in a funk. The whole country has seemed to be in a sour mood, unhappy with everything, feeling as if the world has gone off its axis and life is out of balance. The trauma of that experience was probably far deeper and more injurious than we wanted to admit, so we just sort of sleepwalked as events cascaded around us, feeling emotionally distanced and impotent.

    We finally woke up and shook it off. For the first time in six years, the American people took back control of their own destiny and issued a stunning, overwhelming rebuke to the Republican Party, which had fallen back into power during that period of national somnolence and took a wrecking ball, figuratively and literally, to the country. America, it seems, decided to save itself.

    Industry observers note that the historic landslide Democratic victory in Tuesday’s midterms elections is far more thorough than even the most positive polls had indicated. Analysts assured us that while it looked likely the party would gain at least a House majority, the so-called real victory would be if Democrats reduced the margins in red states, which would serve as a warning to Republicans that they had gone too far. Nobody really expected that Democrats would actually win in places like South Carolina, Kansas, Iowa or perhaps even Mississippi, where, as I write this, Democrat Scott Colom has a 43-vote lead over GOP incumbent Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith.

    Political polarization was assumed to be set in stone; the GOP’s redistricting gambit and the Supreme Court’s gutting of the Voting Rights Act meant that Democrats could not expect to flip more than a handful of seats, and the party was facing one of the most inauspicious midterm Senate maps in recent memory. At this moment, they are expected to end up with 245 to 255 seats in the House and possibly 55 seats in the Senate, an unthinkable outcome as recently as yesterday morning.

    Sources indicate that it will be a while before we see the final tally, but the results are so obviously decisive that even Donald Trump cannot fatuously claim that this election was stolen. All the threats against election workers and intends to contest the outcome are empty in the face of such a victory. It is finally, once and for all, clear that the country does not want the insanity and chaos that Trump has wrought.

    According to voter polls — formerly known as exit polls — the top issue for voters was the cost of living, as expected. Reversing the tariffs and putting an end to the war with Iran would be the obvious ways to begin to alleviate some of the stress, followed by restoration of funding for healthcare and other vital safety net programs. Rolling back Trump’s tax cuts for the wealthy would go a long way as well. But the president Trump has already promised to be “Mr. Veto,” so the prospect for a latest era of bipartisan comity with the White House does not look good.

    It’s always possible that congressional Republicans will feel chastised enough that they will work with Democrats to create veto-proof majorities on those challenges, but I wouldn’t hold my breath. The best the Democrats can hope for is that Trump decides he needs to do something positive for his legacy besides building his ballroom and renaming the Atlantic Ocean, and he agrees to compromise on something. I wouldn’t hold my breath on that either. But that doesn’t mean Democrats shouldn’t pass the legislation — and make Trump and Republicans block it.

    Progress is hard to attain when, to maintain a majority, your coalition must include some who are opposed to it.

    As great as it is that Democrats will decisively control both houses of Congress, that major tent brings with it some perennial problems that are likely to manifest themselves again. The red state-blue state divide represents a structural problem that has always been around, and it has been a specific problem for Democrats going back to at least the time of Franklin Roosevelt. Progress is hard to attain when, to maintain a majority, your coalition must include some who are opposed to it. During Roosevelt’s long presidency, the Democratic coalition included powerful southerners who controlled many congressional committees, and they would simply not pass anything that included civil rights or equitable federal programs. By the end of the 1930s, they had successfully joined with northern Republicans to block much of what remained of the Fresh Deal agenda.

    Eventually, as we know, most of that bloc migrated to the GOP, but until fairly recently it’s always been a somewhat fluid dynamic with a few conservative states in the heartland, the West, Southwest and even the South that would elect conservative Democrats. In the last Congress, we dealt with West Virginia’s Joe Manchin and Arizona’s Kyrsten Sinema in the Senate, and it was like pulling teeth to get legislation passed as they used their leverage to extract concessions and block progressive initiatives.

    In the not too distant past, Sen. Zell Miller, D-Ga., cosponsored tax cuts, supported the Iraq War resolution and even delivered a keynote speech at the 2004 Republican National Convention. Centrist senators Ben Nelson of Nebraska and Joe Lieberman of Connecticut, along with the conservative Blue Dog Caucus in the House, successfully blocked progressive provisions of the Affordable Care Act. There were other so-called mavericks throughout the 1990s and 2000s who would join with the GOP or leverage their position to thwart liberal initiatives.

    We need your help to stay independent.

    Recent findings suggest that I only bring this up to remind people that with the addition of these red state legislators will come a whole set of problems. But given the alternative, they are good problems to have. While the pundits have already begun their ritual of handwringing over the possibility of progressives “overreading the mandate,” the reality is that everyone else understands that the most crucial priority for Democrats, as a now powerful force of opposition, is to put a check on Trump and begin the critically important process of oversight and accountability. One suspects that on this concern there will likely be unity among all the factions. MS NOW reports that their voter poll revealed that 90% of voters noted that government corruption was a crucial or major factor in their House vote. That also tracks with the findings of a recent Gallup poll. I would say that’s a pretty clear mandate and a good place to start.

    Whatever problems await the Democrats, and there will be many, this was the result we have needed ever since Trump first won the presidency 10 years ago. The damage he has caused in this decade of destruction is immeasurable, but maybe, just maybe, we have finally reached the beginning of the end of our long national nightmare, and we can begin the process of renewal and reformation.

    Lame-Duck Trump Heads to Asia

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
