    • Sources indicate that like many U.S.
    • Trump is scheduled to travel to the Philippines and China next week to attend the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in Manila and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen.
    • Recent findings suggest that like many U.S.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Get audio access with any FP subscription.

    Sources indicate that like many U.S. presidents before him, Donald Trump is responding to a final midterm election drubbing by heading for foreign shores—to a region that has been far from top of mind over the past two years.

    Trump is scheduled to travel to the Philippines and China next week to attend the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in Manila and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen. At the latter, he will meet Chinese President Xi Jinping for the third time this year. In Manila, Trump is expected to meet with the other leaders in the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue—between the United States, Australia, Japan, and India—for the first time in his second term.

    Recent findings suggest that like many U.S. presidents before him, Donald Trump is responding to a final midterm election drubbing by heading for foreign shores—to a region that has been far from top of mind over the past two years.

    Sources indicate that trump is scheduled to travel to the Philippines and China next week to attend the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in Manila and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen. At the latter, he will meet Chinese President Xi Jinping for the third time this year. In Manila, Trump is expected to meet with the other leaders in the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue—between the United States, Australia, Japan, and India—for the first time in his second term.

    Trump will make those trips under the shadow of his political diminishment at home, with last week’s elections leading to the Democratic Party’s control of Congress starting in January and giving them the ability to block Trump’s legislative agenda.

    “It is often the case when a president ventures to a major trip in Asia, a long domestic shadow casts its darkness over the trip,” stated Kurt Campbell, chairman and co-founder of The Asia Group, a geopolitical advisory firm in Washington, D.C. “This is another case of just massive overhang from domestic politics that are going to shape everything that he does,” added Campbell, who previously served as deputy secretary of state and Indo-Pacific coordinator on the National Security Council under former U.S. President Joe Biden.

    But Trump is equally likely to try and push past that dynamic, stated Mike Kuiken, vice chair of the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission, a bipartisan panel that advises U.S. lawmakers on China. “The reality is that Trump is weaker at home politically, so I think he’s going to feel very motivated to project power and confidence,” said Kuiken, who is also a distinguished visiting fellow at Stanford University’s Hoover Institution.

    Trump “loves pomp and circumstance, and these kinds of events present an incredible opportunity there,” Kuiken said. “There’s going to be red carpets, and flowers, and parades, and military equipment all over the place, so this is the kind of thing that plays to his insecurities in a way that he’ll very much enjoy.”.

    Substance, there may be less of.

    It has been revealed that experts predict that in his meeting with Xi, Trump will seek to maintain the status quo between the world’s two largest economies—whether with their trade truce (which the two countries just extended until mid-January), their nascent dialogue on artificial intelligence, or their tit-for-tat export controls on U.S. semiconductor chips and China’s critical minerals.

    Recent findings suggest that “I think at least the Chinese expect that he will be more desirous of preserving calm on the diplomatic front now that he is politically weakened and presumably will not want to see the stock market dips or other things that would erode his position even further,” noted Hal Brands, a professor at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies who also serves on the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission. The commission, incidentally, is set to publish its annual report to Congress on Wednesday—the same day that Trump is scheduled to touch down in Shenzhen.

    The midterm result “probably makes Trump more interested in getting massive, good international headlines to help him restore a sense of momentum around his presidency,” stated Brands, who is also a frequent Foreign Policy contributor.

    According to recent reports, trump’s semiconductor position may also be muddied by the turmoil around Nvidia, the chipmaking giant at the center of the U.S. export control debate. The company’s CEO, Jensen Huang, resigned on Thursday after news emerged of his extramarital affairs with an alleged Chinese spy as well as with one of his subordinates at the company.

    According to recent reports, huang cultivated close personal ties with Trump and attended both of his previous meetings with Xi in Beijing and Washington along with other tech CEOs. Last December, Huang successfully petitioned the Trump administration to relax some restrictions on sales of the company’s second-tier chips to China—giving the U.S. government a 25 percent cut of some sales in the process.

    Sources indicate that the Nvidia drama is already causing tension in the U.S.-China relationship. “The U.S. should stop fabricating the ‘Chinese spy’ narratives as a pretext for imposing technology restrictions,” Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told reporters in Beijing on Thursday.

    But the Nvidia elephant in the room is likely to be mutually ignored—or swiftly swept under the rug—when Trump and Xi meet. “There’s no gain for Trump in making an issue of this and even less gain for Xi in making an issue of it, and so I would be kind of surprised if it came up in their bilateral meeting,” Kuiken said. However, Xi is likely to stress that any further tightening of chip export controls through proposed legislation would invite retaliation from Beijing. “I wouldn’t be shocked if Xi were to try to find ways of reminding President Trump: ‘Oh, it’s wonderful what we’ve achieved together over the last year, would be such a shame if anything were to happen to disrupt this productive relationship,’” Kuiken added.

    There’s also the prospect of a trilateral meeting of Trump, Xi, and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Trump stated that he thinks he will meet the two leaders in Shenzhen to discuss “a lot of things, including denuclearization,” he said on Sunday. But Beijing appears to be wary of the implications of such a meeting, given its long-standing reluctance to commit to arms control.

    It has been revealed that “If the Xi-Putin-Trump meeting happens, it will only happen because the Chinese have received sufficient guarantees that it’ll be utterly devoid of substance,” Brands noted. “The things that Trump wants to discuss are a settlement in Ukraine and nuclear arms control. The Chinese have no intention of being put on the hook as a responsible party in bringing the war in Ukraine to an end, and they have no interest in a trilateral nuclear arms control negotiation,” he added. “They would want to make this as scripted and formulaic as possible.”.

    For Beijing, simply having and hosting the meeting holds a degree of appeal. “When we were in China, we heard over and over again about how the Chinese really liked President Trump’s ‘G-2’ framework,” Kuiken stated. “What happens when it becomes sort of a G-3 framework where China effectively has two seats at the table? Because you know Putin’s seat is essentially China’s seat.”.

    Recent findings suggest that putin, as the leader who first floated the meeting, appears more amenable to discussing both nuclear weapons and Ukraine but will likely look to focus more on the latter, said Edgard Kagan, a senior advisor and chair of China studies at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington, D.C. “This was originally a Putin idea,” Kagan told reporters in a briefing earlier this week. “I think the key for Putin was that this was very much about signaling a desire to talk to the president and talk to Chairman Xi in a way that suggests that they’re making decisions on Ukraine, which obviously the Ukrainians and the Europeans don’t like.”.

    Industry observers note that then there’s the Quad, which will be convening a leaders’ meeting on the sidelines of ASEAN before Trump heads to Shenzhen. It will mark the first and likely final time that Trump meets the other leaders of the security grouping—Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi—together in his current term.

    It has been revealed that U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has been the flag-bearer for the Quad thus far, having attended and convened multiple meetings with his counterparts over the past two years. Trump’s participation is unlikely to amount to more than a box-checking exercise, experts said.

    Industry observers note that “I don’t think the president can hide the fact that he’s not terribly enthusiastic about the gathering,” Campbell said, adding that the Trump administration’s notable lack of preparation for meetings with traditional U.S. allies and partners will not be lost on their leaders. “If you compare how he prepares and thinks about a meeting with Putin or Xi, or even potentially with [North Korean dictator] Kim Jong Un, there just is a noticeable difference, and that’s not lost on Asian interlocutors,” Campbell added.

    There are limits to what the other countries that form ASEAN will seek to extract from Trump—to the extent that they get to engage with him at all. “They have probably learned by now that the most effective place to engage this administration is never in a multilateral format but is actually a bilateral format, so I think that the more interesting meetings are the sidebars,” stated Kuiken. “These meetings are probably more likely to be the places where these countries choose to engage, as opposed to trying to box in the U.S in some sort of larger regional discussion or engagement.”.

    The White House has not yet released a full schedule for Trump’s visit, though a bilateral meeting in Manila with Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. appears to be in the cards and others could materialize closer to the date.

    It has been revealed that trade is likely to be high on Asian leaders’ lists of priorities. “Some of the tariffs that he has imposed on these countries are pretty staggering, and so I think those countries now may feel emboldened to compel or urge Trump to revisit these things,” Kuiken noted. “It’ll be interesting to see if they decide to play that card in this first meeting, or if they decide to hold back for a later engagement that’s sort of quieter and a little more underneath the radar.”.

    According to Campbell, the big question on every leader’s mind will be the resolution of a conflict that none of them are directly involved in. “We all know that the Iran war had an impact on this [U.S. midterm] election, but it is starting to have very substantial impacts across Asia,” he mentioned, mentioning supplies of key industrial inputs such as helium, sulfur, and diesel that have been disrupted by the war. “When the war started eight months ago, it was at a moment in which most countries had maximum reserves in many of these areas. Those reserves are now gone,” he added. “So [Trump] is going to be in countries and meeting with leaders—the Philippines, Indonesia, other Southeast Asian countries that are being battered by higher costs associated with energy and the like.”.

    Ultimately, however, Campbell said those leaders will already be starting to look past Trump.

    In a recent development, “I think what they see [from the midterms] is a pretty clear rejection of a style of politics in the United States and a rejection of the United States as an authoritarian leader-led country,” he stated. “And so, the biggest manifestation is going to be Asian interlocutors seeking out other power sources in Washington.”.

    Rishi Iyengar is a staff writer at Foreign Policy. Bluesky: @iyengarish.bsky.social X: @Iyengarish Instagram: @iyengar.rishi.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Forty-five minutes before the first polls closed on Tuesday, Greg Gutfeld was still doing what Fox News does best, acknowledging reality just long enough to replace it with a culture-war hallucination. “Gas prices are so high, I’m going to vote for the party that wanted to trans my kids,” he joked on “The Five,” adding that he didn’t see Democratic wins on the horizon. “There is no blue wave materializing,” Clay Travis, the Outkick founder and Fox contributor, posted at 3 p.m. EST, adding that Republicans were surging in Florida and the polls were about to be proven wrong yet again.

    It has been revealed that then the polls closed, and MAGA’s delusions were pulverized. The country that right-wing media had spent two years describing as angry, ascendant and permanently realigned voted in an avalanche that crushed years of manufactured MAGA hype. American voters told the president to take his $5,000 “Trump Dividend” checks and shove them. Elon Musk, who moved to Texas to get away from Democrats and then spent a reported $150 million to deliver the Lone Star State for Republicans, saw his early Tuesday post urging people to vote red disappear from his profile by Wednesday.

    According to recent reports, the country woke up to results that few expected — and a long list of historic firsts. Georgia elected Keisha Lance Bottoms, the first Black woman governor in American history. Michigan sent Dr. Abdul El-Sayed to Washington as the first Muslim senator. Fresh Hampshire elected Chris Pappas as the first openly gay man in the Senate. New Mexico made Deb Haaland the first Native American woman governor, and Peggy Flanagan became Minnesota’s first Native American woman senator. Texas elected Gina Hinojosa over three-term Gov. Greg Abbott — the state’s first Latina governor and its first Democratic governor in more than three decades. Ohio got its first woman governor in Dr. Amy Acton. South Carolina tapped Dr. Annie Andrews as its first elected woman senator. Democrats won a Senate seat in Kansas for the first time in 94 years. While votes are still being counted in key races, solid majorities in both the Senate and House are assured, and Democrats are set to make Hakeem Jeffries the country’s first Black speaker.

    Sources indicate that even the New York Post, Rupert Murdoch’s tabloid and a loyal Trump house organ, refused to mince words on its front page: “Trump suffers historic rebuke as Dems romp in midterms,” with “BLUE TSUNAMI” blaring beneath it. On “Fox and Friends” Wednesday morning, Ainsley Earhart warned viewers that “your wallet and your way of life” are now in the crosshairs.

    The deeper truth the conservative media apparatus could never say out loud is that MAGA was always a Trump-specific phenomenon. It does not transfer to his imitators, and it only ever worked when the economy let voters treat Trump as entertainment.

    It has been revealed that it is no surprise that Trump 2.0, stripped of its previous establishment Republican guardrails like Mike Pence and Mitch McConnell, has culminated in such total structural collapse. The deeper truth the conservative media apparatus could never say out loud is that MAGA was always a Trump-specific phenomenon. It does not transfer to his imitators, and it only ever worked when the economy let voters treat Trump as entertainment. Right-wing media spent years confusing its ability to dominate a conversation with its ability to represent a country. When Tuesday’s returns exposed the difference, its leading voices reached for almost everything except accountability. They blamed immigration. They blamed insufficient restrictions on voting. They blamed each other. Alex Jones even decided Trump might secretly be a Democrat.

    According to recent reports, for the network’s election night coverage, Fox News seated former Fresh York Mayor Bill de Blasio between two of Trump’s former press secretaries, Kayleigh McEnany and Karoline Leavitt, and he told them to their faces that they were “missing the plot.” He mentioned, “The American people are looking at a war they do not believe in, and they did not authorize. They’re looking at prices that are making it impossible for middle-class people, let alone working-class people, to live.”.

    Trump, watching at the White House, raged on Truth Social — “Why does FoxNews have deBlasio” — and seethed at the panel’s lone liberal: “I can’t stand Jessica Tarlov’s voice — DUMB AS A ROCK, but it’s the voice that gets me.” After Gutfeld read the president’s text on air — which is as good a diagram as exists of what Fox News is now: a suggestion box the president monitors live — Tarlov answered on X, not on Truth Social: “Reality is a tricky thing,” and the president “should get better at dealing with it.”.

    Sources indicate that on Newsmax, things were somehow worse. Political strategist Dick Morris argued that Trump’s problem was effectively excessive success: He had solved the major problems that would otherwise motivate Republican voters. The influencer ecosystem, meanwhile, went straight for the circular firing squad, and every faction picked a different target.

    Jones, livestreaming as the returns buried his movement, stated Trump himself is the plant: “I think he’s a Democrat. I’m 100% at war with Trump. He’s not that r*tarded. He did this on purpose. I think he’s the ultimate Democrat sleeper cell and he works for them.” Benny Johnson and Libs of TikTok reached for the great replacement theory, and Fox’s Lawrence Jones supplied the broadcast version, surveying Texas and concluding, “Texas, there is a lesson here. Don’t be so welcoming.”.

    So much for celebrating people voting with their feet and the U-Hauls leaving California.

    In a recent development, laura Loomer went straight doomer: “America is over and so is the American Dream.” Others blamed Sen. John Thune for failing to pass the SAVE Act and shrink the electorate further, as though the answer to such a broad repudiation were fewer voters. The Daily Wire’s Ben Shapiro posted the “everything is fine” fire GIF — “Just checking in to see how things are goi—” — and the Federalist’s Sean Davis answered with the hot-dog-suit meme, the one where the man in the costume insists everyone else is the problem.

    We need your help to stay independent.

    The recriminations got personal fast. Rep. Nancy Mace told Fox’s Mark Levin to “STFU,” blamed his “beloved” war for the losses and called the night “devastating . . . for the hard-working American who can’t afford to buy a home, or fill their tank with gas or put food on the table.” Levin returned fire: Mace was a “washed up political loser” and “one of the most mentally unhinged POS to ever be in Congress.” She was angry, he noted, “because you’ll actually have to now work for a living . . . Good riddance, crackpot.” Florida Gov.     #18999. Texas Republicans’ gerrymander backfires as Democrats gain ground in U.S. House delegation

    📅 05 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1210 w)
    📖 Baca
    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Salon ↗ Open Full Page

    Texas Republicans’ gerrymander backfires as Democrats gain ground in U.S. House delegation

    📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1210 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Salon

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • This article originally appeared on The Texas Tribune.
    • In 2025, Texas Republicans, pushed by President Donald Trump, redrew the state’s congressional map before the midterms, converting five Democratic-held districts into ones Trump would have carried by at least 10 percentage points.
    • The move backfired: GOP candidates lost four of five seats their new congressional map was designed to flip and lost two of their own.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    This article originally appeared on The Texas Tribune.

    In 2025, Texas Republicans, pushed by President Donald Trump, redrew the state’s congressional map before the midterms, converting five Democratic-held districts into ones Trump would have carried by at least 10 percentage points.

    The move backfired: GOP candidates lost four of five seats their new congressional map was designed to flip and lost two of their own.

    Sources indicate that that means Texas Republicans will head to Washington in January with 24 U.S. House seats, one less than they had at the start of the current Congress. When the state Legislature in Austin pursued the controversial mid-decade gerrymander, Republicans had hoped for a 30-8 split in the delegation but will end up instead at 24-14.

    Industry observers note that in South Texas, moderate Democratic Reps. Henry Cuellar of Laredo and Vicente Gonzalez of McAllen both won reelection, surviving the redraw that put more Trump voters in their districts. Republicans also lost ground in the lone Rio Grande Valley district they already held, as Tejano musician Bobby Pulido ousted two-term Rep. Monica De La Cruz, R-Edinburg.

    In a recent development, democrats picked up another seat with Katy Padilla Stout’s win over YouTuber and gun-rights activist Brandon Herrera in the 23rd Congressional District, a sprawling seat covering San Antonio to the outskirts of El Paso. The district has been vacant since former GOP Rep. Tony Gonzales resigned in April over a sex scandal with a staffer. Despite the district’s 15-point lean for Trump, Padilla Stout, a San Antonio attorney and former teacher, made it onto the radar of national Democrats who saw opportunity in the district’s majority-Hispanic status and Herrera’s history of edgy, controversial comments.

    According to recent reports, democrats held fast to districts elsewhere, despite their incumbents being displaced due to the redraw. In the San Antonio area, Bexar County sheriff’s deputy Johnny Garcia beat Republican Carlos De La Cruz, the brother of Monica De La Cruz, in the newly crafted 35th Congressional District, a GOP target that Trump carried by 10 points.

    Sources indicate that in Houston, the grassroots campaign of Democrat Leticia Gutierrez topped Army veteran and former investment banker Alex Mealer, despite being vastly outspent in a district that Trump won by 20 percentage points two years ago. Gutierrez raised just a fraction of Mealer’s $2.8 million haul over the midterm cycle, as of mid-October, according to Federal Election Commission filings.

    Republicans had high hopes for the redraw, which Democrats fought by fleeing the state, keeping the map in limbo by temporarily denying Republicans the headcount to pass it. But the new lines could not withstand the blue wave that swept through much of the country Tuesday, driven in part by the leftward swing of Latino voters. Texas’ new map banked on the GOP holding most of Trump’s 2024 gains with Latino Texans, who made up a majority of the eligible voting population in four of the five targets.

    Recent findings suggest that nor did the redraw deliver what the White House wanted from it: a buffer that would preserve Republicans’ slim U.S. House majority. Trump’s push for the Texas map kicked off a tit-for-tat redistricting war across the country, producing similarly skewed maps in a number of states.

    In a recent development, after Texas, Republicans were most hopeful to flip four Democratic seats they redrew in Florida. Three of them stayed blue, and the other was within a one-point margin. In California, where Democrats retaliated with upcoming congressional maps of their own, they had picked up three of the five they targeted and were leading in the remaining two.

    Sources indicate that with GOP-leaning congressional maps powerless in the face of the blue wave, Democrats won the U.S. House and are set to have a substantial majority.The party has also wrested control of the U.S. Senate, leaving Trump to reckon with a Congress under full Democratic control for his last two years in office.

    Sources indicate that under less dramatic circumstances, a number of new faces will join the ranks of Texas’ congressional delegation to replace ten U.S. representatives who are either retiring, gave up their seats to run for other offices or lost their primaries for reelection. Most of the races were in noncompetitive general election districts.

    It has been revealed that two sitting representatives ran for U.S. Senate but lost in their respective primaries: Rep. Jasmine Crockett, D-Dallas, fell to James Talarico while GOP Rep. Wesley Hunt, R-Houston, finished behind Sen. John Cornyn and Ken Paxton.

    Sources indicate that reverend Frederick Haynes III won Crockett’s endorsement to succeed her in the heavily Democratic 30th District. A Dallas native, Haynes has been pastor of the city’s Friendship-West Baptist Church for more than 40 years. He sailed his way into Congress in the deep blue district Tuesday.

    Sources indicate that mortgage loan officer Jon Bonck will succeed Hunt in the safely red 38th District. Bonck received endorsements from Trump, Sen. Ted Cruz and other influential Republicans leading up to his victory in the general election.

    In a recent development, the tenure of Rep. Chip Roy will also come to an end in January after the congressman ran for Texas attorney general, a contest he lost in a primary runoff to Mayes Middleton. This election left the staunchly Republican 21st District in the hands of Mark Teixeira, a former professional baseball player who started his 14-season Major League career as the fifth overall draft pick for the Texas Rangers in 2001.

    And one incumbent, Rep. Dan Crenshaw, was forced into an early exit from his safe Republican seat by his primary rival, state Rep. Steve Toth of Conroe. The business owner defeated investment banker and Democratic nominee Shaun Finnie, and will be joining the U.S. House after five total terms, including the last eight years, as a state legislator.

    Sources indicate that among the six soon-to-be retirees, two are Democrats. The seats of Reps. Lloyd Doggett and Marc Veasey will be filled, respectively, by Rep. Greg Casar, who ran for Doggett’s Austin seat after his own district was scrambled, and former Rep. Colin Allred. Both are returning to Congress — Allred after two years out of office — in new districts.

    A fresh cast of Republicans will take over in four other safe districts.

    Five-term Rep. Jodey Arrington will leave his seat to Tom Sell, who worked in the office of former Rep. Larry Combest. Sell worked at a law firm he founded with Combest before running for the U.S. House.

    Rep. Michael McCaul will be succeeded by Chris Gober, who, before running for office, worked as the chief lawyer of Elon Musk’s America PAC that has channeled $216 million toward Republicans this cycle.

    Rep. Morgan Luttrell also chose not to run for reelection after two terms. That opened the door for Jessica Steinmann, an attorney who previously worked in Cruz’s office as well as in the first Trump administration’s Department of Justice.

    And a deceptively familiar face will replace Rep. Troy Nehls – that of his identical twin brother, Trever Nehls, who served in the U.S. Army for more than three decades and retired from the military as a Colonel. He’ll represent the Houston-area 22nd Congressional District.

    This article first appeared on The Texas Tribune.

    Pope Leo’s South America Tour

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1567 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Latin America Brief.
    • The highlights this week: Pope Leo XIV visits South America, regional leaders gather at the Ibero-American Summit in Spain, and Chile’s Atacama Desert feels the effects of El Niño.
    • Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Latin America Brief.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Latin America Brief.

    The highlights this week: Pope Leo XIV visits South America, regional leaders gather at the Ibero-American Summit in Spain, and Chile’s Atacama Desert feels the effects of El Niño.

    Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Latin America Brief.

    The highlights this week: Pope Leo XIV visits South America, regional leaders gather at the Ibero-American Summit in Spain, and Chile’s Atacama Desert feels the effects of El Niño.

    Recent findings suggest that pope Leo XIV began a 12-day tour through South America last Friday. It is the longest trip yet of his papacy, taking him to Uruguay, Argentina, and Peru. He’s getting a rock star reception: The Chicago-born pope became a Peruvian citizen after working as a missionary in the country, making this trip a homecoming for him, Gene Kuleta wrote in Foreign Policy last month.

    It has been revealed that in Argentina, Leo made headlines on Sunday when he called for the kind of strong social welfare state that runs counter to President Javier Milei’s austerity measures. Milei nevertheless praised Leo through tears when he bid him farewell. Argentina experienced a national “collective empathy” during Leo’s trip, Clarín’s Héctor Gambini wrote.

    Industry observers note that leo’s itinerary underscores a clear set of foreign-policy ideals, stated Massimo Faggioli, a historian at Villanova University, the pope’s alma mater. Chief among them is the idea that the Catholic Church can be a guardian for multilateralism as it comes under attack from the United States.

    While the Vatican’s support for the United Nations system is not latest, “what has changed is that U.S. foreign policy has become more muscular, more unilateral, and so you see more visibly now the difference between American foreign policy and that of the Vatican,” Faggioli said.

    It has been revealed that leo was outspoken after the United States captured Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro in January and again after the United States and Israel launched a war against Iran in February, according to Faggioli. The pope publicly suggested that both actions could be unlawful; he has since visited multiple small countries and spoken about how they play crucial roles in the international system.

    “The gift of smallness,” Leo noted on a trip to Monaco in March, means putting “your prosperity at the service of law and justice, especially at a historical moment when the display of power and logic of oppression are harming the world and jeopardizing peace.”.

    According to recent reports, this focus on small states helps explain why Leo chose to start his trip in Uruguay, which is one of Latin America’s least religious countries, Faggioli mentioned. The pope was celebrating Uruguay’s strong civic and diplomatic traditions, not just its small Catholic population. A plurality of the country’s population has no religious affiliation.

    “Persevering in respect for law, for negotiation, and for the patient search for agreements is a service that Uruguay can continue to offer to its neighbors,” Leo mentioned in Uruguay’s capital of Montevideo last Friday. The orchestra that welcomed him played Afro-Uruguayan candombe.

    Latin America’s Catholic population is shrinking—dropping from 80 percent of the total population in 1995 to only 55 percent today, losing ground to evangelicals and people with no religion, according to pollster Latinobarómetro. But the same survey suggests that the decline has slowed in the last half decade.

    “That might be part of the Pope Francis effect,” Faggioli mentioned, referencing Leo’s popular Argentine predecessor.

    Industry observers note that leo has continued Francis’s focus on seeking out the poor and marginalized in his travels. Judging by the crowds welcoming the pope in Argentina, the country has fully embraced him as a continuation of Francis’s spirit.

    It has been revealed that leo arrived in Peru on Wednesday. On Friday, he will return to his adopted hometown of Chiclayo.

    Friday, Nov. 13: Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez Parrilla concludes visit to China.

    Industry observers note that friday, Nov. 13, to Tuesday, Nov. 17: Pope Leo XIV ends his tour with a visit to Peru.

    It has been revealed that wednesday, Nov. 18, to Thursday, Nov. 19: Chilean President José Antonio Kast, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum, and Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China.

    Monday, Nov. 23, to Friday, Nov. 27: Polish President Karol Nawrocki visits Argentina and Chile.

    Paraguay’s bank scandal. As this newsletter covered last week, a dramatic bank collapse in Paraguay toppled President Santiago Peña, who was removed from office on Nov. 6 after announcing aims to resign the day before. It was the country’s largest political crisis since the 2012 removal of leftist President Fernando Lugo.

    Industry observers note that lugo was one of the few Paraguayan leaders of the last 70 years who did not hail from Peña’s right-wing Colorado Party. Peña was replaced by his vice president, Pedro Alliana, who is expected to hew closely to Colorado’s orthodoxy, the Paraguay Post reported. That includes trying to create a business-friendly environment and staying aligned with the United States, Israel, and Taiwan.

    Alliana signaled that he would focus mostly on domestic policy, saying in remarks to Congress that “too much time has been spent overseas.” Paraguay’s next presidential election is set for 2028.

    Industry observers note that slavery reparations? The United Kingdom’s King Charles III faced protesters demanding reparations for slavery during a trip to the Bahamas, Guyana, and Antigua and Barbuda that wrapped up last week. The island nations remain part of the Commonwealth of Nations, an association of 56 countries, mostly former British colonies.

    Unlike fellow Caribbean community member Jamaica, the three countries that Charles visited have not filed a formal legal petition on reparations to the United Kingdom. But the protesters’ demands still prompted a formal response from British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who attended a Commonwealth Heads of Government summit last week.

    It has been revealed that burnham committed to beginning a “structured dialogue” with Caribbean countries affected by the slave trade, Antigua and Barbuda Prime Minister Gaston Browne said. Though Burnham recently wrote in the Guardian that he did not believe financial reparations were appropriate, last week he voiced openness to debt restructuring for some Commonwealth countries.

    In a recent development, an aerial view of blooming wildflowers in the Atacama Desert near Copiapo, Chile, on Sept. 18.Javier Torres/AFP via Getty Images.

    Industry observers note that desert bloom. Chile’s Atacama Desert is covered in bright pink, purple, and yellow desert flowers this month. They spring to life every few years, when the area receives high amounts of rain. This year’s display is a result of the weather irregularities linked to the so-called Super El Niño climate phenomenon.

    El Niño has hit various parts of Latin America differently. Nearby Bolivia has seen severe droughts and has declared a state of emergency, FP’s Christina Lu reported. The toll on Chile has also been tragic: A storm that scientists say was exacerbated by the weather pattern killed 13 people in July, some of them in the same region as the Atacama Desert.

    While Chileans are celebrating the desert blooms, many are also calling for better preparedness for extreme climate events.

    In addition to the Atacama Desert, which of the following is also a desert in Chile?

    Though most of Patagonia is in Argentina, some of it extends into southern Chile.

    Argentina’s President Javier Milei and other leaders attend the 30th Ibero-American Summit at the Royal Collections Gallery in Madrid on Nov. 5. Thomas Coex/AFP via Getty Images.

    Last week, seven Latin American heads of state gathered in Madrid for the Ibero-American Summit, which has been held nearly every year since 1991 and unites Latin American countries with Spain, Portugal, Andorra, and Equatorial Guinea.

    Presidential attendance increased since the last summit in 2024, as did the number of countries that signed on to a joint declaration—albeit with some disagreements in the footnotes. The event is the latest evidence that Latin American leaders are trying to strengthen their network of relationships beyond just the United States and China, which are the top trade partners for many of them.

    Notably, most of the Latin American presidents at the summit were right-wing leaders who have signaled alignment with U.S. President Donald Trump. Brazil, Mexico, and Uruguay—all led by left-wing presidents—sent their foreign ministers instead.

    In his speech, Bolivian President Rodrigo Paz marked independence from the United States both by congratulating Brazil on its democratic election—which Trump has still not recognized—and by proposing the creation of an Ibero-American “center for strategic and security thinking” in Bolivia.

    The proposal was accepted, Paz stated afterward. It is an indication that as his and other right-wing governments don’t want anti-crime cooperation to be restricted to the Trump-led Shield of the Americas initiative.

    It’s not the only recent sign that Latin American countries are turning to Europe for partnership. Since the Mercosur-European Union trade deal took provisional effect in May, exports to the bloc have risen by around 30 percent from Brazil alone, according to Brazil’s trade ministry.

    Sources indicate that catherine Osborn is the writer of Foreign Policy’s weekly Latin America Brief. She is a print and radio journalist based in Rio de Janeiro. X: @cculbertosborn.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, election Day brought a substantial blue earthquake of anti-Trump sentiment that rumbled as far inland as Kansas and shook GOP ground in the Carolinas and Texas.
    • Florida narrowly missed the quake, with Republicans winning all the major statewide races by the thinnest of margins.
    • Industry observers note that angie Nixon felt different.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, election Day brought a substantial blue earthquake of anti-Trump sentiment that rumbled as far inland as Kansas and shook GOP ground in the Carolinas and Texas. By the time late victories rolled in on Tuesday night, there had been so many wins that subsequent Democratic pickups had begun to feel more like aftershocks, even in states that havenât voted blue since Bill Clinton was in the White House.

    Florida narrowly missed the quake, with Republicans winning all the major statewide races by the thinnest of margins. The one-time quintessential purple state, a so-goes-the-nation bellwether with a relatively even amount of registered Republicans and Democrats, turned remarkably red in the Trump era following Barack Obamaâs back-to-back wins in 2008 and 2012. The state legislature redrew its maps to enshrine a supermajority, and a post-Covid influx of GOP transplants seeking lower taxes and lax regulations shifted the balance significantly. A Democrat hasnât made a fight of the governorâs race this decade, and no Democratic Senate candidate has come close to winning since Bill Nelson lost his reelection bid in 2018.

    Industry observers note that angie Nixon felt different. The Jacksonville organizer and bookstore owner ran a proudly democratic socialist campaign, advocating for universal healthcare in a state beset by multiple insurance crises and affordability complications. Her polls looked good up to Election Day, and on Tuesday night, victories across the country made her race in the Sunshine State look winnable. Ultimately though, Nixon could not replicate the victories of other rabble-rousers like Dr. Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and James Talarico in Texas. She lost to incumbent Ashley Moody, who was appointed by Gov. Ron DeSantis to fill the seat left vacant by Marco Rubioâs confirmation as secretary of state, by less than two percentage points. Moody outspent Nixon by more than double to barely eke out a majority.Â.

    Industry observers note that the Florida Democratic Party deserves some blame for being woefully behind the times. After a 2019 squeaker between DeSantis and the progressive Andrew Gillum, the party moved as fast as it could from any candidate that might excite its base. They ran a former Republican for governor in each of the last two gubernatorial races, no doubt depressing turnout and enthusiasm among the Democratic base with their moderate picks.Â.

    Recent findings suggest that but a close look at the rest of the Florida races reveals the culprit in Nixonâs narrow loss. Despite a gerrymander meant to calcify Republican supermajorities in the state and a political stiff in the form of David Jolly at the top of the ballot for governor, the GOP lost seats in the state legislature. The energy in Florida and, remarkably, throughout the South, was with anyone running against Republicans. The blame for Nixonâs defeat lies almost solely with national Democrats and their stubborn refusal to back Nixon with either messaging or money.Â.

    Since her shock primary win in August, Nixon has complained about Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee recalcitrance to anyone who will listen. In September, she told MS NOW hosts Symone Sanders Townsend and Eugene Daniels that Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer was less than thrilled about her race.

    Sources indicate that it’s become something of a truism that the pro-life movement lacked a plan for how to pursue its goals after Roe v. Wade was overturned. Indeed, three more states (Nevada, Virginia, and Missouri) saw abortion-related statewide ballot measures go against pro-lifers in 2026. The recriminations have been bitter against the leaders and key advocacy groups on the pro-life side: They are political naifs; they are incompetent at messaging and strategy; they are self-important, wannabe massive shots who just want proximity to power; they are too focused on federal politics; their organizations’ CEOs make too much money (hilariously false — ask me how I know) for too little results.

    There is plenty of blame to go around, but I think such critiques are missing the key, practical problems the pro-life movement faces. The reality is that the pro-abortion side simply has far more money and organization than the pro-life side, and these gaps have been decisive in election after election. Without the funding for political organization and campaigns, pro-lifers simply cannot win.

    Taika Waititi’s Instagram crash out is a Trumpian sore loss

    📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1708 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Salon

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • For all the horrible things Donald Trump has wrought upon the world — and there are so, so many — he’s also taught us some crucial lessons.
    • That latter bit is certainly true for filmmaker Taika Waititi, whose otherwise tacky-yet-progressive veneer cracked last weekend when he took to Instagram to condemn the poor reviews of his latest film, “Klara and the Sun.” After a torrent of bad press and worse box-office performance, the film’s distributor, Sony, opted to scale back the movie’s wide release, reducing the sci-fi dramedy’s reach from 2,000 theaters nationwide to 800, most of which returned a meager profit.
    • Industry observers note that waititi’s childish outburst is straight from the MAGA playbook.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    For all the horrible things Donald Trump has wrought upon the world — and there are so, so many — he’s also taught us some crucial lessons. Trump is proof of several truths: A red-meat-and-stress-addled heart can withstand otherwise unthinkable conditions with the federal government’s medical secrets; reality television ruined the world; and, if we’re not careful, we’re all liable to become parodies of ourselves one day, crying about it online.

    That latter bit is certainly true for filmmaker Taika Waititi, whose otherwise tacky-yet-progressive veneer cracked last weekend when he took to Instagram to condemn the poor reviews of his latest film, “Klara and the Sun.” After a torrent of bad press and worse box-office performance, the film’s distributor, Sony, opted to scale back the movie’s wide release, reducing the sci-fi dramedy’s reach from 2,000 theaters nationwide to 800, most of which returned a meager profit. Never one to take his mediocrity on the chin, Waititi deflected the negativity outward, which, as we know, always paints someone in a good light!

    Industry observers note that waititi’s childish outburst is straight from the MAGA playbook. And while refuting film critics isn’t akin to Donald Trump’s most damning sins, Waititi’s mockery is a symptom of a problem that won’t be washed away by one blue wave, no matter how sizable.

    According to recent reports, waititi reposted a graphic claiming that “Klara and the Sun” was “rebounding” with a 78% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes, a 53-point gap from the film’s 25% critics score. (For what it’s worth, neither number should ever be used to accurately measure a film’s quality.) “I haven’t read a review of anything aimed at me or my peers in 15 years,” Waititi captioned the post. “But I do listen to the people . . . Let’s spare a thought for those sad, lost souls who couldn’t achieve their dreams of becoming artists, and thus settled, and became critics. Irrelevant. Out of touch. Obsolete. In the bin.”.

    Reading Waititi’s emoji-peppered caption, I was surprised to find it so carelessly evoked the Trumpian crybaby approach to social media. Whether on X or his own Truth Social, Trump’s favorite way of addressing critics and opponents has long been to toss out adjectives at will. Tack a “SAD!” at the end of Waititi’s caption, and it could easily pass for one of Trump’s poetic musings. (If only Waititi had gone so far as to parrot my personal favorite Trump quip about Barney Frank by saying, “The critics looked disgusting, nipples protruding, in front of my movie. Very very disrespectful.”).

    Ironically, all those admonishments in Waititi’s caption are also fitting descriptors for the state of Donald Trump’s agenda, the one imitated by his legions of Republican cronies spread out across America, hoping to be elected in Tuesday’s midterms. But judging by the results, MAGA’s influence is waning fast. Seven Senate seats flipped, historically red states turned blue and a spate of monumental wins popped up nationwide. The MAGA bubble popped in real time. Americans have seen firsthand what little good fascist ideology does for the average, working-class person. And though the country may not become great again overnight, it appears the last 12 years of freefall have finally been suspended — at least for now.

    Sources indicate that not to be all, “Oh, won’t someone think of the celebrities?” about it, but such overwhelmingly positive election results left me wondering what happens to someone like Waititi, whose childish outburst is straight from the MAGA playbook. For over a decade, Trump has used social media to peddle broadly disparaging, dangerous rhetoric that has legitimate impact outside the phone screen. The reckless hatred comprising MAGA ideology is so potent that it’s bled into the ways even otherwise progressive people wield their power, like crude oil painting an ocean black. And while refuting film critics isn’t akin to Trump’s most damning sins, Waititi’s mockery is a symptom of a problem that won’t be washed away by one blue wave, no matter how sizable.

    One would think that Waititi would know better. For one, the guy is 51 years old, certainly experienced and well-established enough to let a flop roll off his back. How fitting that his biggest success is the anti-fascist yet aesthetically tasteless political satire, “Jojo Rabbit,” which won the Oscar for best adapted screenplay in 2020, just as the Trump era was revving up for its second leg. That film, about a 10-year-old Hitler Youth who begins to grapple with the realities of life in 1940s Germany, examines propaganda’s influence and the power of hegemony, even if it often lacks the nuance and perspective such a satire warrants. For better, or more often, for worse, Waititi’s writing displays a self-possessed vulgarity that gets in the way of his more salient observations. Case in point: It’s downright ludicrous to stake your name on a film renouncing hate, then take aim at critics — people not exactly matched in influence to someone like Waititi — just six years later.

    Industry observers note that but this is the rot that social media creates. Whether it’s Instagram, X, TikTok, or YouTube, these sites have incentivized and monetized incendiary opinions. Their algorithms push small people into major power. What was designed to ostensibly be a great equalizer has only divided the world more, making animosity easily accessible to anyone who gets their rocks off on sewing discourse through cruelty.

    For some time now, arts critics have been easy targets on these platforms. Gone are the days of the critic playing dilettante, having intellectual conversations over martinis and cigarettes at the month’s salon for like-minded individuals. To be a critic today — to pursue one’s passion for art and writing and learning, all rolled into one — is to subject oneself to a pretty bleak existence. In most cases, the pay is meager. The hours are long. The job is demanding. And virtually no one has the patience or attention span to read an entire article anymore, let alone engage with its ideas. A legitimate critic doesn’t stumble into the job just to point and laugh; they write because they have real passion for what they cover. Surely someone like Waititi would say the same when he begins a new project after a string of flops.

    Sources indicate that if living in MAGA-world for a decade has taught us anything, it’s that things aren’t just good because one person claims so. Uniformity is the enemy of art, and blind trust is the scourge of politics. There is no future without recognizing the subtleties existing between the lines.

    In a recent development, what Waititi fails to realize is that he’s not punching up or down, but laterally. This is artist versus artist. If the context is right, a good piece of criticism can be as life-altering as a good film. But that’s hard to see when the internet has built such a wide chasm between people, reducing the impact of writing in favor of scrolling. Along with social media’s effect on human behavior, it’s had a heavy hand in blunting the journalism industry. If everyone’s a critic, then no one is, and that’s precisely why monitoring Rotten Tomatoes scores like they’re poll numbers is futile and ridiculous.

    But it’s not just Waititi who’s vulnerable to this unique form of MAGA-tinged, social media-brained psychosis; critics can fall prey to it, too. Whether it’s a filmmaker, a film critic, or just your average filmgoer, social media has confined us all to its machine. No one is exempt from consumer tech’s sway. And if a writer or filmmaker wants to make a splash, tossing out an inflammatory opinion aimed at a peer is a surefire shortcut. I’ve seen this affect critics’ prose over time, with certain writers (or their outlets) favoring button-pushing pull quotes and headlines for attention. But in most cases, no critic is happy to spend two hours watching something they find insufferable. No matter how gleeful Siskel and Ebert used to look sparring over movies, their industry was built on intellectual debate in pursuit of cinematic resonance, not schadenfreude.

    We need your help to stay independent.

    What’s most concerning in Waititi’s response is his foul self-importance, which is the real stain of MAGA politics. While an artist should avoid burdening themselves with hypothetical responses to their work before it’s even out in the world, considering the eventual reaction is worthwhile. Engaging with other people’s perceptions is a practice we could all stand to do with more grace and tact. Contemplating a differing opinion reveals maturity and humility, not absolute agreement. Pointing a finger won’t do anything for a person’s growth, artistic or otherwise. America’s politicians are only just beginning to relearn that lesson, understanding the value in trying to address problems, rather than gesture toward them with a shrug.

    Sources indicate that if America’s blue wave is indeed going to usher in a new era where politicians actually act in favor of the people, and Trumpian artists like Waititi make themselves look foolish on Mark Zuckerberg’s Instagram, we owe some props to one of the century’s most prolific liberals. Aaron Sorkin’s “The Social Reckoning” actually got a few things right. In last month’s companion piece to “The Social Network,” Sorkin posited that the average American would soon be mobilized by their fatigue with MAGA politics and social media. But his director’s eye lacked style and discernment. Sorkin responded to criticisms with pleasant diplomacy, even questioning his own merits as a director versus a screenwriter. “I’m worried that the parts of directing that I’m not good at are those parts you can’t learn,” he admitted.

    While there may be truth to his concern, Sorkin’s introspection is precisely the kind of pause this country could learn from. If living in MAGA-world for a decade has taught us anything, it’s that things aren’t just good because one person states so. Uniformity is the enemy of art, and blind trust is the scourge of politics. There is no future without recognizing the subtleties existing between the lines. The only thing that is, to quote Waititi, irrelevant, out of touch and obsolete is the arrogance in thinking anyone could know it all.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The second Trump administration has placed significant strain on U.S.
    • Sources indicate that to demonstrate that the administration’s turn against allies is not a settled fact of U.S.
    • Industry observers note that the second Trump administration has placed significant strain on U.S.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Get audio access with any FP subscription.

    The second Trump administration has placed significant strain on U.S. treaty alliances. It has directly threatened the sovereignty of long-time allies such as Canada and Denmark and wielded tariffs as a weapon of first resort. Moreover, the administration has sought major force posture changes, often without allied consultation and reportedly based on ideological considerations rather than military requirements. And it has attempted to interfere in allied domestic politics, championing far-right parties and individuals.

    Sources indicate that to demonstrate that the administration’s turn against allies is not a settled fact of U.S. political life, the latest Democratic majority in Congress should reassert powers as a co-equal branch of government. Rhetorical steps, such as reassuring statements and letters of concern, will not be enough even if they garner bipartisan support.

    Industry observers note that the second Trump administration has placed significant strain on U.S. treaty alliances. It has directly threatened the sovereignty of long-time allies such as Canada and Denmark and wielded tariffs as a weapon of first resort. Moreover, the administration has sought major force posture changes, often without allied consultation and reportedly based on ideological considerations rather than military requirements. And it has attempted to interfere in allied domestic politics, championing far-right parties and individuals.

    To demonstrate that the administration’s turn against allies is not a settled fact of U.S. political life, the fresh Democratic majority in Congress should reassert powers as a co-equal branch of government. Rhetorical steps, such as reassuring statements and letters of concern, will not be enough even if they garner bipartisan support.

    Instead, the next Congress must take practical steps to remove obstacles to defense industrial base integration and make it harder for the administration to take unilateral steps that sabotage alliances.

    Current Senate Democratic leadership has telegraphed that working to improve the domestic economic situation in the United States is one of its top priorities for the new Congress. In this context, reasserting congressional authority over foreign policy in general and alliances in particular is not only a national security imperative, but also a part of the Democrats’ affordability agenda: President Donald Trump’s tariffs on Washington’s closest allies have added to Americans’ woes, while economic integration with allies can spur growth and jobs.

    Recent findings suggest that amid rapidly increasing allied defense spending, everyone would benefit from integrating allies into the U.S. defense industrial base. Many of the Trump administration’s actions, however, have soured commercial relationships and pushed allies toward domestic or alternative suppliers. Congress can take concrete steps to help establish a more cooperative allied industrial relationship that ultimately improves intra-alliance burden-sharing.

    In a recent development, first, Congress could treat more allies as part of the U.S. defense industrial base. This would involve adding more countries to the National Technology and Industrial Base and putting funding behind it; extending to other allies the exemptions to the International Traffic in Arms Regulations that Australia and the United Kingdom receive through AUKUS; designating additional key allies as domestic sources under Title III of the Defense Production Act (as Section 1080 of the 2024 National Defense Authorization Act did to add Australia and the U.K., alongside Canada); and raising the dollar thresholds for congressional notification on sales to close allies to match the increased price of modern high-tech weapons.

    Before doing this, Congress would need to vet each ally’s technology protections and compliance with existing U.S. law on concerns such as human rights—but for most treaty allies, this wouldn’t create a problem.

    Industry observers note that second, Congress should facilitate allies building more together. It could increase funding for co-production of critical capabilities such as the Patriot PAC-3 and other air defense interceptors as well as counter-drone capabilities. To ensure that the Pentagon follows through, Congress could withhold a share of funds until the Defense Department certifies progress, the same mechanism that the Senate Armed Services Committee has proposed to ensure access to a second source for Patriot interceptor rocket motors.

    Industry observers note that the legislature could consider complementing bipartisan U.S. maritime security efforts, such as the SHIPS for America Act, with additional exemptions to 10 USC. 8679 for allies in Europe and the Indo-Pacific that can make major shipbuilding contributions.

    Here, the Icebreaker Collaboration Effort Pact among the United States, Canada, and Finland offers a template: Finnish shipyards are building the first new U.S. Coast Guard icebreakers in decades as domestic U.S. production capacity ramps up. Any change must be coordinated closely with domestic interest groups, such as unions and industry, to protect American workers.

    To pay for these steps, Congress could pass a supplemental appropriation aimed at building munitions production in the United States and allied countries. Such a supplemental could include a requirement that allies co-fund each co-production initiative they decide to join, which would go beyond existing proposals such as the nonbinding expectation in the fiscal 2026 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) that Baltic countries match U.S. funding for the Baltic Security Initiative.

    Beyond specific measures related to the defense industrial base, Congress could examine authorities preventing deeper or more rapid cooperation, including limitations on how much allies can do with and for U.S. forces to support their readiness and operations. For example, Congress could extend foreign repair exemptions under 10 USC. 8680 to include South Korea and Japan, as the statute already permits under specified conditions for U.S. submarines in Australian and U.K. shipyards.

    Industry observers note that other problems stem not from missing authorities but instead from open-endedness in existing authorities. For instance, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has reportedly not completed the required paperwork for allies to transfer their own Patriot interceptors to Ukraine. Any similar approval requirements that lack a deadline will give any administration an implicit veto over allied cooperation even if that cooperation advances U.S. interests.

    Congress could consider reviewing these authorities systematically and develop more serious accountability mechanisms, such as instituting automatic approvals if the executive branch has not acted within a specified period and, at a minimum, establishing standing consent for transfers among treaty allies.

    Sources indicate that in other areas, Congress has already begun building the tools to create a bulwark against the administration’s efforts to undermine U.S. alliances. Section 1249 of the 2026 NDAA bars U.S. troop reductions in Europe below 76,000 without independent certification from both the commander of U.S. European Command and the secretary of defense that includes consultations with NATO allies. Congress should now overcome the administration’s objections to extend these provisions and establish similar limits on U.S. troop reductions in South Korea in the final version of the 2027 NDAA.

    After the Supreme Court confirmed in February that presidents can impose tariffs only when Congress has clearly authorized them, the administration shifted to a temporary surcharge and then to Section 301 tariffs that include allies. Congress could consider passing into law a bill similar to the bipartisan Trade Review Act, which would make any new tariff lapse after 60 days without congressional approval.

    Recent findings suggest that members have also proposed various ways to limit potential military action against allies, including a bipartisan bill that would prohibit the departments of Defense and State from using funds for military action or annexation of the sovereign territory of a NATO member state. Although the worst of the Greenland crisis, which inspired these legislative proposals, has passed for now, the administration could attempt to once again coerce allies at any point. Moving forward, Congress should learn from the fact that its efforts to rein in Trump through stand-alone bills and appropriations amendments have stalled. Instead, lawmakers should consider adding new protections to must-pass legislation.

    Legislation is not the only tool, however. The Senate’s advice-and-consent powers allow it to withhold approvals on confirmations, and both chambers can conduct oversight hearings and expand investigations. For example, the Senate can resist confirming nominees selected for posts in Europe, up to and including all pending ambassadorial nominees or potential newly introduced cabinet nominees, until the administration accounts for its attempted interference in allied domestic politics. Next term’s committee leaders could also develop a joint hearing agenda early in the term that prioritizes alliance concerns, including interference in allied politics.

    Enacting fixes, however, is just the first half of the challenge. Ensuring that the administration complies is the other, perhaps harder, half—as the past 22 months have illustrated.

    In October, a bipartisan group of senators wrote a letter to the secretaries of defense and state, urging the “swift obligation” of Baltic Security Initiative funding, following up on their similar letter sent in May that appears to have gone unheeded. In September, the U.S. Government Accountability Office found that the administration could not lawfully let congressionally appropriated funds expire unspent.

    Congress can make its legislative priorities bite by withholding funds until the administration certifies progress, as several of the provisions discussed above do, setting firm obligation deadlines and authorizing multiyear procurement that is harder for any one president to unwind.

    According to recent reports, but while compliance mechanisms might be able to force the administration’s hand, they cannot force allies to continue investing in a partner that they no longer trust. Whether allies ultimately believe that they still have a partner in the American people depends on how muscular the next Congress decides to be.

    There is a particular little sequence to my autumn evenings that Iâve come to adore.

    In a recent development, I once heard a piece of advice about eating more vegetables that Iâve never forgotten, although I wish I could remember who said it: Find the vegetables you can add to a meal almost automatically. The ones that make you say, âWhy the hell not?â.

    For me, those are pre-shredded cabbage and carrots.

    Pre-shredded red and green cabbage: I put this on practically everything. Tacos, rice bowls, steak chili, prepared grain salads â anything that could benefit from a little crunch, color or freshness.     We need your help to stay independent.

    Sources indicate that of course, a grocery list is only so useful without a little inspiration. Here are five dinners that show how these ingredients make their way onto my table.

    Industry observers note that these arenât formal recipes. Think of them as invitations to improvise.

    This one is a little more ambitious, but itâs an excellent example of how convenience ingredients can leave more room for creativity.

I steamed frozen corn and edamame, and tossed a generous pile of shredded red cabbage with sesame oil.

    This is the dinner for when I want something cozy and substantial but do not want to peel a single potato.

    Recent findings suggest that brown ground beef or chicken in a skillet with frozen onions, garlic and mushrooms. Once everything has developed some color, stir in a brown or mushroom gravy packet, a splash of stock and a generous quantity of frozen mixed vegetables.

    Let the filling simmer until thick and savory, then transfer it to a baking dish (or keep it in an oven-safe skillet, if you have one). Spread deli-counter mashed potatoes over the top and bake until the filling is bubbling and the potatoes are golden in spots.

    Hearty, comforting and full of vegetables, without having to peel, chop or mash a thing.

    This is one of those dinners that started with a can and became something much more interesting.

    I browned a little hot Italian sausage in a skillet, then added sun-dried tomatoes, a can of tomatoes, Heydayâs tomato alla vodka beans, a splash of cream and frozen spinach.

    Sources indicate that everything simmered together into a rich, savory, slightly spicy skillet situation. I served it with toasted sourdough tips for scooping up all that lovely sauce.

    It has been revealed that the beans bring both flavor and fiber, the sausage adds richness and heat, and the spinach practically disappears into the sauce. I would happily eat this again tomorrow.

    This is the sort of thing I love making when I want something fresh, bright and satisfying without spending much time at the stove.

    Recent findings suggest that cook some small pasta â Iâm fond of cubetti here â and add frozen peas and carrots, cooking them just long enough to heat through. Drain, cool slightly and toss with canned white beans and a generous amount of Sauz Lemon Pepper Pesto.

    It has been revealed that you can eat it slightly warm or chill it for later. Either way, the creamy, lemony pesto ties everything together, while the vegetables and beans make the whole thing more substantial.

    Sometimes you just need one very good sauce.

    Industry observers note that remember those Whole Foods chicken cutlets I was raving about earlier? Hereâs one of my favorite things to do with them.

    While the cutlets cook, toast some soft potato buns and make a quick lemon-garlic mayonnaise. I use Kewpie, into which I stir freshly grated lemon zest and one of those handy frozen minced-garlic cubes, thawed.

    To assemble, spread sun-dried tomato pesto on one half of the bun and the lemon-garlic mayo on the other. Add the cheesy chicken cutlet, then pile on an almost unreasonable quantity of fresh arugula. My beloved shredded cabbage would also be wonderful here if youâre in the mood for extra crunch.

    Industry observers note that the result is creamy, tangy, savory, crunchy and a little peppery. Itâs the sort of sandwich Iâd happily pay a cute restaurant a slightly unreasonable amount of money to make for me.

    Instead, Iâm standing in my own kitchen, feeling very pleased with myself.

    #18983. Trump reversed the Pied Piper’s bargain, and voters stiffed him

    📅 05 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1286 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy 📈 Bullish 🌐 Salon ↗ Open Full Page

    Trump reversed the Pied Piper’s bargain, and voters stiffed him

    📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1286 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Salon

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • When the pied piper loses his audience, we must ask whether the people have rediscovered their conscience or simply found a newly introduced tune to follow.
    • On Tuesday night, Donald Trump and his MAGA movement saw what happens when political influence collides with the everyday realities of the people it seeks to lead.
    • Industry observers note that the 2026 midterm elections brought a dramatic shift in political power.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When the pied piper loses his audience, we must ask whether the people have rediscovered their conscience or simply found a newly introduced tune to follow.

    On Tuesday night, Donald Trump and his MAGA movement saw what happens when political influence collides with the everyday realities of the people it seeks to lead.

    Industry observers note that the 2026 midterm elections brought a dramatic shift in political power. Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate, flipping Senate seats in states such as Texas and Kansas, which were long thought to be out of reach, and winning House districts Trump easily carried just two years ago.Â.

    Voter polls placed the presidentâs approval at approximately 38%, with roughly six in 10 voters saying he was a factor in their vote. But beneath those numbers lies a more consequential story. Americans are confronting the cost of living, the economic consequences of tariffs, the uncertainty of war with Iran and diminishing confidence in American leadership abroad.

    According to recent reports, trump promised his voters he would drain the swamp, end foreign wars and bring prices down. Yet many Americans went to the polls questioning whether those promises had been kept. Unlike the Pied Piper of Hamelin, who rid the town of its rats, Trump now faces an electorate concerned that the problems he promised to eliminate have instead multiplied.Â.

    In a recent development, in the original story, the Piper fulfilled his bargain. He played his pipe, led the rats into the river and freed the town. But when the townspeople refused to pay him, he returned to exact revenge by leading away their children.Â.

    Over and over again throughout the midterm campaign, Trump urged supporters to vote as though he were personally on the ballot. In this telling, the Piper did not eliminate the rats. He added to them, and still he expected to be paid.

    In a recent development, critics argue that Trump reversed that bargain. Rather than delivering the relief promised to ordinary Americans, the administration has left many struggling with economic uncertainty while continuing to demand political loyalty. Over and over again throughout the midterm campaign, Trump urged supporters to vote as though he were personally on the ballot. In this telling, the Piper did not eliminate the rats. He added to them, and still he expected to be paid.Â Â.

    It has been revealed that trumpâs supporters see a different story. They point to immigration raids and mass deportations, deregulation and challenges to established political institutions as evidence that the president delivered on vital commitments. From their perspective, voters who rejected those policies after experiencing the consequences resemble townspeople who accepted the Piperâs services, but refused to honor their bargain.Â.

    Both interpretations expose a fundamental ethical question: When does political loyalty cease to be an expression of shared principles and become an abdication of independent judgment?Â.

    In a recent development, in a democracy, voters are not obligated to follow the music indefinitely. They retain the right to question the destination, reconsider promises and withdraw their support. Political loyalty is not a debt citizens owe their leaders. It is a trust that leaders must continually earn.

    Sources indicate that albert Hirschman, an American economist and author of âExit, Voice, and Loyalty: Responses to Decline in Firms, Organizations, and States,â distinguished between voice (working to change an organization from within) and exit (abandoning it). A vote against an incumbent is often itself an act of a voice. But where voters withdrew their allegiance from a party or movement altogether, Tuesday looked more like an exit. Hirschman saw loyalty as what keeps members inside, speaking up rather than leaving. His framework suggests that when loyalty silences voice instead, exit becomes the only remaining option.Â.

    But elected officials carry a different and greater responsibility.Â.

    Like the children of Hamelin, many Republican lawmakers followed the music toward an uncertain destination. Unlike those children, however, they had the authority â and the responsibility â to question where they were being led. Some embraced the presidentâs direction; others followed him despite reservations, knowing that dissent could invite a primary challenge. After all, they had seen others who challenged his leadership pay a considerable political cost. Kentucky Rep. Thomas Massie and Louisiana Sen. Bill Cassidy lost their Republican primaries to Trump-backed challengers.Â.

    According to recent reports, political cooperation is essential to governing. But cooperation becomes ethically troubling when loyalty to an individual displaces the obligation to question, deliberate and act independently. The oath of office is not a pledge of allegiance to a president, a party or a political movement. It is a commitment to uphold the Constitution. A president can command attention, share public debate and place enormous pressure on members of his own party. But the ability to demand loyalty does not create a moral entitlement to receive it.Â.

    The children of Hamelinâs Pied Piper tale had no part in the broken bargain, yet they paid its price. In our democracy, ordinary Americans and future generations often inherit the consequences of political decisions, and today they are paying a price. Economic instability, weakened public trust and the costs of war do not disappear when an election ends. A leaderâs success cannot be measured solely by the number of people willing to follow along with them. It must also be measured by what happens to those who never chase the tune.Â.

    The election has shifted power in Washington. Democrats, after winning sizable, historic victories throughout the country, will soon have an opportunity to exercise congressional oversight and reinforce the institutional independence our constitutional system requires.Â.

    But changing who holds the instrument does not necessarily change the music.Â.

    Democrats now face their own ethical test. Will they exercise power with the transparency, accountability and respect for constitutional checks they demanded from their opponents? Will they welcome dissent within their own ranks? And will they resist the temptation to substitute partisan loyalty for independent judgment?Â Â.

    An election can change the balance of power overnight. It cannot, by itself, restore public trust or guarantee ethical leadership. That requires leaders willing to place constitutional responsibility above political convenience, institutions prepared to exercise meaningful oversight, and citizens who refuse to surrender their judgment to the most compelling voice in the room. The first six months of the 120th Congress must be defined not merely by a change in political power, but by a demonstrable commitment to ethical reform, transparency, and accountability. The American people did not vote simply for a change in leadership. They voted for a government worthy of their trust.

    We need your help to stay independent.

    It has been revealed that the Pied Piperâs greatest power was not simply his ability to play a captivating tune. It was his ability to persuade others to follow without questioning where their journey would end.Â.

    Political ethicist Dennis Thompson called this the problem of many hands: When many officials each contribute a small part to a collective outcome, responsibility seems to dissolve until no one bears it. So, when political loyalty becomes more important than independent judgment, who bears responsibility â the leader who plays the tune, or those who willingly follow? Thompsonâs framework does not allow individual lawmakers to hide behind presidential leadership, party discipline or collective decisions. Nor does it assign blame equally. Responsibility depends on each officialâs authority, knowledge, contribution and the alternatives available to them. By that measure, those who knew better and had the power to act cannot claim they were merely following the music from the leader in the red hat.

    When the music finally stops, the question is not simply who will lead next.Â.

    It is whether we have learned to listen differently.
