    • DePetris is a fellow at Defense Priorities and a syndicated foreign affairs columnist at the Chicago Tribune.

    Recent findings suggest that if there’s one subject that unifies the Democratic Party after their midterm election victory this month, it’s ending the war in Iran. Chuck Schumer, who will likely return as Senate Majority Leader when the next Congress is gaveled into session on January 3, declared that terminating the conflict was at the top of his to-do list. The top House Democrat, Hakeem Jeffries, echoed that sentiment: “We need to end the reckless and costly war of choice in Iran. That’s been a commitment that we’ve made.”.

    Industry observers note that at first glance, none of these remarks are particularly surprising. Throughout the midterms, the Democrats pegged the nagging cost of living and higher energy prices stateside to the war that’s occurring thousands of miles away in the Persian Gulf. It turned out to be a winning political strategy. Compelling President Trump into ending hostilities by filing another War Powers Resolution on the Senate floor or by cutting off funds for the war would just be a logical extension of what the party ran on.

    Daniel R. DePetris is a fellow at Defense Priorities and a syndicated foreign affairs columnist at the Chicago Tribune.

    On Tuesday night, two things happened at once, and the country will be tempted to remember only one of them.

    Industry observers note that the first made me go quiet at my kitchen table. Chris Pappas won election to the U.S. Senate in Upcoming Hampshire, becoming the first openly gay man ever sent to that chamber, and part of the margin that handed Democrats the Senate. In Indiana, J.D. Ford, the first openly gay person ever elected to that stateâs legislature, unseated a Republican incumbent and is headed to the House. In Texas, of all places, James Talarico beat Ken Paxton to become the first Democrat to win statewide in more than thirty years, after a campaign in which anti-LGBTQ+ messaging was reportedly Paxtonâs single largest category of advertising, and in which the vice president of the United States stood on a stage and used âgayâ as a punchline against him. Talarico is straight, and he won anyway.

    According to recent reports, and on Long Island, in a district Donald Trump carried, a gay Democrat named Chris Gallant, whose private photographs were leaked against him precisely because someone believed that seeing him would be enough to end him, came within about two points of flipping a seat the forecasters had rated safely Republican. He conceded the election on Wednesday, down by roughly 6,700 votes in the closest race of the incumbent Republican Nick LaLotaâs career. In the same breath, Gallant called LaLota a brother in arms and told the district he was still their neighbor, which is to say he refused the shame he was supposed to feel from the photo leak to the very end. Whatever that is, it is not the story of a man sunk by leather. It is the story of a man who nearly won the unwinnable while carrying the exact weight that was supposed to be disqualifying.

    In 2026, you cannot reliably win an American election by making a manâs gayness, real or invented, the center of your campaign. Republicans tried it in Texas and lost the whole state. They tried it on Long Island and watched a red seat nearly flip.

    Put those results next to one another and a sentence forms that would have been unimaginable a decade ago: In 2026, you cannot reliably win an American election by making a manâs gayness, real or invented, the center of your campaign. Republicans tried it in Texas and lost the whole state. They tried it on Long Island and watched a red seat nearly flip. The oldest weapon in the drawer â the one that raised me, the one that could empty a lunch table in the 1990s â is losing its edge at the ballot box. Voters keep looking at the openly gay candidate and sending him to Washington.

    That is the headline, and it is real, and I am not going to let anyone talk me out of being moved by it.

    But here is the second thing that happened Tuesday night. In the same hours, often on the same ballots, and it is the part the rainbow-wave coverage is already rushing past. In Arizona and Nebraska, voters approved measures to bar transgender girls from girlsâ sports. In Colorado, two measures aimed at transgender young people, one on sports and one restricting certain surgical care for minors, are narrowly passing. In Washington State, an initiative to keep transgender girls out of girlsâ sports passed comfortably. The same electorate that refused to punish a Senate candidate for being gay reached down the ballot and punished trans kids for existing.

    This is the thing I need people to see before the celebration hardens into a story we tell ourselves. The contempt did not disappear on Tuesday. It relocated. A political movement that has learned it can no longer win by hating gay men has not given up the strategy. It has updated the target. The MAGA machine that aired the Paxton ads and laughed at Vanceâs joke is the same one now writing ballot measures about 11-year-olds, because cruelty still tests well when it is aimed at the group with the least power to answer back. Gays are simply the part of the community that got powerful enough to be left alone.

    According to recent reports, I know this pattern in my body, because I have watched it my whole life. The fear moves. First it was the plague, then it was the gay man as predator, then it was marriage as the end of the world, and each time the broader culture eventually got bored or ashamed and the fear went looking for a new address. Right now the address is a trans child in a locker room. The people who found that child did not arrive by accident. They are the same people, running the same play, because it is the only play they have ever had.

    In a recent development, so I want to be careful about the victory lap, even as I take one. It is a genuine and hard-won thing that Chris Pappas will be a senator and J.D. Ford will be a congressman, and that a straight man in Texas could not be destroyed by being called gay. Those wins are not small, and the people who did the work to make them real earned every bit of the joy.Â.

    According to recent reports, but a movement does not get to accept its own seats at the table while the youngest and most defenseless members of its own community are voted off the field in four states on the same night. This is not a win we get to keep cleanly. It is a split screen, and if we only look at our half of it, we become exactly the kind of people who could be bought off with a little representation while someone else pays the bill.

    We need your help to stay independent.

    The refusal to be ashamed won some rooms on Tuesday. I felt it. The task now is to extend that refusal to the people the machine has decided to hunt next, to say as loudly for trans kids what the voters of New Hampshire and Indiana and Texas just stated for us: that you do not get to make a personâs existence a punchline, or a wedge, or a ballot measure. We learned that lesson about gay men the slow and brutal way. The whole point of learning it is to spare the next group from learning it alone.

    Chris Gallant did not quite win. But he came close enough to prove the old weapon is dulling. The question Tuesday really asked is whether we will hand the people wielding it a newly introduced one, or finally take the thing out of their hands.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Today, after 31 years, we are saddened to announce that Salon is ceasing publication.

    Itâs difficult to find the right words for the end of something that has meant so much to so many people. Salon was never just a website. It was an idea about what journalism could be, born at a moment when the internet was still a largely unexplored frontier.

    When Salon introduced in November 1995, the web was a very different place. A small group of journalists set out to create something original: a publication with a strong voice, a curiosity about the world and a belief that the internet could bring journalism and readers together in new ways. They helped pioneer a form of journalism that would come to define an entirely new era of publishing.

    Recent findings suggest that over three decades, Salon has brought together politics, culture, criticism and ideas in a way that was distinctly our own. Our journalism examined power and politics, questioned assumptions, surfaced stories that deserved attention and made room for perspectives that were too often overlooked. Our writers and editors helped shape conversations about the forces changing our lives. The work was never simply about keeping up with the news. It was about making sense of it.

    Industry observers note that the history of Salon is also the history of the people who made it. We are profoundly grateful to the journalists, editors, photographers, producers, designers, business teams and countless other colleagues who brought this publication to life across its many chapters. To the founders who imagined it, the staff members who built it, the contributors who gave it their voices and the alumni who carried its spirit into the world: Thank you. Salon’s legacy belongs to all of you.

    In a recent development, the business realities of independent digital journalism have changed profoundly over the years. After careful consideration, we have reached the difficult decision that our publishing model is no longer sustainable. We know this news will be deeply disappointing to many of you, and we share that sadness.

    Thirty-one years is a remarkable run, but what matters most is what happened during those years: the journalism, the ideas, the voices, the conversations and the community that grew around them. Salon helped demonstrate what digital journalism could be and could become. We hope that legacy will continue to matter long after today.

    Industry observers note that thank you for being part of our story. It has been an extraordinary privilege.

    Privatize Air Traffic Control

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (682 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nationalreview

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that thank goodness we’re still two weeks away from Thanksgiving.
    • It has been revealed that over the weekend, more than 18,000 flights were canceled when the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), the agency that oversees America’s air traffic control system, ordered a nationwide ground stop.
    • In a recent development, this was the second nationwide ground stop since 9/11.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that thank goodness we’re still two weeks away from Thanksgiving. Otherwise, Steve Martin and John Candy’s long trek home would have become a near-universal experience.

    It has been revealed that over the weekend, more than 18,000 flights were canceled when the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), the agency that oversees America’s air traffic control system, ordered a nationwide ground stop. No plane was allowed to take off from a U.S. airport for over four hours. The stoppage was necessary when the FAA’s telecommunications network suddenly failed, apparently caused by a faulty update to its decades-old tangle of copper wiring.

    In a recent development, this was the second nationwide ground stop since 9/11. The previous one happened less than four years ago, in January 2023, and was also caused by technical difficulties. Republican lawmakers blamed the Biden administration last time; now, Democrats are faulting the Trump administration. But the FAA’s antiquated infrastructure isn’t a partisan issue. It’s the institutional consequence of having an unaccountable bureaucracy manage the skies.

    Recent findings suggest that unlike almost every other major country, the U.S. federal government funds and operates air traffic control directly. Congress must appropriate its budget each year, and controllers must work without pay when the government shuts down. Infrastructure investments are subject to political timetables. Meanwhile, the FAA is expected to regulate the very system that it runs.

    It has been revealed that usually, it wastes no time in dodging responsibility. Immediately after the grounding, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy — who oversees the FAA as part of his department — placed the blame on Congress and past administrations for not adequately funding upgrades to the agency’s aging infrastructure. Yet the FAA received $12.5 billion from last year’s reconciliation law for that purpose. Earlier this month, it requested $30 billion more. Now, Duffy claims that he really needs $50 billion to get the job done. And we thought airlines’ add-on fees were bad.

    Sources indicate that improvements don’t have to be so costly. The FAA has spent a quarter century trying to switch its network from copper wires to fiber-optic cables. Its counterpart up north, Nav Canada, completed most of the same transition in just 18 months.

    The fundamental difference? Nav Canada was spun off from the national government in 1996 as a nonprofit corporation. The organization is funded entirely by user fees from the airlines and private aircraft that rely on its systems, not general taxes, and it’s structured to be accountable to both private stakeholders and the government. When it needs to finance capital projects, Nav Canada doesn’t have to wait for approval. It can simply glitch bonds and recoup the cost over the long run.

    The results are impressive. Research finds that privatization lowered costs and boosted productivity for the aviation sector, especially compared with the FAA. Safety has greatly improved, and Nav Canada leads in technological advancement. Dozens of countries have since followed Canada’s lead toward an independent, commercial operator.

    Passengers wait at a terminal after the FAA issued a national ground stop following the agency’s earlier report of serious air traffic control communications problems, at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport in Atlanta, Ga., November 13, 2026.

    In a recent development, america almost joined that list in 2017. That year, legislation gained traction in Congress that would have transferred air traffic control to an independent entity while retaining the FAA’s oversight role. Regrettably, the plan was shot down by the labor union representing controllers, which feared losing the federal government’s generous protections and benefits. Private aircraft owners also opposed it to avoid paying user fees they are presently exempt from, keeping the revenue burden on commercial flyers.

    Industry observers note that aside from placating these entrenched interests, there is no good reason to keep air traffic control in government hands. The public utility model has proven safe and effective elsewhere, and the FAA has shown once again that it can’t measure up. Free the aviation system from political gamesmanship, and watch dependability soar.

    The Editors comprise the senior editorial staff of National Review magazine and nationalreview.com.

    During NATO’s formative years, the U.S. military commitment to the old continent was a tenuous thing. Dwight Eisenhower, appointed the first supreme allied commander of Europe in 1950, argued—amid a vicious debate in Washington over committing additional divisions to Europe—that American forces should only act as a bridge until Europe stepped up to defend itself. If the United States still had troops in Europe 10 years hence, he said in 1951, then the trans-Atlantic project would be a failure.

    Germany Rearmed: The Return of War and the End of Illusions, Liana Fix, Oxford University Press, 216 pp., $34.99, November 2026.

    Ike’s forecast, it seems, was wrong on both counts. Seventy-five years on, roughly 80,000 U.S. troops remain on the continent. Yet few would regard the alliance as a failure. The U.S. military commitment succeeded in guaranteeing Europe’s freedom and keeping the Soviets at bay. But Europe never fully shouldered the burden of its own defense.

    Old assumptions, however, are finally changing. Squeezed by both a volatile Washington and voracious Moscow, Europe has finally awoken to its security dilemma: Its defense spending has nearly doubled in six years in real terms, from 242 billion euros in 2020 to 454 billion euros in 2026. If by 2035 Europe fully meets its NATO military expenditure target—spending 3.5 percent of GDP on defense (compared to the little more than 2 percent that it spends today)—then the surge in annual spending will rival the scale of the Marshall Proposal relative to Europe’s GDP.

    As Council on Foreign Relations scholar Liana Fix argues in her incisive latest book, Germany Rearmed, the central protagonist in this story is Berlin. Germany has doubled defense spending since 2021 and accounts for more than a quarter of the European Union’s increase over that period. Based on its current budget, by 2029, Germany will spend more on its military than France and the U.K. today spend combined.

    Recent findings suggest that but is a rearmed Germany, in fact, a good thing for Europe and the world? Fix makes a compelling case that Berlin shedding its “myth of pacifism” is in the best interest of both Europe and the United States. But risks abound. A militarily empowered Germany has centrifugal potential, threatening friction with prickly France and anxious neighbors in Central and Eastern Europe if the rearmament is not executed within a broader European framework. And if the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party eventually takes the reins of what will be one of the world’s most powerful militaries, it would reawaken historical nightmares.

    Sources indicate that germany Rearmed gives proper airing to the consequences and challenges of German rearmament, often left unanalyzed amid general backslapping about surging European defense spending. The U.S. commitment to Europe is ultimately unsustainable at current levels as Washington focuses on growing threats in the Pacific—and given its isolationist spasms at home. And Europe, with Germany as its backbone, has the overwhelming means to check a revanchist Russia—Germany’s economy is roughly two times the size of Russia’s, and the EU’s is nearly 10 times its size.

    According to recent reports, but policymakers in Europe and Berlin should take heed of Fix’s advice. She argues that Germany needs to do a better job of Europeanizing its rearmament—in force structure, spending on a Europe-wide military industrial base, and joint funding—or it risks undermining European cohesion as the United States draws down.

    Industry observers note that west Germany participates for the first time as NATO’s 15th member in Paris, France, on May 9, 1955. AFP via Getty Images.

    Recent findings suggest that germany’s recent rearmament push, at first blush, may appear as a sudden break from the past. In popular perception, the allied occupation after World War II underwrote an enduring German aversion to military power, just as in Japan—whose own story of U.S. occupation and political transformation is beautifully told in John W. Dower’s Pulitzer-winning Embracing Defeat. The Western security architecture during the Cold War then reinforced German passivity: Lord Hastings Ismay, NATO’s first secretary-general, allegedly described NATO’s purpose as to “keep the Russians out, the Americans in, and the Germans down.”.

    This “myth of pacifism,” according to Fix, has permeated German history ever since: from Chancellor Willy Brandt’s Ostpolitik of the 1970s to the Wandel durch Handel (“change through trade”) approach to Russia and China adopted under both Chancellors Gerhard Schröder and Angela Merkel. At seemingly every opportunity, Germany prioritized diplomacy and economic engagement over military power, believing the former to be more attuned to the future. This belief hardened after 1989, when Germans concluded (correctly) that the Soviet collapse owed more to Mikhail Gorbachev’s reforms than to U.S. President Ronald Reagan’s military flexing.

    Recent findings suggest that crucially, as Fix observes, the German body politic has no grand military tradition to lean on, unlike its European neighbors. The United Kingdom can look back nostalgically to its days of ruling the waves. France’s defiant Gaullist military tradition is having its moment in the sun in the wake of Julian Jackson’s masterful book De Gaulle, adapted into a recently released blockbuster biopic. Germany, for obvious reasons, can’t draw from its 20th-century military history; even Prussian militarism is viewed skeptically with the hindsight of what followed.

    But Fix provides nuance to this myth of pacifism, arguing that Germany was in fact no stranger to hard power after WWII. West German defense spending surpassed 3 percent of GDP through the mid-1970s, and even after the Cold War, the Bundeswehr fought in out-of-area operations in both the Balkans and Afghanistan, where it lost 55 soldiers—a fact little remembered in Germany today.

    Quibbles aside, Germany has undeniably entered a newly introduced relationship with its military. In addition to the doubling of defense spending over the past five years, polling from fall 2024 indicated that 73 percent of Germans wanted to invest more money in European security and 65 percent supported a spending target of 3 percent of GDP or higher.

    It has been revealed that german Chancellor Friedrich Merz and U.S. President Donald Trump speak at the G-7 summit, in Evian, France, on June 16.Christian Hartmann / POOL / AFP via Getty Images.

    Industry observers note that while many commentators would gladly attribute this wake-up call to Russian President Vladimir Putin’s brutal invasion of Ukraine, Fix inconveniently but convincingly credits U.S. President Donald Trump’s return to the White House as the real catalyst.

    After Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine, German Chancellor Olaf Scholz claimed grandiloquently in his “Zeitenwende” speech that “the world … will no longer be the same as before.” But while his 100 billion euro special defense fund was a good first step, disbursement was slow, and it wasn’t followed by other bold moves.

    In a recent development, only in 2025, with Chancellor Friedrich Merz facing a hostile Washington, did Germany finally turn a corner. Between 2025 and 2029, Germany intends to spend a total of 649 billion euros and reach annual spending of 3.5 percent of GDP—up from just 1.15 percent in 2015, the year after Russia’s annexation of Crimea.

    Referring to Russia’s second invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and the United States’ reelection of Trump in 2024, Fix memorably writes that “history had to repeat itself twice for Germany to abandon the ‘myth of pacifism’ and to seriously begin rearmament.”.

    It’s a remarkable feature of our turbulent era that the breakneck rearmament of Germany is considered, in the main, a beneficent thing. Economists surveying the many challenges of slowing European growth and flagging competitiveness point to continental rearmament as a sole bright spot: a fiscal stimulus surpassing COVID-era spending that may boost sagging European productivity growth by 0.25 percent per every 1 percent of GDP spent on defense, if focused on research and development as well as equipment rather than military pensions and personnel, according to estimates from the Kiel Institute.

    According to recent reports, and Germany is undoubtedly the most consequential player in the story of Europe’s broader rearmament. With French bond markets quaking, Germany is one of the only countries with the fiscal headroom to spend, with a debt-to-GDP ratio of 64 percent. Germany’s contribution to increased spending will also invariably be Europe’s largest, given that its economy is a third larger than that of the U.K. and 50 percent larger than France. And its industrial prowess positions it well to play the role of Europe’s arsenal.

    But what kind of military power will Germany be? Here Fix rightly throws up notes of caution. Thus far, Germany’s rearmament has largely been a national one, with spending at the German rather than EU level and funding largely going to German defense players. This trajectory risks fragmenting Europe’s military production, while also enhancing Germany’s own preeminent power within the continent—inviting suspicion and potentially exacerbating European divisions. It’s hard to envision outright conflict between Germany and its neighbors, but a more assertive Germany backed by hard power may more forcefully push its own foreign agenda over, say, Poland or France. The U.S. security blanket helped keep a lid on these rivalries since World War II; if Washington retreats from the continent, competing national priorities may sharpen with the steel of military spending.

    The country’s cinema has recently taken a very dark turn.

    Fix’s solution, which is a compelling one, is for Germany to rearm inside either a more European NATO or a broader European security architecture: spending at European level where possible on shared platforms, inside a more integrated European command, and across a continent-wide military industrial base. Such “Europeanized” spending would allay concerns about the contortions in power caused by German rearmament. It would also reassure allies wary of an AfD ascension in Berlin: tied into a NATO or European architecture, a remilitarized Germany would have a harder time pursuing an overtly nationalistic military agenda.

    Sources indicate that the question of Washington’s future role on the continent still presents a broad conundrum. Fix wrote Germany Rearmed in 2025 and early 2026, and the rawness of the Trump administration’s provocations on trade and Greenland shines through. She argues that Washington is “never going back” and that the future trans-Atlantic relationship under either Democrats or Republicans will resemble “a patron-client relationship more than an alliance, with no preferred treatment for Europeans.”.

    Sources indicate that this likely over-indexes on the wrecking ball of the Trump administration’s first two years. After the Republicans’ drubbing in the midterms, and considering that Trump’s favoritism toward Putin’s Russia and Xi Jinping’s China is idiosyncratic even within his party, the possibilities of U.S.-European reconciliation are higher than she lets on. Brussels and Washington will still have overwhelming shared interests come a newly introduced U.S. administration in 2029, especially as Europe finally awakens to the threat of surging Chinese exports and barrels into a trade conflict with Beijing over the coming years. More likely is a United States that is less bullying and extractive, whether a Republican or Democratic administration, and remains committed to NATO and Article V—even if it pushes for Europe to shoulder more of its defense burden while gradually winding down its troop commitment.

    Fresh reservists of the Bundeswehr train at Camp Aulenbach near Baumholder, Germany, on Sept. 15. Andreas Rentz/Getty Images.

    This matters because it should inform how Europe rearms. Replacing core U.S. enablers, such as space-based intelligence and integrated air and missile defense systems, would be a costly endeavor that would eat up a tremendous amount of European capacity and take up to a decade. The International Institute for Strategic Studies puts the cost of fully replacing US capabilities at more than $1 trillion.

    A more prudent wager is that a future United States will maintain its nuclear umbrella over Europe and the backbone of critical NATO capabilities while Europe builds capacity in complementary areas such as ground forces, missiles, unmanned systems, and munitions. Betting on even limited U.S. staying power may seem foolhardy at the moment, but the alternative would be an expensive distraction that Europe can ill afford.

    Sources indicate that the greater threat to European security and cohesion is more likely to come from within. The AfD now leads every national poll in Germany, averaging 29 percent to the Christian Democratic Union/Christian Socialist Union’s 19 percent. Its path to the chancellery as German elections approach in 2029 remains narrow given that Germany maintains a strong political firewall against the party in light of history. But the AfD agenda should terrify us: The party has an affinity for Russia and China, and it advocates for even greater defense spending of 5 percent of GDP in pursuit of national sovereignty.

    However unlikely an AfD-run Germany may be, populist convulsions within Europe are certain. Fix spends little time on the rise in France of the far-right National Rally, which appears poised to win the French presidency in the spring. How a right-wing France in the engine room of Europe would affect broader rearmament is a question that should be top of mind in Brussels today.

    The implications of German rearmament are vexing, and the recent surge in spending represents easy yards. But for a remilitarized Germany to truly enhance European security, it must surrender more of its own power, decision-making, and even defense-industrial spending to the rest of Europe. Otherwise, Europe will have answered Eisenhower’s challenge 75 years on only to produce a more fractured continent as the United States pulls back.

    #18970. China’s Economics of Denial

    📅 05 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2781 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foreignaffairs ↗ Open Full Page

    China’s Economics of Denial

    📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2781 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

    ⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Oliver Melton is a Director with Rhodium Group’s China practice.
    • Logan Wright is a Partner at Rhodium Group and leads its research on China’s economy and financial markets.
    • Beijing’s Theory of Success in the Face of Failure.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Oliver Melton is a Director with Rhodium Group’s China practice.

    Logan Wright is a Partner at Rhodium Group and leads its research on China’s economy and financial markets. He is the author of the book Broken China: How the Economic Miracle Shattered and What it Means for the World.

    Beijing’s Theory of Success in the Face of Failure.

    According to recent reports, china has correctly diagnosed its most pressing economic problems. The Chinese Communist Party has acknowledged that its economy relies too much on investment and exports and that persistently weak household consumption is the core threat to future growth. The leadership also knows that this imbalanced growth model is causing trade friction with developed and emerging economies alike and will continue to do so. They know there is a growing chorus of economists (including many quiet voices in China) raising the alarm that, if Beijing does not make major changes soon, China will face ever-slower growth, cascading trade disputes, and potentially stagnating household income.

    It has been revealed that but what is puzzling is that the country’s leaders are not acting. Beijing has confirmed only modest intends to boost household consumption and domestic demand, and its overall economic strategy remains essentially unchanged—focused on expanding investment in manufacturing, especially in advanced technologies and fresh strategic industries.

    Theories abound as to why Beijing has chosen to ignore the warnings. Many speculate that Chinese leader Xi Jinping is not receiving accurate information or that he and his closest allies have abandoned development as a priority in favor of national security goals or a desire to control the commanding heights of global industry. Others argue that Beijing knows what it should do, but political or institutional constraints prevent it from taking decisive action.

    In a recent development, in truth, while these factors all play a part in shaping policy, the real explanation is far simpler. The party is sticking to this path because the leadership believes it is working. It sees the same troubling data—including rising external surpluses, weak consumption, slower household income growth, weak credit demand, rising unemployment and underemployment, and persistent deflation—but it has reached wildly different conclusions about what these developments indicate and what Beijing should do in response.

    Chinese economic policy is nested within a methodical planning process, which is meant to ensure that short-term pressures do not distract from long-term priorities. The problem is that the long-term strategy is predicated on the belief that control of advanced technologies and industry will trigger a new round of high-speed growth. This economic strategy can best be understood as a Marxism-infused misapplication of neoclassical economic development theory: Beijing is obsessed with control over technology and physical capital and believes that its ultrahigh levels of investment will accelerate productivity gains and wage growth. But a disproportionate focus on manufacturing and technology cannot increase productivity or wages if those investments are decoupled from the needs of the market and trends in aggregate final demand. This is especially true in a country as large as China—already the world’s largest exporter—that cannot rely on further exports to fuel growth.

    According to recent reports, china’s worldview treats development as equivalent to capital accumulation and sees productivity as determined by the control and deployment of technology. It posits that the growth of the service sector, higher wages, and higher consumption are the consequences of that physical underlying foundation—they follow naturally in later stages of the development process once the productive industries have flourished. In this conception of economic development, the right strategy is always more investment, more industry, and more technology. The role of the state is to ensure that household savings and industrial profits are recycled through the state-owned banking system or government-guided capital into priority investments rather than frivolous activities, such as services or consumption. The resulting structural imbalance that weakens household income growth, the service sector, and public services was thus not an accident; in China’s economic development theory, this is seen as self-discipline that will pay off with more rapid long-term development.

    A key corollary to this view is that the government’s macroeconomic management must guide resource allocation proactively through hands-on intervention, not impassively through interest rates and exchange rates. The state can harness the dynamism and ambition of markets to promote efficiency and innovation in defined spaces, but it is the government’s job to identify the correct focal points for investment to ensure that priority sectors grow at maximum speed and then to intervene to ameliorate imbalances when they inevitably arise.

    In this conception of macroeconomics, the economy consists of a massive input-output table where every cell in the matrix is a sector that consumes other cells’ outputs and provides inputs to other producers. If there is an imbalance in supply or demand for certain products—which becomes evident in high or low prices—it may be because of overinvestment in the producing sector or underinvestment in downstream consuming sectors. Government policy seeks to increase output and steadily lower prices by facilitating investment and production throughout the matrix, adjusting the pace and balance of resource allocation as needed if one cell’s output exceeds the demands of the others. The goal is not to develop overcapacity or low profitability in these targeted sectors, but the optimal path for rapid development will inevitably push sectors in that direction.

    According to recent reports, beijing has followed this playbook closely. When, for instance, the real estate sector collapsed in 2022 and the structural imbalances in China’s economy became too substantial to ignore, Beijing responded by increasing its efforts to micromanage credit flows, reversing experiments with interest rate liberalization and financial market reforms while tightening oversight of capital markets and industrial policy funding. Central bank relending facilities now channel low-cost bank loans to prioritize industrial upgrading and equipment purchases for targeted sectors. Thousands of government-run equity funds provide low-cost capital to firms that support a web of industrial and technology strategies. State-owned enterprises intervene to help boost valuations in the stock market, and regulators prioritize firms in strategic sectors for fresh listings. When a sector is overinvested, policy campaigns such as “anti-involution”—a neologism that describes a basket of discordant policies to resolve overcapacity—are deployed to slow future investment, buttress profitability by fixing prices, or set standards to restrict market entry in a bid to slow output while the other cells in the input-output tables catch up and restore balance over time.

    In a recent development, although hard to comprehend in the context of a market economy, some aspects of this approach have an understandable internal logic in China, especially at a micro level. The collapse of the property sector—roughly a quarter of GDP at its peak—sent massive shock waves through very specific supply and demand pathways in the economy. It made sense for Beijing to calibrate policy for the affected sectors and think in terms of input-output tables as it designed its responses. The frequency of bubbles in China’s equity, commodity, and property markets over the past 15 years has left policymakers deeply wary of accommodative monetary policy for the entire economy, which helps explain why they are experimenting with more targeted tools aimed at specific sectors.

    Likewise, a certain level of triumphalism in Beijing is understandable, given that Chinese companies are breaking into pole positions in major conventional industries, such as autos and telecommunications, and many others are poised to thrive in cutting-edge sectors, such as robotics and biotechnology—all in the wake of a massive hit to GDP. For a generation of economic policymakers who cut their teeth trying to revitalize a moribund planned economy in the 1990s and the first decade of this century, the emergence of world-leading (often private) firms is definitive evidence that Beijing has found a winning recipe. From this perspective, Beijing is also dismissive of foreign complaints about unfair market interventions or trade imbalances as the sour grapes of rich countries that had grown accustomed to rent-seeking technology monopolies.

    Recent findings suggest that china’s leaders also see some deflation as the fruits of hard-won efficiency gains: the elimination of bottlenecks, economies of scale in manufacturing clusters, construction of world-class infrastructure, improved logistics, and removal of market barriers that have lowered costs up and down manufacturing supply chains. One-off cost reductions from efficiency gains or the abrupt loss of construction activity must be digested by the economy, they would argue, not offset by stimulus. And while foreign commentators and dignitaries warn of growing trade pushback, the data tells a surprisingly different story: China’s export growth barely slowed as the Trump administration imposed sweeping duties and the European Union set up defenses against a handful of sectors, such as electric vehicles.

    The core problem with China’s economic strategy, however, is that aggregate domestic demand consistently falls far short of domestic supply. Chinese planners’ input-output tables will not balance unless domestic workers are buying the goods that China’s industries produce. Otherwise, everything else must be exported, often at lower prices. The leadership understands this in principle but believes that the control of advanced industries and technology will, ipso facto, cause productivity to rise, sustain economic growth into the future, and generate higher wages and therefore higher consumption.

    Industry observers note that this is the flaw in Beijing’s approach—the dangerous legacy of vestigial Marxism and misapplied neoclassical growth theory. In reality, state intervention in markets can depress overall productivity and workers can see flat wages even when China succeeds at promoting advanced industries.

    In a recent development, it is true that capital and technology create productivity gains in well-functioning market economies. But the causality usually breaks down if resources are allocated by policy interventions that are divorced from returns on investment. The control or ownership of advanced industries does not inherently cause economic growth, because they are far too small a share of the economy. Instead, latest products or technologies generate productivity when they are distributed and used throughout the economy in ways that improve efficiency or increase output. It is not the success of a robotics firm that leads to efficiency gains, for example, it is the deployment of its robots in factories to save production costs—namely by displacing workers—and boost output. If those benefits do not exceed the true cost of the new industrial robots—even with layers of subsidies—then the net effect is not positive, no matter how impressive the factories themselves are, or how successful the robotics firm itself appears.

    The use of fresh production technologies also requires a degree of creative destruction that Beijing’s own industrial policy interventions have inhibited. When governments, not price-conscious firms, make technology and investment decisions, policymakers are not just gambling that they know better than the market how to boost long-run performance. They are also betting that they know how to use those technologies to create innovative new business models. Yet in China, state influence over resource allocation has ossified markets, especially by reducing bankruptcies, in ways that limit the fruits of innovation and efficiency gains in the broader economy. Additionally, much of China’s industrial policy aims to build self-reliance, which, by definition, focuses on duplicative investments that buttress domestic industrial prowess without necessarily adding efficiency.

    Moreover, even though China’s many layers of industrial policy have helped launch successful companies and built an impressive fleet of ultramodern factories, there are also tremendous inefficiencies and waste that never make the headlines. Overall productivity must be calculated comprehensively, evaluating the net output gains against all the industrial subsidies, bad debts, foregone profits, and indirect support for investment that the government has provided. The reality is that China’s aggregate success rate is far lower than the shining stars would suggest: the remarkable global reach of electric vehicle and battery makers such as BYD, CATL, and Li Auto masks the dozens of failed companies that generated nonperforming loans and ate up unprofitable capital subsidies throughout the bulk of the sector and its supply chain. It is far from obvious that the net return on investment from industrial policy spending, estimated by the International Monetary Fund to be up to four percent of GDP, is positive, and it could be deeply negative, despite pockets of success.

    Industry observers note that finally, Beijing is betting that superefficient manufacturing and success in strategic industries will eventually lead to higher wages, which will then cause consumption to surge. It is true that productivity growth causes real incomes to rise in a competitive market economy. But if investments in labor-saving technologies are driven by state policy, not returns on investment, wages can fall even as firms become more efficient. Rising household income requires a key intermediate step: employment, which is not a core characteristic of China’s capital-intensive, advanced manufacturing investment strategy. Indeed, state funding has helped China—a middle-income economy—become a world leader in high-tech “dark factories” that operate without distracting human accommodations, such as light. This may increase output in prized manufacturing cells in the input-output tables, but if demand for labor is not growing in aggregate, the whole equation starts to fall apart.

    Still, the most pernicious consequence of Beijing’s economic model is entrenched deflation. The focus on expanding production combined with China’s weak consumer demand has caused the producer price index to fall for longer than it has risen over the past decade. This is a far larger threat to China’s economy than a mere nuisance of sectoral imbalances. Deflation reduces private-sector credit demand; undercuts incentives for new investments; and crushes employment, wage expectations, and, therefore, consumer confidence, which leads to weaker domestic demand—not in carefully demarcated input-output relationships but throughout the economy. Deflation also saps fiscal revenues and puts pressure on financial institutions in ways that severely limit the state’s capacity to act decisively the longer it lasts. Deflationary pressures in China also spill over to the global economy through cheaper exports and a weakening real exchange rate, driving more tensions between Beijing and its trading partners.

    Recent findings suggest that there is immense risk in falling behind the curve in fighting deflation, but Beijing is not likely to change course if it continues to believe its strategy will boost productivity and jumpstart domestic demand in the long run. Some analysts speculate that Beijing could be forced into a reappraisal of its vision in response to unemployment pressures or the proliferation of foreign trade friction, but it has already shown its cards. The accumulation of unemployment, underemployment, and low wages for Chinese households and workers are already significant, yet Beijing has responded with only modest latest household subsidies and incremental investment in social services. Likewise, as external trade tensions have risen, Beijing has managed these country-by-country disputes as diplomatic issues, through a mix of threats and negotiations, to preserve the bulk of China’s export markets.

    The decision to pursue short-term Band-Aid measures for a weak labor market and foreign trade tensions is confusing at first pass. For a government laser-focused on self-reliance and eliminating foreign dependencies, it is a curious strategy to become ever more dependent on foreign demand—over which Beijing has little control—as its primary driver of economic growth. Likewise, for a regime that is obsessed with social stability, it would seem prudent to focus more on wages and labor demand. Yet the strategy makes a degree of sense when viewed from the leadership’s perspective that China is in a transitional period. It may be unpleasant and difficult, but it is an unavoidable step on the path to a technology-led growth model.

    Recent findings suggest that the leadership’s current confidence in this transition process means that it could be many years before the warning signs, already visible, become persuasive internally. This all but guarantees that Beijing will continue to defer action while deflationary pressures and external trade tensions build. Deflation and weak corporate profitability are already eroding China’s fiscal revenues, which have basically been flat in nominal terms since 2019. Deflation and the growing debt burden are also corroding the financial system, which will ultimately require large write-offs and recapitalization from the government budget to prevent credit growth from slowing further. A $54 billion bank recapitalization just took place two months ago, with little effect on lending.

    Beijing’s ideological commitment to its industry- and technology-focused development strategy is creating a dangerous cycle that will likely produce weaker consumption, slower income growth, and even greater trade friction with the rest of the world. Moreover, in the face of such challenges, China’s economic leadership is compensating by expanding state intervention in the economy in ways that further undermine market forces and the independence of the private sector. At this rate, even if the leadership eventually recognizes the need to change strategy, China may not have the fiscal or financial space to rebalance the economy toward a more sustainable and diversified growth model.

    #18969. Let’s Stop Fighting Gravity in U.S.-Canada Trade

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (166 w)

    Let’s Stop Fighting Gravity in U.S.-Canada Trade

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (166 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Nationalreview

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • U.S.-Canada trade is a little like gravity.
    • Trade negotiations between the two countries had been suspended, but the midterm results may be an opportunity to press forward as Democratic wins in both the House of Representatives and Senate shift the political calculus.
    • Hendrik Brakel is the former chief economist of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce and former chief economic adviser to the leader of Canada’s Official Opposition.

    U.S.-Canada trade is a little like gravity. You can push against it, but the size and proximity of the U.S. economy and the convenience of a G-7 market like Canada always pull us back together.

    Trade negotiations between the two countries had been suspended, but the midterm results may be an opportunity to press forward as Democratic wins in both the House of Representatives and Senate shift the political calculus. President Donald Trump seemed to warm to the idea of a deal on the campaign trail. Some analysts are suggesting a deal is imminent, and Prime Minister Mark Carney stated Canadian and U.S. teams would be working to deliver a deal “in the coming weeks” following a “good conversation” with Trump.

    Hendrik Brakel is the former chief economist of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce and former chief economic adviser to the leader of Canada’s Official Opposition.

    Daniel Dorman is the managing editor and director of operations at the Macdonald-Laurier Institute in Ottawa.

    Nvidia, Spies, and the Art of Economic Espionage

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2087 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways

    Prefer to listen? To hear this entire conversation, and more episodes in the weeks ahead, follow Ones and Tooze wherever you get your podcasts.

    The semiconductor manufacturer Nvidia, which had until recently been the most valuable company in the world, was thrown into turmoil this past week.     The semiconductor manufacturer Nvidia, which had until recently been the most valuable company in the world, was thrown into turmoil this past week. Company founder and CEO Jensen Huang resigned upon allegations that he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy and subsequently intervened to sell Nvidia chips to her China-tied company, despite U.S. regulations in place to prevent China’s access to the technology. The scandal has put a spotlight on the widespread international practice of economic espionage—and also on the Trump administration’s susceptibility to corruption.

    What is the difference between industrial espionage and economic espionage? Is the tech elite particularly vulnerable to this type of spying? And will China be successful at incorporating any AI technologies that it managed to steal?

    Those are just a few of the questions that came up in my recent conversation with FP economics columnist Adam Tooze on the podcast we co-host, Ones and Tooze. What follows is an excerpt, edited for length and clarity. For the full conversation, look for Ones and Tooze wherever you get your podcasts. And check out Adam’s Substack newsletter.

    Cameron Abadi: What are the differences exactly between industrial espionage, economic intelligence, and economic espionage?

    Adam Tooze: In general understanding, industrial espionage is above all targeted at particular businesses by, more often than not, other businesses but sometimes by governments. And it’s about accessing commercial secrets, business secrets, business strategies, business technologies. And it involves various types of subterfuge or illegal action.

    It has been revealed that economic espionage is sort of blurred into that zone, because it also involves various types of subterfuge. But when we say economic espionage, one immediately thinks of governments. Why is that? I think because when we think of businesses, we think of private economic activity and profit. But when we use the word “economy,” we immediately start thinking about GDP and national interest. And so, the sorts of information that are being targeted there might be more to do with technologies of general strategic interest. So that will be different from industrial espionage or purely commercial espionage.

    According to recent reports, and then an example of economic intelligence would be, say, wartime efforts on the part of the British who are aiming a strategic bombing program against Germany and therefore need to understand how the German economy functions and built an economics intelligence wing of the British military war effort so as to organize that. And that ranged from people who were architectural historians who knew which cities would be inflammable if you dropped incendiary bombs on them all the way through to an understanding of the input-output diagram, the supply chains.

    Sources indicate that and it involves, more often than not, open-source information. It doesn’t involve any subterfuge at all. And so economic intelligence kind of blurs into the world that we’re in, of economic reporting, of newsletters, of regular updates. The Economist magazine has what it used to call the Economist Intelligence Unit, which was presumably very well-connected journalists doing studies.

    Recent findings suggest that and I think the allegation in the Nvidia case sits most squarely in the domain of economic espionage. Yes, it targets a particular business and the top man in that particular business, the charismatic figurehead, indeed, of the entire hardware side of AI. So it would seem that it sits somewhere on that boundary.

    Industry observers note that I don’t think the allegation, however, is that Jensen Huang’s lover was doing this with a view to commercially profiting herself. I think the suggestion is that it’s MSS, the Ministry of State Security, which is doing this on behalf of the Chinese state.

    It has been revealed that CA: Jensen Huang is noted to have fallen prey to a honey-trap method of espionage, in which a spy creates a sexual relationship to later exploit it. Is our current economic elite in tech companies particularly susceptible to this form of espionage?

    Sources indicate that AT: It’s impossible not to speculate about the ego makeup of Silicon Valley engineers. It wouldn’t, after all, be surprising if there was a desire for compensation for a whole variety of inhibitions, which no doubt are introduced at various stages in many people’s careers during their extraordinary efforts in very recondite zones of technical expertise. So, the nerd gone wild at the head of a company, the loneliness of people in that kind of position, all of this, I think, no doubt plays a role.

    In a recent development, but then I was thinking, actually sociologically, and I came to this strange realization, because I spend quite a lot of time in hotels because of this weird existence that I have. And I was thinking to myself, if a senior soldier goes to a hotel, on the face of it, you’re kind of wondering what the senior soldier is doing in a hotel, right? If a senior civil servant, pretty much whichever government they work for, goes to a really glamorous hotel, again, you’d be asking yourself, how can they afford that? That’s not really where they belong, right?

    So suddenly, you realize that the whole zone of high-end, expensive, relatively exclusive hospitality that presumably provides the most attractive zone for this kind of entrapment, the actors for whom it arouses zero legitimacy challenges, zero need for explanation at all, in fact it’s completely normal and taken for granted, are high-level business figures.

    Recent findings suggest that in fact, the entire conference circuit, where people stay, the blending in those spaces of leisure and business activity, including pools and gyms and eating and drinking as a matter of course, in fact, isa kind of mandate for many businesses. I’ve gone to a lot of these investor conferences, and it’s quite clear that networking is an absolutely required option, right? There’s no excuse for just withdrawing to your room and getting on with your life, which I’d want to do most of the time.

    And so presumably, this is precisely the world in which this works. I mean, business people systematically expect to be wined and dined. They expect to be courted. They constantly struggle to draw the line between reasonable inducements and bribery. That is an essential part of their business. And many of them, of course, have very strict codes of ethics. But it’s a matter of record that those shift all the time.

    And they’re much more like, in that sense, the Chinese Communist Party than they are like, you know, conventional civil service jobs in the West, where it’s just quite clear that accepting any kind of gift in any form is just off-limits. No one in the civil service is regularly invited to glamorous parties where there’s a mixture of more or less formally clad, in some cases scantily clad, different types of interaction. And so it’s a kind of recipe for stress on this fault line, I would have thought. And it’s purely sociological, it’s not a matter of psychology at all.

    CA: There’s clearly a distinction between pursuing the acquisition of technologies through espionage of this kind versus productively absorbing that technology upon having acquired it. How does that distinction apply right now to China?

    AT: I think this is the whole game, actually. The real reason to be worried is that China has a demonstrated and extraordinary capacity to incorporate. In other words, it’s a near-peer. And that’s precisely what makes it so alarming to Western security officials, is that there’s absolutely every reason to think they can, yeah. And furthermore, leapfrog, even. Give them half a chance and there’s every single reason to think that they can generalize it, make it cheaper, speed it up.

    There are differences, obviously, because what Nvidia does or what Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Firm does or what the lithograph makers do is literally special source. Like, no one has ever done that anywhere, ever, in the entire world in the history of humanity. So whether you can replicate that is an open question. But that’s presumably what the Chinese aren’t going to do anyway. They’re going to make their own version that’s more suitable to their circumstances.

    Recent findings suggest that and it’s critical to know—and we don’t know what’s actually happened in this case—but there are certain critical problems that it’s interesting to know how other people solve them, because it helps you to think about how you should solve them in your own terms. And that is why I think the Chinese case is so significant, because they have a demonstrated capacity to do that. And it really varies—in regard to transport engineering, cars, railways, solar, batteries, there has already been hugely successful leapfrogging; the game is over. With regard to chips, it’s a slightly different story, and I think that speaks to the fact that the technological demands are just so mind-blowingly high.

    It has been revealed that but that does contrast very significantly with the Soviet Union, which at different periods in its history demonstrated greater- and lesser-degree capacity to incorporate technologies that it acquired through espionage. So around the atomic bomb program, there was a quite a high capacity to incorporate. Then of course in rocketry, they become world-leading. And they do that like the Americans by capturing German rocket scientists and then incorporating their knowledge into what was already a high-functioning military industrial system in the Soviet Union that was wasteful of people’s lives but was generative of a whole series of incredibly innovative, very, very powerful and effective weapons.

    Recent findings suggest that but more generally, it’s a remarkable instance of just how little can get transferred, because after all, the Soviet Union was the beneficiary, after ‘45, of a huge wave—this is the untold story of German reparations after World War II, absolutely gigantic, and they take the form principally of dismantling. So vast amounts of German equipment are shipped to the Soviet Union where, I don’t think it’s merely apocryphal to say, an awful lot of it just rusted and was not fully incorporated into the Soviet system.

    Now, in earlier stages, they had done much better. So in the ‘30s, the Stalinist industrialization program is heavily dependent on American expertise and on German expertise funded in part by export guarantees from the Weimar Republic that helped to fund this flow.

    So it wasn’t consistently rubbish at incorporating, but it certainly wasn’t the powerhouse of creative imitation, adaptation, modification, and improvement that China is, to an extent that nowhere else in the world can match, right?

    That’s the extraordinary thing. They can iterate, they can modify, they could incorporate at a pace that no one else in the world—in almost all areas of production—no one else can match. And so, then if you feed that with privileged insider information, then you’d expect really large-scale effects.

    Recent findings suggest that cameron Abadi is a deputy editor at Foreign Policy. X: @CameronAbadi.

    Adam Tooze is a columnist at Foreign Policy and a history professor and the director of the European Institute at Columbia University. He is the author of Chartbook, a newsletter on economics, geopolitics, and history. X: @adam_tooze.

    The Latest Congress Can Repair Civil-Military Relations

    📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2110 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • FEAVER is Professor of Political Science and Public Policy at Duke University and the author of Thanks for Your Service: The Causes and Consequences of Public Confidence in the U.S.
    • HEIDI URBEN is Professor of the Practice and Associate Director of Georgetown University’s Center for Security Studies in the Walsh School of Foreign Service.
    • Industry observers note that peter D.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    PETER D. FEAVER is Professor of Political Science and Public Policy at Duke University and the author of Thanks for Your Service: The Causes and Consequences of Public Confidence in the U.S. Military.

    HEIDI URBEN is Professor of the Practice and Associate Director of Georgetown University’s Center for Security Studies in the Walsh School of Foreign Service.

    How It Can Reclaim Its Constitutional Powers.

    Industry observers note that peter D. Feaver and Heidi Urben.

    Sources indicate that article I of the Constitution gives Congress sweeping powers to raise, maintain, and equip the armed forces. But the current Congress has done little to use these powers. The intense, frenetic activity of the past two years has undone established norms for military professionalism and may shape civil-military relations for a generation. Yet it has been led almost entirely by the executive branch with little meaningful involvement or pushback from Capitol Hill.

    The next Congress will face great pressure to reverse course and in doing so could shore up the historical norms of American civil-military relations. The concern today is not a military that is defying civilians—the traditional bogeyman of American political leaders since the founding of the Republic. Rather, the fear is that the thousands of changes, large and small, that the executive branch has so rapidly imposed on the military may end up undermining the professional ethic on which the U.S. form of civilian control depends.

    The incoming Congress can push U.S. civil-military relations in a healthier direction by overseeing the executive branch more actively than its predecessor. It can also help restore trust with both the military and the American public if it focuses on providing greater transparency, takes a more assertive role in conducting defense policy, reinforces the military’s nonpartisan professional ethic, and establishes a newly introduced bipartisan commission to reinvigorate the military profession. Congress has the power and authority to improve civil-military relations. The new session, starting in January, is its chance to use them before the damage becomes irreversible.

    When Pete Hegseth was sworn in as defense secretary, in 2025, he had strong views on the changes he wanted to make, alleging the military had lost its warfighting focus because of misguided priorities and “wokeism.” He has pursued those changes with a zeal not seen since Robert McNamara held the office from 1961 to 1968. Hegseth has reshaped the senior officer ranks: he has fired or removed nearly two dozen senior general and flag officers, and he has gotten rid of more than one-quarter of all four-star generals, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, and the chiefs of the U.S. Air Force, Army, and Navy. He has fired, removed, or pulled from promotion lists approximately 80 general and flag officers, a disproportionate number of whom are women or racial minorities. Hegseth has justified those removals in the vaguest of terms, which has convinced most observers that the real reason amounts to little more than because these officers followed the lawful orders of the previous administration. No previous defense secretary has removed such large swaths of the officer corps who honored their oaths to the Constitution and faithfully implemented policies decided by their civilian superiors.

    Sources indicate that hegseth has moved rapidly, largely ignoring traditional bureaucratic practices, including rigorous staff reviews and close involvement of congressional stakeholders in changing the trajectory of the Pentagon’s policymaking and in conducting military operations. Amid ongoing questions about the legality of the boat strikes the Trump administration ordered against suspected drug traffickers last fall as well as civilian casualties in America’s war with Iran, it is critical to note that Hegseth had already fired the senior, most experienced military legal advisers—sending a warning shot across the bow of younger judge advocates—and begun a significant overhaul of the Judge Advocate General Corps. Ever since the My Lai massacre during the Vietnam War, when U.S. soldiers committed war crimes by killing hundreds of unarmed Vietnamese civilians, the JAG Corps had been empowered to help U.S. personnel abide by the laws of armed conflict. By demoting senior legal advisers and selecting less qualified personnel in those positions, however, the military’s legal voice is more marginalized today than it has been since the Vietnam War. The Trump administration has also centralized decision-making, including by placing routine actions in highly classified channels that minimize opportunities for input and deliberation.

    Hegseth has done all of this—and much more—with essentially no pushback from the uniformed military or Pentagon bureaucracy. On the one hand, this demonstrates just how strongly officers accept the principle of civilian control—a posture reinforced precisely because Hegseth has proved willing to punish even unsupported allegations of military insubordination. On the other hand, his actions have had a chilling effect across the force, creating an environment in which the military is reluctant to offer candid advice or uphold its professional standards and values when they are at odds with administration priorities. Indeed, in a highly unusual move, former government officials have publicly called for military leaders to do more to stand up to the Trump administration, even at the cost of undermining civilian control. As we argued in Foreign Affairs in 2024, however, the military cannot save democracy; only Congress and the courts can and should check presidential power.

    Hegseth has enjoyed the unwavering support of President Donald Trump. But the real secret to Hegseth’s success in imposing his agenda on the Pentagon has been the unwillingness of the current Congress to exercise its Article I responsibilities or defend its traditional prerogatives. The incoming Congress can take a different approach by using its power to build trust, transparency, and accountability.

    Most pressing, Congress should exercise its ability to appropriately scrutinize defense policymaking, much of which has been shrouded in secrecy under the Trump administration. The current Congress has held very few oversight hearings, and the ones that have taken place have been exchanges of insults rather than of information. When secrecy is genuinely needed, of course, Congress can concern classified briefings and hold closed hearings. But open hearings, when properly conducted, are necessary in cases in which Congress is entitled to answers, for example, about military personnel policy.

    In the case of the boat strikes in the Caribbean and the eastern Pacific, Congress needs to know what advice senior military commanders and their JAGs offered, and it must understand how JAG firings affect the process by which commanders discern the lawfulness of military operations. Thus far, the Defense Department has provided only superficial explanations of its actions that basically amount to “we did this because we thought it was necessary.” Such justifications fall far short of what the Constitution envisions as the best way to hold the armed forces accountable: open debate that subjects policies to rigorous scrutiny. Greater transparency would also bolster public confidence in defense policy and remove pressure on the military to have to act as a potential savior of the Constitution.

    Congress should also faithfully fulfill its “advice and consent” function established in Article II, which authorizes the Senate to review and confirm presidential nominations and promotions. Hegseth’s unprecedented intervention in the meritocratic promotion process has dramatically altered the military’s upper echelons. Congress has normalized this interference, perhaps unwittingly, by approving Hegseth’s altered promotion lists with voice votes and little inquiry.

    In a recent development, the president and the defense secretary must retain the right to remove officers in whom they have lost confidence. But Congress has the right to know why a change was made, and it needs to ensure that promotions and removals follow established law and procedures rather than ideological or partisan considerations. Because Congress created the process for meritocratic promotions, it can push the executive branch to adhere to that process. It should mandate that the defense secretary provide a written explanation, supported by documented evidence of misconduct or derogatory information, for any off-cycle removals of senior officers and restore senior officers’ promotions, which would limit unjustified removals and uphold the merit-based selection process. Improving transparency in personnel policy will have one further salutary effect: it will help retain those qualified military personnel who are wondering whether they should give up on a military career that could be derailed by politicized and capricious promotion decisions.

    According to recent reports, in addition, Congress has a responsibility to police the well-established principle and practice that the uniformed military must stay away from partisan politics. The military has largely tried to uphold this norm, even as civilian political leaders have sought to draw it into partisan debates. Each time, for instance, Hegseth attacks the Biden administration before military audiences, most of whom served during the Biden era, he unwittingly further degrades the nonpartisan ethic on which service members’ oaths of office—and thus their subordination to his own policies—depend. It sends a message that embracing partisan rhetoric is key to career advancement and signals to the public that the military is not a neutral constituency. Congress can police the executive branch’s politicization of the military through inquiries, hearings, and even measures that prohibit the use of appropriated funds for events that treat military audiences like campaign rallies. Members of Congress can also call out for censure uniformed military personnel who behave in a blatantly partisan fashion regardless of whether they support or oppose the party the member supports.

    Most ambitiously, Congress should reclaim its role in making defense policy rather than only providing oversight. Legislative deference to the executive in times of war is not unique to Trump’s second term, but Congress should close loopholes that allow presidents to expand their power unchecked. If Congress wants to provide a legal justification to allow the use of force in Iran or against drug traffickers in the Caribbean or the eastern Pacific Ocean, it should do so. If it believes these actions are unlawful, however, it must use its legislative powers to constrain them. Similarly, Congress should amend the Insurrection Act to clarify and restrict the domestic use of military force. The president must retain the ability to respond to true national emergencies, but Congress should narrow the criteria for deployment of troops on U.S. soil to avoid potential abuse.

    Sources indicate that even as it becomes more active, Congress must strenuously avoid involving the military in a partisan war. Members of Congress should not press the military to criticize the president or the defense secretary in the made-for-social-media-outrage hearings that have become commonplace in Washington. It is right and proper for Congress to ask members of the military to share their personal and professional opinions on key strategic questions. But too often, politicians try to turn officers into combatants in their partisan battles, hiding behind the armed forces to defend partisan agendas or attacking military leaders who have simply carried out the lawful orders of a president from another party. Above all, Congress should not ask the military to be a check on civilian power. Only other civilians have the authority to do that.

    Congress cannot solve longer-term challenges through the day-to-day legislative process. But it has other tools to more holistically improve civil-military relations and identify the most essential reforms. The time-honored strategy is to set up a nonpartisan blue-ribbon commission to analyze problems, draw attention to their importance, and recommend solutions. A national commission on the state of the professional military ethic, co-chaired by three respected individuals—one with experience in a Republican administration, one with experience in a Democratic administration, and one retired senior military leader—would have the freedom to investigate how recent developments, including attempts to politicize the military and sustain a high tempo of operations, have affected the force. At a minimum, the commission should explore impacts on recruiting and retention; professional military education, fellowships in civilian institutions, and general and flag officer development; the JAG Corps’ ability to provide commanders with candid, independent legal advice; and the state of the National Guard.

    The current Congress has not shown enough interest in exercising its own powers. The next one can make a clean break and rediscover the body’s ability to carry out the functions that are necessary to improve civil-military relations. The fresh Congress can demonstrate its commitment to fulfilling its responsibilities by providing ordinary legislative oversight in the raising, maintaining, and equipping of the armed forces. And on thorny issues that require a bigger response, Congress can start the reform process by creating a national commission to lay out an agenda for action. Even after two years of enormous strain that has eroded best practices in civil-military relations, the next Congress is well positioned to reverse the slide and shore up Americans’ faith in a nonpartisan, professional military that is essential to democracy.

    Sources indicate that in mid-July 2006, NPR’s foreign editor dispatched me to Beirut. Israel and Hezbollah were waging an all-out war after militants debuted a cross-border attack from Lebanon, killing eight Israeli soldiers and capturing two more. Israeli bombs pounded Lebanon’s ports, roads, and bridges, while Hezbollah rained missiles down on northern Israel. Believing his country had the upper hand, Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Olmert wanted to finish off Hezbollah once and for all and had convinced the George W. Bush administration to hold off calling for a ceasefire.

    I was in my hotel room working on a story with a Lebanese translator when then-U.S. Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice appeared on TV, suggesting the conflict was an opportunity to remake the region. She added that the attacks—which had already led to more than 300 Lebanese deaths and would go on to kill over 1,000 people in Lebanon and 121 Israeli soldiers—were the “birth pangs of a upcoming Middle East.”.
