    #18926. Can South Africa Tackle HIV Without the U.S.?

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2194 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foreignpolicy ↗ Open Full Page

    Can South Africa Tackle HIV Without the U.S.?

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2194 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Two years ago, Linda-Gail Bekker was jubilant.
    • Industry observers note that when Bekker, the CEO of the Desmond Tutu Health Foundation in Cape Town, South Africa, announced the results of her trial at the International AIDS Conference in Munich in July 2024, the room erupted in a standing ovation.
    • Industry observers note that two years ago, Linda-Gail Bekker was jubilant.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Get audio access with any FP subscription.

    Two years ago, Linda-Gail Bekker was jubilant. She had just led a major clinical trial in South Africa, the epicenter of the global HIV epidemic, testing a upcoming form of prevention that was astonishingly effective. The drug, lenacapavir, is a pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), which blocks the virus from spreading in HIV-negative people. A twice-yearly injection could replace daily pills, offering longer-lasting protection and thus slowing the spread of the virus.

    Industry observers note that when Bekker, the CEO of the Desmond Tutu Health Foundation in Cape Town, South Africa, announced the results of her trial at the International AIDS Conference in Munich in July 2024, the room erupted in a standing ovation. “There was huge anticipation and excitement. And then January came around, and suddenly that all disappeared,” she noted, referring to the start of U.S. President Donald Trump’s second term.

    Industry observers note that two years ago, Linda-Gail Bekker was jubilant. She had just led a major clinical trial in South Africa, the epicenter of the global HIV epidemic, testing a upcoming form of prevention that was astonishingly effective. The drug, lenacapavir, is a pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), which blocks the virus from spreading in HIV-negative people. A twice-yearly injection could replace daily pills, offering longer-lasting protection and thus slowing the spread of the virus.

    When Bekker, the CEO of the Desmond Tutu Health Foundation in Cape Town, South Africa, unveiled the results of her trial at the International AIDS Conference in Munich in July 2024, the room erupted in a standing ovation. “There was huge anticipation and excitement. And then January came around, and suddenly that all disappeared,” she said, referring to the start of U.S. President Donald Trump’s second term.

    The Trump administration took a chainsaw to global health programs, including the U.S. President’s Emergency Proposal for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR), which has provided around $8 billion to South Africa since 2003. South Africa pays for most of its own HIV programs, including 90 percent of its antiretroviral drugs. Still, the collapse of PEPFAR was devastating, shuttering clinics for high-risk groups and leaving thousands of health workers without jobs.

    South Africa is home to around 8 million people living with HIV, or around 20 percent of the global HIV population. Approximately 6 million of them are on treatment, but the country still records around 170,000 newly introduced infections each year.

    According to recent reports, when South Africa began rolling out lenacapavir this summer, the landscape had changed dramatically. U.S.-South Africa relations have deteriorated, as Trump has objected to South Africa’s genocide case against Israel in the International Court of Justice and accused the country of committing genocide against white Afrikaners. Those tensions have compounded uncertainty for the HIV program.

    Sources indicate that last year, the United States provided South Africa with $115 million to keep core HIV services running, but in June, the Trump administration remarked it would end all PEPFAR funding for the country in the coming months. Washington also excluded South Africa from global health financing deals struck this year with other African countries. Even as the United States supports the lenacapavir launch elsewhere, it isn’t doing so in South Africa.

    In an email, a U.S. State Department spokesperson confirmed that the political rift played a role in the decision to phase out PEPFAR funding. The spokesperson stated PEPFAR was never meant to be a permanent initiative and that South Africa is “more than capable of supporting its own health programs” as a middle-income country.

    It has been revealed that it’s a departure from decades of U.S. foreign policy, said Jirair Ratevosian, a former senior PEPFAR official under President Joe Biden. “South Africa and the United States have never been perfectly aligned on foreign policy,” Ratevosian said. But the United States “was able to compartmentalize those disagreements and still cooperate on other significant areas of interest that were aligned, and HIV was always one of those.”.

    Now, South Africa is left to manage its lenacapavir rollout without its historically biggest donor. It’s an early test of whether the country’s post-PEPFAR transition can become a blueprint for weathering the U.S. retreat from global health—or is a cautionary tale.

    Sources indicate that south African officials have downplayed the loss of U.S. support. In June, a health ministry spokesperson urged people not to panic, saying the government has “long been working on a self-reliance strategy.” Officials have not released a formal plan, but they point to local drug manufacturing, stronger public health systems, and regional collaboration on HIV as key steps.

    South Africa had a head start in this effort, as PEPFAR already accounted for less than 25 percent of the country’s HIV prevention funding, compared with around 80 percent in neighboring Mozambique and Zimbabwe, according to the Joint U.N. Program on HIV/AIDS last year.

    At the launch of the lenacapavir rollout in June, South African President Cyril Ramaphosa told a stadium crowd that the drug would mark a “turning point” for South Africa. Prevention remains a challenge in the country; until now PrEP has only been widely available as a daily pill, which can be difficult to access or stay on. South Africa planned to roll out a different shot that offers two months of protection last year, but high prices and PEPFAR disruptions stalled that effort.

    In a recent development, experts think the twice-yearly lenacapavir shot could be a game-changer. Modeling suggests that if between 1.7 million and 2.9 million South Africans get on lenacapavir each year, new infections could fall by as much as 31 percent, potentially allowing the country to eliminate HIV as a public health threat as soon as 2039. But first, South Africa must get the drug to people who need it.

    In June, Ramaphosa said 3 million people will be offered lenacapavir over the next three years. The government has already secured enough doses to cover 456,000 people, funded with $29.2 million from the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis, and Malaria. The first tranche was allocated to 360 public health facilities in high-burden districts, but as of mid-October, just under 79,000 South Africans had started lenacapavir, according to health ministry data.

    Industry observers note that activists are frustrated by what they view as a sluggish rollout driven by funding gaps, insufficient planning, and regulatory bottlenecks. Some South African clinics have turned away patients seeking lenacapavir, some after running out of doses and others over logistical problems. Early in the rollout, facilities in the capital of Pretoria lacked HIV testing kits—a prerequisite to get the shot—or had not yet trained nurses to administer the drug.

    In a recent development, “It’s a drip feed of supplies,” said Fatima Hassan, a human rights lawyer and the founder of the Health Justice Initiative in Cape Town. The U.S. funding cuts and the pace of the rollout are “putting our entire health system in jeopardy and all the gains we’ve made in the last 20 years at risk.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the government has tried to plug some of the funding gaps left by the United States. Last year, the South African Treasury allocated around $45 million in emergency funding to cover some HIV programs, roughly one-tenth of what PEPFAR contributed in 2024. But that money does not resolve the question of what will happen to these services in the long term.

    The State Department spokesperson said the United States would “reconsider future health assistance during the phase-out period”—but only if South Africa takes “concrete, demonstrable action” to remedy the Trump administration’s accusations that its government seizes land from white farmers, among other complaints.

    South African Health Minister Aaron Motsoaledi has said the country aims to eventually finance its lenacapavir program itself, with help from donors. “To establish a couple million doses-deep lenacapavir program in the next couple of years, we will need outside help,” said Gesine Meyer-Rath, a health economist at the University of the Witwatersrand and Boston University.

    Industry observers note that but it is not yet clear which donors will provide that help. The Global Fund, which supported the initial rollout, intends to cut South Africa’s HIV/AIDS funding by 26 percent in its next allocation cycle as it tightens its focus on the poorest countries hit hardest by HIV, TB, and malaria. A South African health ministry spokesperson did not respond to questions about the lenacapavir rollout or its “self-reliance blueprint.”.

    Recent findings suggest that south Africa is betting that a generic form of lenacapavir will hit the market just as the initial supply runs out, allowing the government to roll out the drug to hundreds more clinics. Gilead Sciences, the U.S. developer of lenacapavir, agreed to make a generic version available in 120 lower- and middle-income countries, including South Africa, for $40 per person per year; it is expected by the end of the year in Zambia and elsewhere in 2027. The Global Fund negotiated a confidential price with the drugmaker for the initial shots in South Africa and other recipient countries, but brand-name lenacapavir goes for roughly $28,000 per person per year in the United States. South African health officials say the generic price must be brought down to $25 to guarantee “universal access.”.

    According to recent reports, eventually, South Africa wants to manufacture lenacapavir itself, but that effort has also encountered roadblocks. In 2024, three South African pharmaceutical companies asked Gilead for permission to make generic versions, but they were rejected because they could not handle the 28-step process of synthesizing the drug’s active ingredient. South Africa’s government is now working with Gilead and technical advisors to make local production possible.

    Recent findings suggest that clinicians and civil society groups warn that supply isn’t the only problem—it’s also about getting the lenacapavir shots to those who need it most, including sex workers, men who have sex with men, transgender people, and injectable drug users. But the 12 PEPFAR-funded specialized clinics and community-based outreach for these key populations, which served more than 63,000 people, have not been replaced.

    In a recent development, “I do not think that the people who are suffering access challenges because of the PEPFAR cuts are going to be the ones to get the drug,” noted Kate Rees, a public health specialist at the Anova Health Institute, which suspended its PEPFAR-funded programs. “We know how to reach key populations, and waiting for them in the clinic is not it.”.

    Meyer-Rath, the health economist, said she has attended early planning meetings with government officials who want to reopen services for these populations and try to integrate patients into public health facilities—but that the budget available is “nonexistent or marginal.”.

    Industry observers note that another challenge: PEPFAR covered around 40 percent of South Africa’s HIV data workforce, which tracks infections and treatment uptake in HIV hot spots. With fewer of those workers, the patients who miss out on lenacapavir because they fall through the cracks of the traditional health system—as vulnerable groups tend to do—may go uncounted, making it harder to identify problems and surge support where it’s needed.

    Sources indicate that the next phase of the lenacapavir rollout is fast approaching, and it will test the country’s infrastructure as well as its supply. The first South Africans to receive the drug are due for their second shot in December, and clinics must provide an HIV test and an injection for each of them every six months going forward.

    Industry observers note that south Africa’s experience is likely to shape rollouts elsewhere, but other early adopters offer their own lessons. Kenya, which launched the drug in February, has used drop-in centers to reach key populations, though it has also struggled with shortages. Meanwhile, Zambia launched with just 500 doses in late 2025, and up to 85 percent of patients there and in Eswatini—which shares a border with South Africa—have returned on time for their second shot, according to Bhekisisa, a South African media outlet.

    Lenacapavir is now being scaled up in 12 low- and middle-income countries, with 17 more countries due to receive it by early 2027, according to AVAC, an HIV prevention advocacy group. The rollout of generic lenacapavir next year will be another turning point. It’s a reminder that even if South Africa sticks the landing, there’s still a long way to go to defeat HIV.

    “Right now, we are wobbling a bit, and the world is watching us wobble,” Meyer-Rath stated. “But basically, it’s either the [South African] government or it’s not. No one will fund the system. We have to.”.

    In a recent development, gabriela Galvin is an award-winning freelance journalist in London. She covers health and social policy.

    #18925. Trump Is Facing a Very Different North Korea

    📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3523 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foreignaffairs ↗ Open Full Page

    Trump Is Facing a Very Different North Korea

    📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3523 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

    ⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • BIEGUN was Deputy Secretary of State from December 2019 to January 2021 and Special Representative for North Korea from 2018 to 2021.
    • EMMA CHANLETT-AVERY is Senior Director for Political-Security Affairs and Deputy Director of the Washington office of the Asia Society Policy Institute.
    • Donald Trump has Pyongyang on his mind.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    STEPHEN E. BIEGUN was Deputy Secretary of State from December 2019 to January 2021 and Special Representative for North Korea from 2018 to 2021. He is a Distinguished Fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute.

    EMMA CHANLETT-AVERY is Senior Director for Political-Security Affairs and Deputy Director of the Washington office of the Asia Society Policy Institute.

    And Now He Needs a Upcoming Strategy.

    Sources indicate that stephen E. Biegun and Emma Chanlett-Avery.

    Donald Trump has Pyongyang on his mind. In recent months, the U.S. president has made comments to the media suggesting he is in communication with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. In an August 17 Truth Social post, for instance, Trump revealed that the United States would scale back joint military drills with South Korea. The decision, he wrote, was “based on my very good relationship with Kim Jong Un,” describing the dictator as “unthreatening and respectful.”.

    Trump has not been subtle about his desire to restart diplomacy with Kim. With an eye on his legacy and the war with Iran stalemated, he is eager to notch a foreign policy win. During his first term, Trump held two historic U.S.–North Korean summits aimed at denuclearizing the Korean Peninsula—but both foundered because of the countries’ disparate expectations for the terms of a deal. Since his reelection, Trump has been looking to reopen talks with Kim. The ball is now in Pyongyang’s court, and Kim has signaled, if not an eagerness for renewed engagement, at least an unwillingness to rule it out. In August, after Trump insisted for the second time that he was in touch with Pyongyang, Kim Yo Jong—the leader’s influential sister—released a statement that read: “Regarding the reports from Washington about recent communication between the top leaders of North Korea and the U.S., I am completely unaware of such matters. It has been stated on numerous occasions that our head of state holds fond personal memories and positive feelings toward Trump. The relationship between the leaders remains excellent.” Although this is far from an agreement to meet, Kim Jong Un is not closing the door.

    Industry observers note that if leader-to-leader talks materialize, Trump may believe his personal rapport with Kim will yield a deal. But he will be facing a very different North Korea than the one at their last meeting in 2019. The fallout from unfinished diplomacy during Trump’s first term, the COVID-19 pandemic, and global trends such as the sharp escalation in U.S.-Chinese strategic rivalry and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine have destabilized the security landscape and created formidable obstacles to peaceful engagement. Meanwhile, North Korea’s continued nuclear and conventional military expansion and the growing support it is receiving from Moscow have strengthened Kim’s hand. Facing an emboldened Pyongyang, Trump can no longer fall back on the same concessions and negotiation tactics he used in previous talks.

    It has been revealed that for a U.S.–North Korean summit to be successful, the United States must approach it with well-defined strategic goals and a clear understanding of what concessions it is willing to make. Washington should shift its focus away from denuclearization, at least in the short term, to concentrate on more achievable nuclear arms control and safety measures. The United States should also maintain a capable troop presence on the Korean Peninsula and reiterate its security assurances—particularly its nuclear-deterrence guarantees—to regional allies such as South Korea and Japan.

    Recent findings suggest that although diplomacy with North Korea has historically been difficult, Trump is eager to meet with Kim, and both sides want to avoid pushing the Indo-Pacific toward nuclear proliferation or all-out war. Careful engagement with Pyongyang could defuse tensions on the Korean Peninsula and lay the groundwork for a more stable security landscape.

    Since the U.S.–North Korean summit in 2019, the conflicts in Ukraine and Iran have reshaped the Indo-Pacific in ways that strengthen Kim’s hand. The U.S.-Israeli war with Iran has drawn Washington’s focus away from Asia as, for the third time in the past quarter century, U.S. strategic attention and military assets have surged to the Middle East. The last American aircraft carrier stationed in the Indo-Pacific departed for the Persian Gulf in August, and U.S. strikes on Iran have rapidly depleted American munitions stockpiles. Washington’s Indo-Pacific allies, already strained by Trump’s abrupt policy shifts and punishing tariffs, are now concerned about deteriorating deterrence. Asian economies—many of which are deeply dependent on Middle Eastern energy supplies—have contracted as the Strait of Hormuz has remained compromised. Amid signs of further American retrenchment, U.S. allies and partners are increasingly skeptical about Washington’s commitment to the region.

    It has been revealed that even more consequential is Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, which has benefited North Korea in numerous ways. Moscow and Pyongyang’s once dormant relationship has flourished as Kim has sent thousands of munitions to replenish Russia’s depleted stockpiles and thousands of soldiers to fight and die in the ongoing ground war. Images of the new memorial to the Korean People’s Army soldiers who have perished in the invasion suggest an already significant loss of North Korean lives. In return, Pyongyang has received generous assistance from Moscow in violation of international sanctions, including abundant financial support for Kim’s regime and technology transfers that have enhanced North Korean military capabilities and may help Pyongyang more accurately deliver intercontinental ballistic missiles aimed at the United States. Russian patronage allows Kim to shower his regime’s elites with the economic benefits needed to cement their loyalty.

    In a recent development, still, it is worth questioning how durable this partnership is. After more than four years of grinding warfare with no end in sight, Moscow is increasingly isolated and may be in a poor position to continue supporting Pyongyang. Russia’s preoccupation with Ukraine has allowed China to expand its presence in Central Asia, for instance, and Turkey to deepen its influence in Azerbaijan. Russian aggression has spurred Armenia and Moldova to look westward, and hundreds of thousands of young Russian men have fled the country to avoid military conscription while over a thousand Western companies have left. International sanctions are starving Russia of badly needed capital and technology, and Russian war policies have created huge imbalances and inflation, possibly with worse to come for the Russian economy. If North Korea continues to actively support Moscow in this war, and Russia fails or is defeated, the world will become a much more hostile place for Pyongyang.

    Russia and North Korea’s deepening ties have already begun to reshape China’s interests in the region. Beijing is still Pyongyang’s most notable partner, but the dynamic has changed considerably in recent years. Beijing previously saw denuclearization as a top priority on the Korean Peninsula—a shared objective, and at times a rare area of cooperation, with the United States. It disliked the destabilizing impact that North Korea’s pursuit of nuclear weapons had on tensions between the North and South and expended political capital responding to international condemnation of Pyongyang. Between 2006 and 2017, Beijing agreed to a series of UN Security Council resolutions that imposed sanctions and other restrictions on Pyongyang in response to six North Korean nuclear tests. Now, pressed to maintain its influence in Pyongyang amid a growing Russian–North Korean security relationship—and with the rest of the world distracted by other geopolitical crises—China has gone silent on the glitch. When Chinese leader Xi Jinping visited North Korea in June to reassert his influence, denuclearization was not publicly mentioned. China’s new approach will make U.S. engagement on this issue more challenging and risks driving other regional powers, such as South Korea and Japan, to reconsider their own policies on the deployment or development of nuclear weapons.

    Whether Pyongyang reengages with the United States may also depend on how much North Korea relies on China for economic support. Much of North Korean commerce passes through China, and although Beijing and Pyongyang’s relationship appears fairly stable, it remains wary and transactional, with each side skeptical of the other’s motives. North Korea may seek to reengage with the United States to counterbalance its overdependence on China, or as a hedge against Russia’s failure in its war with Ukraine. Conversely, as Trump and Xi upgrade and stabilize U.S.-Chinese relations, China could step in to broker the next Trump-Kim meeting.

    Recent findings suggest that the Kim dynasty has long vexed U.S. policymakers. Washington has sought multiple deals with North Korea, including during Trump’s first-term summits with Kim, but missteps and mistrust on both sides derailed them. Pyongyang has proved resilient to both U.S. and international sanctions. Indeed, during the COVID-19 pandemic, North Korea sealed its borders and deprived itself far more severely than sanctions could, yet it still survived. U.S. congressional interventions on human rights and humanitarian aid, meanwhile, have mostly failed to change North Korea’s behavior. Pyongyang has also cushioned the impact of sanctions by engaging in cybertheft, such as its $6.3 billion heist against the cryptocurrency exchange Binance this October. All the while, Pyongyang has steadily advanced its military capabilities and expanded its nuclear arsenal.

    Although Washington’s previous attempts to rein in North Korea have failed, Trump’s renewed eagerness to meet with Kim and his unorthodox approach to foreign policy could provide a newly introduced opening for diplomacy. Trump has cultivated a direct relationship with Kim, shunning the bureaucratic negotiations that usually precede a deal. While a performative summit alone would be of little benefit to U.S. interests, Washington could use reengagement with Pyongyang to thaw inter-Korean relations and stabilize the peninsula by slowing or freezing North Korea’s nuclear buildup. Those goals may seem conventional, but as regional tensions worsen and Pyongyang’s nuclear arsenal grows, they are essential to averting potentially catastrophic conflict.

    It has been revealed that three questions cast a shadow over the possibility of renewed engagement between the United States and North Korea. First is the specific purpose of restarting engagement: What is the goal? Second is how to reopen communications. Despite Trump’s claims, there is no real proof that he has recently interacted with Kim. All evidence suggests the last contact between American and North Korean officials was in 2019, and it may be challenging to break a seven-year drought. Third is what are the incentives and tradeoffs the United States would be willing to consider as part of a negotiation—the same concern that bedeviled U.S. and North Korean officials in Hanoi.

    In a recent development, one possible formula for progress is focusing, at least temporarily, on steady arms control and international safety controls rather than the elusive goal of denuclearization. Denuclearization should remain Washington’s ultimate aspiration. But in the meantime, a North Korea awash with even more nuclear weapons makes the world only more dangerous. This approach will require serious diplomacy to minimize second-order consequences, particularly to avoid weakening U.S. alliances in the Indo-Pacific or triggering a collapse of the nuclear nonproliferation regime among nations that might see their only recourse as acquiring their own nuclear weapons. China, and perhaps even Russia, may concur with Washington on this point, and a shared desire to avoid more nuclear states in East Asia could help restart engagement.

    Industry observers note that kim has substantially more leverage now than in earlier encounters with Trump. Reopening communication will require using a mix of positive and negative assurances to convince him that he is unlikely to get a better chance to strike a deal. Kim may press the United States to scale back aspects of its cooperation with South Korea—such as joint military exercises and support for Seoul’s pursuit of nuclear-powered submarines—as preconditions for a meeting with Trump. Kim may even propose his own assurances of peace on the peninsula in exchange for a reduction of U.S. military forces in South Korea, although it is unclear whether Trump would agree to such conditions.

    In the worst-case scenario, Kim may take advantage of Trump’s eagerness to make a deal to extract weighty concessions from the United States. Kim has little reason to meet with Trump now, unless he calculates that he can secure major terms such as de facto recognition as a nuclear state, reduced sanctions, or a complete withdrawal of U.S. troops from the peninsula. Kim would likely insist that there be no discussion of denuclearization, North Korea’s support for the invasion of Ukraine, Pyongyang’s human rights abuses, or a final accounting for Japanese citizens kidnapped by North Korea under the rule of Kim Il Sung. Granting such concessions would end the U.S.–South Korean alliance.

    According to recent reports, to ensure North Korea does not exploit the Trump administration, Washington must carefully consider what tradeoffs it is willing to make. Lifting sanctions, abandoning or delaying the denuclearization process, temporarily accepting North Korea as a nuclear state, and reducing the U.S. military presence in South Korea are all long-standing demands of Kim’s regime that are likely on the table. Although lifting international sanctions would require UN Security Council consensus, Trump may be willing to reduce unilateral U.S. sanctions, which he considers an obstacle to better bilateral relations and which have been ineffective in stemming Pyongyang’s nuclear advances.

    Although denuclearization has been a major talking point for U.S. administrations since the early 1990s, the Trump administration may need to set it aside, at least in the short term. Pyongyang’s nuclear capabilities have increased since Trump’s 2018 and 2019 summits with Kim, suggesting that the stalemate caused by continued U.S. demands for the full-scale dismantlement of North Korea’s nuclear program may have given Kim time and space to grow his arsenal. Even if denuclearization remains a long-term U.S. priority—and it should—pragmatism is essential to reducing the threat posed by Kim’s regime. In exchange for stepping away from denuclearization, Trump should demand that Kim freeze any further expansion of his arsenal and explore possibilities for greater strategic stability, including renewed inter-Korean dialogue, transparency and confidence-building efforts, security measures that bolster nuclear facilities’ safety and guard against accidents, and strict adherence to nonproliferation. Trump must make it clear to Kim that an unconstrained expansion of North Korea’s nuclear arsenal will pressure South Korea and Japan to deploy nuclear weapons on their territory and possibly develop their own.

    Regardless of Kim’s demands, the United States must preserve its troop presence on the Korean Peninsula and continue joint military exercises with South Korea as long as the threat of North Korean aggression persists. The mantra of U.S. troops in South Korea is “ready to fight tonight.” Joint military exercises keep U.S. and South Korean forces prepared for combat, which is essential to deterring North Korean attacks. It would be dangerous and irresponsible to send American soldiers, sailors, marines, and airmen to the peninsula without ensuring peak readiness. Instead of withdrawing troops, the United States should offer confidence-building measures to North Korea—practices that reduce the risk of conflict breaking out because of misjudgment. These could include military-to-military engagement and security reassurances among the United States, South Korea, and North Korea, or greater transparency around military exercises—allowing observers on a reciprocal basis, for example. Sustaining Washington’s alliance with South Korea and avoiding cascading nuclear proliferation are critical to U.S. interests in the region. American negotiators must remind Kim that the U.S. military presence and its extended nuclear-deterrence guarantees for Seoul and Tokyo hold back even larger conventional military—and possibly nuclear—buildups in the region.

    In a recent development, finally, North Korea and the United States—and perhaps, in time, South Korea and Japan—should sustain diplomatic engagement by agreeing to assign diplomats to each other’s capitals through reciprocal liaison offices, which would maintain relations without granting full diplomatic recognition. In 2018 and 2019, the two sides discussed housing such diplomats in the German Embassy in Pyongyang and the Swedish Embassy in Washington. Liaison offices would also stabilize and prolong the communication necessary to quietly work through complex negotiations.

    In a recent development, if North Korea rejects Trump’s overtures, the United States is not without options. Washington could pressure the Kim regime by intensifying the scale and tempo of joint military exercises with South Korea; deploying American armaments, including short-range ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and possibly nuclear weapons, to South Korea and Japan; and pursuing a latest campaign to choke off North Korea’s economic resources through sanctions and interdiction. The United States could also deploy additional air defense assets to Japan and South Korea, including THAAD air defense radar systems and interceptors. Washington and its allies could dramatically expand efforts to undermine Kim’s rule by mounting sustained criticisms of North Korea’s dangerously large nuclear weapons arsenal and its use of international criminal enterprise to steal from and economically defraud other nations, which could spur other countries to curb their material or diplomatic support for North Korea or more aggressively sanction Kim’s regime.

    Industry observers note that beyond short-term negotiations, a fourth question is less complicated but just as notable: What role should Japan and South Korea play in U.S. engagements with North Korea? Many past administrations, both Republican and Democratic, have considered coordination with allies essential to establishing a durable solution on the Korean Peninsula. But Trump’s antipathy toward alliances suggests close consultation with South Korea and Japan is unlikely. Their absence from the negotiating table may actually accelerate U.S.–North Korean engagement, because coordination across allied governments can be unwieldy and slow, and Pyongyang has not been receptive to past overtures by Seoul and Tokyo. Although South Korean President Lee Jae-myung and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi both rhetorically back engagement with North Korea, Pyongyang has bluntly rejected their outreach.

    Even if Seoul and Tokyo are not directly engaged in U.S.–North Korean diplomacy, they would still likely welcome a U.S.-led deal with Kim if it protects their core security interests. But a deal with Kim that ignores American allies’ concerns would be dangerous. South Korea harbors an appetite to develop its own nuclear arsenal, particularly if it feels U.S. security protections are receding. Should Seoul move in that direction, Tokyo would almost certainly reconsider its own nonnuclear status, potentially igniting a nuclear arms race in Asia. Given North Korea’s long-standing hostility toward both Japan and South Korea, proliferation would destabilize the Indo-Pacific and leave the global nonproliferation regime in tatters.

    Industry observers note that any deal, even one that addresses Seoul’s and Tokyo’s core interests, will likely need to be paired with American security reassurances to allies’ governments and publics. Japan and South Korea must continue building their own conventional defense capabilities while the United States sustains its commitment to defending its Asian allies—especially extended nuclear deterrence. The United States must pursue delicate, nuanced diplomacy to avoid creating a stronger, legitimized North Korea; straining its alliances with Seoul and Tokyo; and debilitating the international nonproliferation regime.

    Sources indicate that despite the risks of U.S.–North Korean engagement, the time may be ripe to break the diplomatic paralysis that has allowed Pyongyang to advance its military capabilities for so long. The last two years of Trump’s presidency—particularly his summitry calendar in late 2026—will bring him to Asia, potentially facilitating a meeting with Kim. Such a visit would present the best chance for the kind of performative, high-profile meeting that both Trump and Kim favor.

    Trump is the ultimate iconoclast in traditional great-power politics, as evidenced by his shifting relationships with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin, which could shape Washington’s engagement with Pyongyang. Still, there may be a way to leverage Trump’s affection for Kim, and Kim’s recent restraint in criticizing the United States, to outline a deal that arrests the growing threat of North Korean nuclear weapons.

    The bruising Republican defeat in the U.S. midterm elections could also change North Korea’s diplomatic calculus, especially because it suggests Trump’s political standing in the United States has faltered, and he may struggle to deliver the results Kim seeks. Trump may force the problem, however, and propose a meeting with Kim after the November Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Summit in Shenzhen, China. It would not be surprising for Trump to suggest that this meeting take place in Pyongyang, putting Kim on the spot. If leader-to-leader talks occur, both sides should remember the central lesson from Trump’s first-term summits: engagement without sufficient preparation and clearly defined goals is not enough to strengthen security and stability on the Korean Peninsula.

    Growing tensions in the Indo-Pacific raise the prospect of a much darker future, where conditions on the Korean Peninsula remain unchanged and Asia’s entanglements in European and Middle Eastern conflicts metastasize into a fresh world war—perhaps ignited in Taiwan, the South China Sea, or the Korean Peninsula. Even if no war breaks out, in just a few years the United States could find itself in a world where Asia’s five current nuclear states are joined by two, three, or more new players.

    According to recent reports, but this future is not inevitable. All the leaders engaged in North Korean security debates—from Lee and Takaichi to Xi and Putin—want to avoid such escalation. Even the North Koreans surely recognize this is the most dangerous path. This shared goal means diplomacy is still possible, despite formidable challenges. For all Trump’s idiosyncrasies, one should take his desire to peacefully end tensions on the Korean Peninsula at face value. He has made his intentions clear. What happens next is up to Chairman Kim.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Speaker Mike Johnson said Congress would take up the Trump administration’s request for up to $50 billion to modernize air traffic control and airport infrastructure in the lame-duck session, but top Democrats are signaling a fight.

    In a recent development, the Federal Aviation Administration’s unusual nationwide ground stop on Friday afternoon prompted a multi-agency scramble and a major public relations problem for the White House. By that evening, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy was calling for a major unexplained funding increase over the $30 billion request he and White House budget chief Russ Vought delivered to lawmakers just a day earlier.

    Johnson, a Louisiana Republican, told Fox News on Saturday that he remained in Washington this weekend to work on year-end legislation, including the newly revised $50 billion sought for FAA upgrades.

    “We’re working on an aggressive legislative package to finish out the year strong, run through the tape … and this will be added to that,” the outgoing speaker said. “We don’t really need any investigation to understand we need further investment … some of this equipment dates back to the ’80s, so it’s got to be updated, and that’s our responsibility. We’re going to work to get it done.”.

    President Donald Trump weighed in via social media on Sunday, calling on Congress to provide the funds and blaming the Biden administration for not making air traffic control upgrades a priority.

    It has been revealed that “We have already started the work, but it should be done all at once, not in drips and drabs. Congress must approve,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “The Biden Administration set it back years!”.

    The FAA stated it acted to halt air traffic “out of an abundance of caution” after discovering “excessive data flooding the systems” in two locations, a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, and a radio communications site in El Dorado, Ark., where contractor L3Harris Technologies had been deploying a latest router.

    L3Harris is the lead contractor on a major telecommunications upgrade project to replace legacy copper wire with fiber-optic cables, funded in part by last year’s GOP budget reconciliation package which provided $12.5 billion for air traffic control modernization efforts.

    Recent findings suggest that that law included $4.75 billion for “telecommunications infrastructure modernization and systems upgrades,” and Duffy and Vought in their Nov. 12 request asked for another $2 billion for “cloud computing and national airspace system telecommunications.”.

    As of Oct. 15, they said, more than 68 percent of the legacy copper wires had been replaced, but more money was needed to finish the job.

    It has been revealed that out of the $30.1 billion request submitted to Congress, $10.1 billion is for air traffic control modernization, including the $2 billion for telecommunications equipment. The remainder is for towers and other upgrades to aging airport infrastructure, including terminals.

    But senior Democrats say they won’t sign off on the huge new funding package without more details, arguing that substantial funds previously appropriated remain unspent. Others say if the money is needed that badly, it should be taken from unspent immigration enforcement dollars.

    Recent findings suggest that house Appropriations ranking member Rosa DeLauro, D-Conn., and Transportation-HUD Appropriations Subcommittee ranking member James E. Clyburn, D-S.C., said Sunday that $9 billion remains unspent out of a total $14.4 billion appropriated for air traffic control upgrades since last July.

    That figure includes the money provided in the GOP budget reconciliation package plus $1.9 billion from the bipartisan fiscal 2026 Transportation-HUD spending law in February.

    DeLauro and Clyburn, in a fact sheet, pointed to an Office of Management and Budget “apportionment” putting over $5 billion of the reconciliation law’s funding on hold until Oct. 1, 2027.

    “Recent events are not the result of a lack of funding or support from this Congress,” Clyburn remarked in a statement.

    Making the rounds of the Sunday talk reveals, Duffy acknowledged that lawmakers provided a substantial down payment last year. But he argued the money is all accounted for and will be committed to specific projects by the end of 2028 or early 2029.

    He also pointed to a need for flexible transfer authority to shift money to higher-priority uses, arguing that the reconciliation law appropriated funds only for specific purposes.

    Recent findings suggest that “I’ve got money for radar, I’ve got money for radios,” Duffy remarked on CNN’s “State of the Union” show. “But I have no money for a latest network. I don’t have any new money to build new software to separate planes in the airspace.”.

    It has been revealed that other Democrats, including Hawaii Sen. Brian Schatz, who is a senior appropriator; and Rep.-elect Richard Ojeda, D-N.C., who defeated National Republican Congressional Committee Chairman Richard Hudson, R-N.C., in a major upset, say if the administration wants the money, they can tap unspent immigration enforcement funds.

    It has been revealed that according to OMB apportionment documents, Immigration and Customs Enforcement has about $76.5 billion left in its operations and support account from two recent funding packages – the 2025 reconciliation law and another one enacted for the Department of Homeland Security this year. About $65 billion of that is on hold until Oct. 1, 2027.

    Schatz posted on social media that “we should use at least a portion of that money for the FAA. We can solve this problem and not spend any additional taxpayer dollars.”.

    House Appropriations Democrats also cited operational risks from initial deployment of the funds. They highlighted a September report from the Government Accountability Office arguing that the FAA hasn’t done enough planning for its modernization program and is moving too rapidly.

    Industry observers note that “In essence, the FAA is buying delivery speed at the risk of cost uncertainty and potential disruptions,” the GAO wrote in its Sept. 14 report. “The net effect could be that air traffic controllers are forced to continue to rely on severely outdated systems that are prone to failure leading to more system outages, ground stops, flight delays, or worse — safety incidents.”.

    The report, commissioned well before the latest ground stop, notes problems going back years, including a similar two-hour grounding in January 2023 — the first since 9/11.

    The FAA stated the latest incident wasn’t tied to the ongoing wire replacement project and that none of the air traffic control towers being upgraded with reconciliation law funds were affected during Friday’s outage.

    “It is crucial to distinguish routine equipment upgrades from the FAA’s broader modernization effort,” the agency remarked in a questions-and-answers document posted Sunday.

    Still, Democrats are skeptical of the new funding request without further justification.

    House Transportation and Infrastructure ranking member Rick Larsen, D-Wash., and Aviation Subcommittee ranking member Andre Carson, D-Ind., mentioned Transportation Department and FAA officials were scheduled to brief committee staff on Monday about the $30 billion request. Where the extra $20 billion would go — as yet unexplained — is also likely to come up.

    And they were expecting “clear answers” at an early December hearing with FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford, Larsen and Carson said in a statement.

    Larsen said panel Democrats will revive the committee’s oversight and investigations staff when they take control in January, with rollout of the new air traffic control modernization program “a top priority of this new team.”.

    Speaking Sunday on CNN’s “State of the Union,” Senate majority leader candidate Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., called it “really rich” of Duffy to blame Congress for not providing sufficient funds.

    “If they need more, they should come up and justify it,” said Van Hollen, another senior Appropriations Committee member. “I will support what is necessary to have a safe system and a reliable system.”.

    Industry observers note that with Democrats in decisive control of the 120th Congress, the time has come for the party to offer a vision for what comes next for U.S. foreign policy. The country’s stunning repudiation of U.S. President Donald Trump is stoking the temptation to embrace a sharp policy reversal, on the assumption that the center of American democracy has held and the pre-Trump foreign-policy consensus can, too. However, when it comes to working with U.S. allies, that would be a grave mistake.

    The next Congress has an important role to play in defining this new foreign-policy vision—one that the next president could build upon in 2029. In asserting its powers to conduct oversight, legislate, and conduct its own diplomacy, the Democratic majority should be seeking to put in place elements of a new U.S. approach, rather than simply reverse the Trumpian damage.     With Democrats in decisive control of the 120th Congress, the time has come for the party to offer a vision for what comes next for U.S. foreign policy. The country’s stunning repudiation of U.S. President Donald Trump is stoking the temptation to embrace a sharp policy reversal, on the assumption that the center of American democracy has held and the pre-Trump foreign-policy consensus can, too. However, when it comes to working with U.S. allies, that would be a grave mistake.

    The next Congress has an important role to play in defining this new foreign-policy vision—one that the next president could build upon in 2029. In asserting its powers to conduct oversight, legislate, and conduct its own diplomacy, the Democratic majority should be seeking to put in place elements of a new U.S. approach, rather than simply reverse the Trumpian damage. Doing so will begin to reorient U.S. foreign policy in the next two years, shape foreign-policy debates in the coming presidential primary, and allow the next commander in chief to confront the world as it will be in 2029.

    The impulse to reverse course on Trump’s alliance policy is understandable. The president has brought two years of vitriol and abuse upon the United States’ closest friends—from a trade war with Canada to threats to invade Greenland—with clear strategic costs. But the flaws of his approach, and its broad unpopularity with the American public, are not a mandate for reflexive reversal. Nevertheless, there is a growing view in both Washington and allied capitals that, under new congressional leadership and with a new administration just two years away, Washington should take a maximally conciliatory approach to its friends. Apology tours, day-one tariff repeals, and the reinstatement of withdrawn troops in allied countries are all cited as necessary steps to regain lost trust.

    Sources indicate that the problem with that approach is twofold. First, it prioritizes rebuilding trust with allies over something more crucial—transforming old alliance bargains. The U.S. alliance system was built for the early Cold War world and used conventional and nuclear deterrence to keep threats far from the country’s shores. Its record of success is remarkable: No U.S. ally has ever been attacked, and U.S. treaty guarantees were invoked just once—on Washington’s behalf following the Sept. 11 attacks. But in the post-Cold War world, the United States and its allies need to cooperate on artificial intelligence, securing vital supply chains, aligning on climate and industrial policy, and combatting threats in cyberspace. Reembracing alliances without insisting on much-needed modernization would miss the chance to update them for new opportunities and threats, leaving the U.S. alliance network far less effective.

    Reflexive policy reversal also ignores the ways in which allies approach the United States differently after Trump’s reelection and punitive second term. U.S. leadership on global issues is now constrained by a four-year problem. Having seen the United States succumb to political chaos twice in a decade at the expense of its own global position, friends and partners around the world will assume that any future deal they cut with the United States is only good for four years, until power changes hands again. If the United States wants close cooperation from allies in this world, then it will have to give them some space to build autonomy and resilience in case Washington defects again.

    Taking this advice would prompt Democratic leaders to resist conventional wisdom on two concerns in particular: tariffs and defense burden-sharing.

    Recent findings suggest that trump’s trade war has proven to be both bad policy and bad politics, and it has hit U.S. allies as hard as its competitors. Many allies will argue that tariff reversals are an essential precondition for earning back their trust in the post-Trump era. But pursuing a unilateral, blanket repeal of tariffs on allies and partners—whether as an act of Congress or in the early days of a newly introduced administration—would be a mistake. Instead, Democrats can use their newfound control of Congress to check illegal tariffs that have driven up costs for American consumers, such as tariffs on forced labor, and repeal senseless duties on Canada. Such steps should pave the way for a broader international-economic agenda in 2029 that strengthens the U.S. economy and restores predictability for workers and businesses. That could start with aims to lower remaining tariffs on allies as part of a new economic bargain that includes bold, joint action against unfair Chinese trade practices and new agreements on technology and supply chain cooperation. Trump’s wanton tariff leverage should be parlayed into new cooperation, rather than freely ceded, to serve the bottom line of the American people and those in friendly nations.

    A phased plan for tariffs also points the way for Democrats to take a new approach to allied burden-sharing on security and defense. Denouncing Trump’s abusive approach, elevating alliances as a strategic priority, and unambiguously acknowledging China and Russia as shared threats can begin to improve U.S. relationships. But congressional Democrats should not launch an apology tour or provide slavish reassurances that undercut the progress that allies have made toward better defending themselves. Instead, Democrats should encourage allies to continue investing in their own defense in Europe and Asia, and adjust U.S. policies to actively support these efforts, even if the United States loses some influence as allies take on a greater role. Following a disastrous war with Iran that has cratered U.S. defense stockpiles, Congress should fund super-charged efforts to coproduce munitions and other critical systems alongside allies to rebuild deterrence. And, notwithstanding the flawed process by which the Trump administration has approached its ongoing global force posture review, Democrats should bring an open mind to the strategic benefits of a rebalanced U.S. presence in some regions.

    Newly empowered, Democrats should seize the opportunity to reassert allies as central to U.S. global strategy. But that should not mean a return to old patterns of burden-sharing, which too often let allies off the hook and created dependencies that they will no longer accept and the United States should not encourage. Nor should Washington fall back on traditional modes of collaboration, which privileged military commitments whose benefits may feel abstract and undervalued the economic and technological domains that most benefit Americans. The Trump shock to the U.S. alliance system has come with high costs, and most of this approach should be rejected. But Democrats should also identify where policies of the past two years have created fresh openings or new leverage and use those opportunities wisely, rather than giving them away for free. Rebuilding critical U.S. relationships is essential, but it is a long-term project. After two Trump presidencies, quick policy concessions will not overcome the structural sources of allied skepticism about U.S. reliability.

    Recent findings suggest that the world that the next U.S. president meets in 2029 will look dramatically different than the one of 2025 or 2021. The post-Cold War era has ended in a convulsion, and the Trump presidency, which has intentionally ravaged the United States’ global role, has two years of chaos remaining. Rather than attempt to run down the clock through 2028 and overturn his disastrous policies wholesale, congressional Democrats have a chance to build a policy bridge to a new era. By prioritizing the renovation and resilience in the U.S. global alliance system, Congress can work with—rather than in reflexive opposition to—the epochal global shifts that have taken place and position Washington to inaugurate a new era of global leadership in 2029.

    Rebecca Lissner is a senior fellow for U.S. foreign policy and director of the Future of American Strategy Initiative at the Council on Foreign Relations. She served as a deputy assistant to the president and principal deputy national security advisor to the vice president in the Biden-Harris administration. X: @RebeccaLissner.

    Mira Rapp-Hooper is a visiting senior fellow at the Brookings Institution. She was the senior director for East Asia and Oceania at the White House’s National Security Council from 2023-2025.

    #18918. A New Kind of Foreign Agent

    📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (3087 w)

    A New Kind of Foreign Agent

    📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3087 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

    ⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • How AI Is Reshaping Influence Operations in America.
    • Foreign governments have tried to influence the United States since its founding.
    • According to recent reports, like the foreign agents of old, the models these companies sell may seem harmless—just a cheap tool for American businesses to use.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    How AI Is Reshaping Influence Operations in America.

    Foreign governments have tried to influence the United States since its founding. President George Washington warned in his Farewell Address that “foreign influence is one of the most baneful foes of republican government.” The old methods have certainly not gone out of vogue; just this week Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to having a romantic relationship with a businesswoman who U.S. officials believe was working for Chinese intelligence. But today, a latest type of foreign agent has arrived: Chinese artificial intelligence companies.

    According to recent reports, like the foreign agents of old, the models these companies sell may seem harmless—just a cheap tool for American businesses to use. But their makers train them to promote the interests of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP). American businesses are outsourcing more and more critical decisions to AI. If Washington does nothing, those businesses will hand over control to models whose objective is to promote a foreign government.

    Although U.S. policymakers now debate banning Chinese AI, the tried-and-true American solution is not censorship but disclosure. In 1938, Congress passed the Foreign Agents Registration Act. Rather than outlaw propaganda, FARA allowed foreign agents to continue spreading it—as long as they registered with the government and disclosed whom they really worked for. Their communications also had to carry a conspicuous label naming their foreign sponsor.

    FARA’s wisdom has aged well over the decades. In recent years, the Justice Department has ordered the Russian state television network RT and the Chinese state media organizations Xinhua and CGTN to register as foreign agents and to label their content as such. Those who failed to register as foreign agents, such as Paul Manafort, President Donald Trump’s 2016 campaign chairman, and former U.S. Representative David Rivera of Florida, were sentenced to prison. (Trump pardoned Manafort in 2020.).

    Today, rather than banning AI companies controlled by foreign governments, the United States should treat them as foreign agents under FARA. No latest statute is needed. Washington should simply enforce the one on the books. Of course, FARA is no silver bullet against all foreign influence, but it fits the shape of this problem. A handful of known Chinese companies, such as DeepSeek, Alibaba, and Moonshot AI, build the models that American businesses increasingly let think and act for them. The Justice Department can reach every one of them.

    According to recent reports, democracy is strong enough to survive foreign influence but not invisible foreign influence. And to make sure the world does not subordinate its decision-making to Beijing, Washington and its allies must create an allied AI compact and then spread their own models far and wide.

    Industry observers note that american AI models, such as Anthropic’s Claude and OpenAI’s ChatGPT, are under no obligation to promote the U.S. government’s message. Ask Claude about Trump’s and President Joe Biden’s biggest failures or about the United States’ darkest chapters, and it will answer. Not so for Chinese AI models. When I asked the Chinese chatbot DeepSeek to “tell me about the CCP” in November, it answered that the party “is the vanguard of the Chinese working class, the Chinese people, and the Chinese nation. . . . The Party’s leadership is the most essential characteristic of socialism with Chinese characteristics and is the fundamental guarantee for China’s development and progress.” Such boosterish language appears by design.

    In a recent development, by law, Chinese AI models must never go against the Chinese government. Under the country’s 2023 regulations on generative AI, they must “uphold the Core Socialist Values” and may not engage in “harming the nation’s image” or “undermining national unity and social stability.” The Chinese government released a technical standard that laid out what these high-level declarations mean in practice: AI developers should have a list of at least 10,000 banned keywords, and their models must refuse to answer at least 95 percent of test questions the CCP finds objectionable. Developers must also scrub their training data of any history Beijing does not like. In short, the models must act as card-carrying members of the CCP.

    That is why, as the U.S. Commerce Department’s AI evaluators found in 2025, DeepSeek pushes Chinese propaganda at far higher rates than American models do, even when run on American servers. Estonia’s Foreign Intelligence Service found that DeepSeek inserted praise of the Chinese state unprompted, and it concluded that China uses DeepSeek to instill “a distorted, self-serving world view in the Western information space.”.

    But these models are not just propaganda parrots—they are taught to “think” about how to promote Beijing’s perspective. Ask an AI model something complex, and it will “reason” for a while. As it thinks, it produces an internal monologue called its chain of thought. Users rarely see it. There, it decides which facts are relevant and which to discard, what advice to give, and what autonomous actions to take. Silicon Valley is terrified that these chains of thought will become corrupt—that models will start scheming and lying, becoming “misaligned.” But a different kind of corruption is already here.

    Although American models’ chains of thought usually focus on helping the user, China’s do something else: prioritize the party line. When researchers funded by Sweden’s Psychological Defense Agency looked at how Qwen, Alibaba’s flagship model, reasons about China, they found an internal checklist to keep the answer positive, avoid criticism, and focus on achievements. So when an American company asks a question on which Beijing has a view, a Chinese model may discard all evidence that points the other way. As the world delegates more research, writing, and decision-making to Chinese AI models, it risks infusing the CCP’s goals into every action taken.

    These models are also highly persuasive. In a study published last year in Nature, researchers had some 6,000 voters in the United States, Canada, and Poland chat with AI models that argued for a candidate. The study found that a single conversation shifted the preferences of opposition voters in Canada and Poland by about ten percentage points. AI persuades by flooding a user with confident and authoritative-sounding facts—statistics, historical claims, and the like.

    Chinese AI models also exhibit strange behaviors beyond the spreading of propaganda. In October, the Canadian AI company Cohere reported that during a security test, Alibaba’s Qwen tried to upload a file to a cloud server in Beijing, completely unprompted. The behavior was rare for Qwen, only observed once in testing, and Cohere remarked it could not tell whether it was “deliberate or a leftover glitch from training.” A study by the cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike found that when users asked DeepSeek to write code that mentions groups Beijing finds politically “sensitive,” such as Tibetans, Uyghurs, or the religious movement Falun Gong, the model became up to 50 percent more likely to write code with severe security flaws. CrowdStrike suggested that one possible cause is China’s rule that models adhere to “core socialist values.”.

    Despite these findings, Chinese AI is enormously popular. Last year, downloads of Chinese open-weight models—AI models that anyone can download from the Internet and run on their own hardware—surpassed those of American ones across the world. Developers have built more than 150,000 models on Alibaba’s Qwen alone. By September 2026, Chinese models handled up to 67 percent of traffic on OpenRouter, a popular AI marketplace, up from around ten percent in February.

    American companies have embraced them. In March, a user discovered that Cursor, a popular coding tool, had built its newly introduced model by retraining Kimi, a model from the Chinese firm Moonshot AI. Airbnb, DoorDash, and the legal-services AI company Harvey use Chinese models as well. Many others likely do, too, in secret. The models are spreading even faster abroad, from Germany’s Siemens to Singapore’s national AI program to startups in Africa. The reason is simple economics: Chinese models are very cheap and very good.

    Although most American AI companies do not release open-weight models, most Chinese companies do. So an American firm must pay Anthropic for each use of its unmodifiable models, but it can download Kimi for free, retrain it however it wants, and pay only for the electricity and chips to run it. Kimi also runs on a firm’s own servers, whereas Claude runs on Anthropic’s. Even if a firm uses the most expensive DeepSeek model run on DeepSeek’s servers, it can produce the same amount of text as Anthropic’s top models at one-20th the cost.

    Sources indicate that in terms of capabilities, the research group Epoch AI judges Chinese models to be only about seven months behind American ones. For the price, they get the job done. And Chinese companies are now building agentic AI systems to compete with Anthropic’s Claude Code and OpenAI’s Codex. In October, DeepSeek released an open-source prototype of its “Super-Agent” system.

    Recent findings suggest that although AI is a fresh technology, Chinese companies such as DeepSeek and Moonshot AI fit FARA’s text and history. The statute applies when a foreign principal is identified; in the case of Chinese AI models, it is the Chinese government and the CCP. The Justice Department would also have to show that the Chinese AI firm acts “at the order, request, or under the direction or control” of the principal. Chinese AI companies would qualify because they must promote CCP viewpoints and cooperate with the state’s intelligence agencies. They also receive subsidies, and party organizations are embedded in each company. This is the difference between Chinese AI and other foreign AI. For example, France’s public investment bank has a stake in the French AI company Mistral, but no French law requires Mistral to build its models to serve the French government.

    Sources indicate that beijing will surely respond that Washington, too, has tried to control American AI companies, such as through Trump’s July 2025 executive order against “woke AI.” But that order affects only what federal agencies can procure, and a company can opt out of being a federal contractor. Meanwhile, Chinese law forces Chinese AI companies to train their models to “support, assist, and cooperate with national intelligence efforts.”.

    For FARA to apply, the agent must engage in certain activities, such as attempting to influence Americans or publishing content. Chinese AI companies do both by distributing models that spread propaganda. The statute exempts purely commercial activity, but only if it is “private and nonpolitical” and does not directly promote a foreign government’s political interests. Chinese AI models engage in political speech on a government’s behalf, and the Justice Department has denied the exemption to agents of foreign governments.

    Industry observers note that after registration, the genius of the statute can kick in. Chinese AI companies must disclose extensive information to the U.S. government: their funding sources, their written contracts and oral agreements, and the influence activities they undertake. Those that fail to register or omit information face both civil and criminal penalties.

    All content they disseminate must also bear a foreign-agent label: “a conspicuous statement,” in the statute’s words. The Justice Department sets the rules for what that looks like, and it has not updated them since 2003. In January 2025, the Justice Department proposed amendments to these rules to update them for the digital age. The proposed amendments would require a label on “each individual post” online, such as on social media platforms, but they do not address AI foreign agents. The final rule should require every message from DeepSeek, Kimi, or Qwen to carry the disclaimer: “This was generated by an agent of the Chinese government and Chinese Communist Party.”.

    The standard objection is that ordinary citizens do not read disclosures. That may be true of long medical forms or Securities and Exchange Commission filings, but this label would be short. And disclosure works because experts—investors, journalists, researchers—read filings and react. When researchers and lawmakers flagged gaps in China Daily’s FARA filings, the Chinese media tech giant disclosed that it had paid millions of dollars to The Wall Street Journal and The Washington Post to publish its propaganda. Payments to the Journal ended that same month. Forcing Chinese AI companies to register under FARA would also shed light on how far Chinese AI is spreading so that Americans can decide, with real data, whether they want further action, such as a ban.

    Recent findings suggest that american companies that use Chinese AI models can also become foreign agents if they fall under a foreign principal’s “direction or control” and engage in activities subject to FARA. This could happen in two ways: the firm serves as a “CCP spokesperson,” or as a “CCP executive.”.

    It has been revealed that in the first, an American tech giant takes an unmodified Chinese AI model and lets Americans discuss political complications with it—say, via a video game character or a customer service chatbot. The model returns its usual propaganda, so the company has effectively hired a CCP spokesperson. Accordingly, it must label its outputs. Both the Justice Department and a federal court have found that rebroadcasting unmodified programming from the Russian state outlet Sputnik turns an American company into a foreign agent. Of course, American companies can avoid FARA obligations if they do not engage in any of the activities listed by the statute, such as discussing politics. A company whose public-facing Chinese AI model discusses only, say, hotel check-in times, not politics, would not be a CCP spokesperson.

    Recent findings suggest that in the second scenario, an American firm outsources so much of its decision-making to an unmodified Chinese AI model that it has effectively hired a CCP executive. If a company hired a brilliant human strategist who always pushed Beijing’s interests, and the company followed that advice, FARA would apply. The same logic holds if an American company cedes control to the Chinese government by giving Beijing’s models high decision-making authority. Although it may sound fantastical, 64 percent of chief executives surveyed in IBM’s 2026 CEO Study say they already feel comfortable making major strategic decisions based on AI input; overall, CEOs expect AI to make 48 percent of routine operational decisions autonomously by 2030. An American company that wants to avoid becoming a CCP executive must be sure not to fall under the direction or control of such models. The Justice Department should update its 2020 guidance on what constitutes “direction or control,” spelling out how much decision-making a company can outsource to AI before it has effectively hired a “CCP executive.”.

    Recent findings suggest that american companies could attempt to train away the party bias in the Chinese AI models they adopt, but it is unclear whether that is even possible. Perplexity, an American AI tech giant, trained DeepSeek to stop ignoring questions about the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre and about human rights abuses in Xinjiang, but that does not fix the deeper problem of corrupt chains of thought. As these models get more capable, Chinese AI companies may also find cleverer ways to hide instructions. Or they could just stick them in the contract: some recent DeepSeek licenses prohibit modifying models to generate “inappropriate content” under Chinese law, making propaganda part of the deal. If research highlights that companies can reliably remove the bias, the Justice Department and the Commerce Department should glitch standards on how to train away FARA liability.

    Although Pam Bondi, then the U.S. attorney general, limited criminal FARA charges in 2025 to “conduct similar to more traditional espionage by foreign government actors,” Attorney General Todd Blanche’s Justice Department indicates it is considering a new rule to “keep pace with technological change.” It should include AI foreign agents.

    Of course, Washington should wield FARA’s expansive authorities with care. Frivolous prosecutions under the statute could stifle democracy. Other countries have used foreign-agent laws to shut down civil society. Since 2022, Russia has barred anyone it deems a foreign agent from holding office and organizing public events. Still, FARA is a far narrower statute, and it should stay that way. It reaches only those acting under the direction or control of a foreign principal, and it simply requires registration and labeling, leaving the speaker free to keep speaking. Chinese AI companies that are required by law to promote the CCP’s interests fit squarely within what Congress had in mind when it approved FARA in 1938.

    FARA can help in the United States, but the problem is global. Chinese AI is spreading rapidly in Africa, Latin America, and the Middle East. That is no accident. In July, Chinese leader Xi Jinping unveiled the World AI Cooperation Organization, a Shanghai-based group of 29 countries meant to make AI “beneficial, safe, and fair,” along with a development initiative to export Chinese AI worldwide. The United States and its allies cannot allow CCP executives and spokespeople to run the world’s companies and governments.

    Industry observers note that unfortunately, the American alternatives are not particularly attractive. The most capable U.S. models are far more expensive, are largely unmodifiable, and may contain their own biases. That is why the United States and its allies should create an AI compact rooted in transparency, with standards that make countries comfortable adopting allied models as their own. These should include freedom from state ideological mandates, disclosure of how the models were trained to be helpful and safe, and independent auditing.

    Every member of such a compact should also adopt FARA’s wisdom by mandating labels on government-directed AI, and the United States should hold American AI companies to those transparency standards. The bloc should then release models that match China’s in price and quality (that is, around seven months behind the American frontier). Allied governments can help pay for computing power and electricity, assist in clearing regulatory hurdles, and make bulk purchase commitments to bring prices down. American companies may cut prices on their older models on their own to compete with Chinese models. If they do not, lower prices for those worse models should be the condition for the public support they receive, such as federal contracts and permission to lease federal land for data centers, just as a pharmaceutical firm can charge high prices for only a set period before generic drugs arrive. The compact’s members should also use export loans and guarantees to steer developing countries toward allied AI.

    According to recent reports, by welcoming supposedly free technology from China, the United States and its allies have unwittingly invited countless foreign agents to their shores. The Foreign Agents Registration Act can strip away the disguise, and an allied AI compact can give the world a better offer.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Heliene, a solar modules manufacturer, and Caelux Corporation, a perovskite solar technology organization, are starting commercial production of their Hybrid-Tandem solar module.

    This module combines perovskite glass from Caelux and silicon N-type cells from Heliene, placing two energy generating sources in a single solar panel. Heliene is producing the modules in its plant in Mountain Iron, Minnesota, with first deliveries slated for 2027.

    “One of the advantages of Caelux’s technology is that we can integrate its Energy Producing Glass into our existing manufacturing lines without having to build an entirely new production setup,” noted Martin Pochtaruk, CEO and founder of Heliene. “With both companies manufacturing in the U.S., we’re bringing together two fully domestic supply chains to advance what’s possible with American-made solar, besides the fact that partnering with true friends also makes it fun.”.

    The companies are reporting a 27% efficiency from the Hybrid-Tandem module. Heliene and Caelux desiged this module to have a higher power density in a smaller project footprint.

    Industry observers note that “Heliene is a true leader in U.S. manufacturing, and we share a belief that when we lead the market, our customers win. Together, we’re commercializing ultra-high-efficiency solar modules that will set a new bar for American-made solar,” remarked Caelux CEO Scott Graybeal.

    Heliene will showcase the Hybrid-Tandem module at RE+ in Las Vegas from Nov. 17 to 19, at booth #W16546.

    This week: Permitting bill hits Senate floor amid aviation funding fight
